For a monument built with copper tools, cord, wood, and water, this is a remarkable achievement. Chapter 9 explains how it might have been done. For the moment, note that the precision shows the effort and skill of the builders. They were not accidental, and not sloppy. They were committed to getting it right.

The outside

When finished, the Great Pyramid was covered with an outer casing of fine white limestone from the Tura quarries across the river, with joints so tight that Herodotus and later visitors reported that the whole structure looked like one continuous surface. The casing blocks were cut and dressed on-site, and the final smoothing was probably done from the top down after the core was complete. The sides sloped slightly inward at their centers, a feature that can be seen from the air when the sun is low, producing a subtle eight-sided shape. Egyptologists are not sure whether this was a deliberate refinement or a settling effect.

Most of the casing is gone. Medieval builders in Cairo stripped it for buildings and, in some accounts, an earthquake in 1303 loosened many stones, which were then reused. A few casing stones survive at the base on the north side, and the stretch of the casing still stands at the top of Khafre's pyramid next door, giving us a sense of what the original looked like.

At the apex, the pyramid was crowned by a capstone called a pyramidion. The original is lost. Some researchers suggest that it was covered with a thin layer of gold or electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, which would have caught the sun, but there is no direct evidence for this. Later Egyptian pyramidia, for example from the pyramids of the Twelfth Dynasty, were made of black granite and inscribed with sun symbols.

Entering the pyramid

The original entrance is on the north face, about 17 meters above the ground, in a gabled limestone frame. A narrow, sloping corridor, the Descending Passage, runs about 105 meters down through the masonry and into the bedrock, ending in a rough, unfinished chamber about 30 meters below the base. This Subterranean Chamber was never completed. Why the builders left it unfinished is unknown, but the most common view is that the king's plans changed during construction, and the burial was moved higher up in the pyramid.

A short distance inside the Descending Passage, a second corridor, the Ascending Passage, branches off and climbs upward. In its lower part, the entrance to this passage was blocked by a series of three large granite plugs, designed to be slid into

place after the funeral, sealing the upper chambers. The plugs are still there. When the caliph's workmen entered the pyramid in the ninth century, they could not break the granite, so they dug a tunnel around the plugs through the softer limestone to reach the passage beyond. That tunnel, the Robbers' Tunnel, is the one visitors use today.

The Ascending Passage opens into a spectacular space, the Grand Gallery.

The Grand Gallery

The Grand Gallery is perhaps the finest piece of architecture in the Old Kingdom. It is a high, narrow corridor, about 47 meters long and 8.6 meters tall, rising at the same slope as the passage below, about 26 degrees. Its walls are made of polished limestone, and they rise in seven stepped overhangs, each course projecting inward by about 7.5 centimeters beyond the one below. At the top, the ceiling is only about a meter wide. The result is a corbelled vault: a sort of pointed stone arch.

Along each side at the floor are shallow ramps, with rectangular holes cut into them at regular intervals. Their purpose is debated. Some propose that they held wooden beams that helped to store the granite plugs before they were released. Others see it as part of the structure's ritual symbolism. Whatever the purpose, the gallery is a masterpiece of stone engineering, and it was built to carry heavy loads. Above it, the pyramid's weight presses down, and the corbelled walls transfer that weight sideways and downward in a controlled way.

At the upper end of the Grand Gallery, a high step leads to a low, narrow antechamber and then to the King's Chamber.

The King's Chamber

The King's Chamber is a plain rectangular room, about 10.5 meters long, 5.2 meters wide, and 5.8 meters high. It is built entirely of red granite from Aswan, with walls lined with polished blocks and a flat ceiling made of nine huge granite slabs. Above these are five further low chambers, called relieving chambers, separated by more granite slabs. The topmost has a gabled roof of limestone. Together the granite beams and the stacked layers help to spread the weight of the masonry overhead to the sides, protecting the chamber from crushing.

The estimated weights of the granite slabs above the chamber range from about 25 to about 80 tonnes each. The total weight of the nine ceiling slabs alone is perhaps 400 tonnes. Moving and lifting them more than 40 meters above the base is one of the great engineering feats of the project, and we will come back to it in Chapter 12.

The only object in the room is a granite sarcophagus, lidless and cracked at one corner. It is slightly too big to have been brought in through the entrance passage, so it must have been placed there during construction, before the chamber was roofed over. It is carved from a single block of red granite and sits aligned with the north-south axis of the pyramid. The lid, if there was one, is lost. In 1837 the explorer Howard Vyse, searching for hidden chambers, used gunpowder to blast his way into the relieving chambers above the King's Chamber. In the

topmost of those chambers, he found red-painted graffiti left by the work gangs, including the cartouche of Khufu. These inscriptions are among the best direct evidence that the pyramid was built in Khufu's time.

The Queen's Chamber and the shafts

Back at the lower end of the Grand Gallery, a level passage leads horizontally to a smaller room that has been known for centuries as the Queen's Chamber. The name is a medieval misnomer. It does not seem to have been intended for a queen, and the queens of Khufu were buried in separate small pyramids beside the main one. The room has a high, gabled roof, and in the east wall, a tall niche that is corbelled. The niche may have held a statue, but no one knows.

From the north and south walls of both the King's Chamber and the Queen's Chamber, narrow shafts about 20 centimeters across lead outward. The ones in the King's Chamber emerge at the outside of the pyramid. The ones in the Queen's Chamber stop short of the surface. They were discovered in 1872 by the engineer Waynman Dixon, who noticed a crack in the wall and followed it. The shafts have since been explored with robots, in 1993 and 2002, and with a miniature camera, in 2011. In the southern shaft of the Queen's Chamber, the first robot found a small limestone door with two copper handles. In 2002 a robot drilled through it and found another door behind it. In 2011 a robot with a flexible camera, called Djedi, saw painted marks on the back of the door, in red ocher. No one knows what they mean.

The shafts are often described as "air shafts," but the Egyptians had no need to ventilate a sealed tomb. A more likely explanation is that they have a religious function, perhaps allowing the king's spirit to leave the pyramid and ascend to the sky, and they may also have been aligned with certain stars. We will come back to this in Chapter 15.

KEY POINT

The Great Pyramid has three chambers at three levels: the unfinished Subterranean Chamber in the bedrock, the so-called Queen's Chamber in the middle, and the King's Chamber high up. This arrangement suggests that the plan changed at least twice during construction as the builders moved the burial chamber upward.

The complex around the pyramid

Like all pyramids, the Great Pyramid was part of a complex. On the east side stood a mortuary temple, of which only the black basalt paving survives. From its entrance a long causeway, partly roofed and decorated with relief carvings, ran down to a valley temple near the harbor. The causeway has been largely destroyed, but its foundations have been traced for several hundred meters.

Next to the pyramid are three smaller pyramids for queens, labeled G1a, G1b, and G1c, and a small cult pyramid just southeast of the main one. Five pits cut in the bedrock around the pyramid once held boats. Two of them, on the south side, were sealed with limestone slabs. In 1954, the Egyptian archaeologist

Kamal el-Mallakh opened one of them and found a complete ship, 43.6 meters long, made of Lebanese cedar, which had been taken apart in 1,224 pieces and carefully packed. It was rebuilt over years and displayed in a museum beside the pyramid. The first ship was moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2021. A second pit, opened in the 1980s, held another disassembled ship, which an Egyptian-Japanese team has been studying and restoring.

Around the pyramid, in neat grids, are the tombs of Khufu's family and his court officials, arranged in what archaeologists call the Eastern Field and the Western Field. Most are mastabas. They contain some of the finest early reliefs, and several held the strange limestone "reserve heads," portrait heads without bodies that were placed in the burial shafts.

The overseer: Hemiunu

Among the tombs in the Western Field is that of Hemiunu, Khufu's nephew and his vizier. Among his titles was "Overseer of all the king's works," which makes him a good candidate for the chief architect or project manager of the Great Pyramid. His tomb, labeled G4000, is one of the largest in the cemetery. In its serdab, archaeologists found a life-sized limestone statue of him, now in Hildesheim, Germany. It shows him as a heavy, seated man with a rather stern expression and the folds of fat that indicated a person who ate well, which marked social status in ancient Egypt.

It is not safe to say that Hemiunu designed the pyramid single-handedly, and no plan or drawing survives. But the overlap

of his titles and his status within the court makes him a plausible candidate for the person who directed its construction.

How long did it take?

If Khufu reigned for about 23 to 27 years, and work on the pyramid presumably began early in his reign, the construction could have taken about 20 years. This is the figure usually given, and it matches an old claim by Herodotus. The evidence from the logbook found at Wadi al-Jarf, which we will meet in Chapter 11, dates work on the casing stones to around Khufu's 26th or 27th year, which suggests that the pyramid was nearing completion at that time.

Assuming the 20-year figure, simple arithmetic tells us how fast the work must have been. With about 2.3 million blocks to place, and working perhaps 300 days a year, the crew had to place about 380 blocks a day. If they worked ten-hour days, that is roughly 38 blocks an hour, or one block every one and a half to two minutes, day after day, for two decades. That is a stunning pace, but it was possible with a large, well-organized workforce working on many fronts at once, since the quarrying, hauling, dressing, and laying all happened in parallel.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Blocks per day. 2,300,000 blocks ÷ (20 years × 300 days) = about 383 blocks per day. At 10 working hours, 383 ÷ 10 = about 38 blocks per hour, or one every 1.6 minutes. Early courses at the wide base would go much faster because most of the blocks lie there; the final courses near the top would go much slower because fewer blocks were needed.

Khufu and the memory of the Great Pyramid

Khufu's reputation has been a matter of controversy for 2,500 years. Herodotus, writing around 450 BCE, said that Cheops was a tyrant who closed the temples and forced all of Egypt to work for him, and that he even forced his own daughter into prostitution to raise money. The story is a legend, and not a reliable one. Contemporary evidence suggests that Khufu was a powerful king who commanded a sophisticated state and whose workers, as we will see in Chapter 13, were fed, housed, and given medical care.

Khufu's name lived on. He was venerated for centuries, and a cult of the king was maintained at Giza, especially in the Late Period, when the Egyptians looked to the Old Kingdom as a golden age. By the time of the Greeks and Romans, tourists were visiting the pyramid and carving their names on it. The Great Pyramid has been a site of pilgrimage for more than four thousand years.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu (c. 2589–2566 BCE) at Giza as the centerpiece of a vast complex. Its original height was about 146.6 m and its base side about 230.3 m; it contains roughly 2.3 million blocks. Its interior includes the Descending Passage, an unfinished Subterranean Chamber, the Grand Gallery, the so-called Queen's Chamber, and the granite King's Chamber with five relieving chambers above it. Work-gang graffiti, nearby tombs, and the Wadi al-Jarf logbook tie it securely to Khufu.

CHAPTER 6

The Giza Plateau: Khafre, Menkaure, and the Sphinx

Three pyramids, one great statue, and a necropolis that was a city of the dead.

Today, when people say "the pyramids," they usually mean the three at Giza. They stand in a diagonal row along the edge of the plateau, with the Great Pyramid of Khufu to the northeast, Khafre's to the middle, and Menkaure's, much smaller, to the southwest. Around them are smaller pyramids, temples, tombs, and the Sphinx. To understand the whole, we need to walk through the plateau as the Egyptians planned it, and to look at how it changed over about eighty years.

After Khufu: a short, strange interlude

When Khufu died, his throne passed to his son Djedefre, who ruled for about eight years. Djedefre did something unexpected. He moved the royal necropolis north to Abu Rawash, a few kilometers from Giza, and started his own pyramid there on a high, isolated hill. It was planned as a large monument, but it was left unfinished, and in later centuries it was quarried so heavily that only a stump remains.

Djedefre is a significant figure for another reason. He is the first king known to have used the title "Son of Ra" as part of his royal name. A fine quartzite head of Djedefre, in the Louvre, is

among the best royal portraits of the Old Kingdom. Some Egyptologists have wondered whether the Great Sphinx might even have been made in his image, though most favor his successor. We will come to that.

There may have been a family dispute. The tombs of some of Khufu's heirs suggest a complicated succession, and Djedefre's reign is short. But the evidence is too thin for confident conclusions. What matters here is that, after Djedefre, the royal necropolis moved back to Giza.

Khafre's pyramid

Khafre was another son of Khufu. He ruled for about 24 or 25 years, from around 2558 BCE, and built the second-largest pyramid at Giza. In its original form the Pyramid of Khafre measured about 215 meters on each side and stood about 143.5 meters tall. It was only three meters shorter than Khufu's. It was also steeper, at an angle of about 53 degrees 10 minutes, and it was built on a higher part of the plateau, so that from certain angles it looks taller than the Great Pyramid.

That is a good example of how perspective can deceive. From the Cairo side, to the northeast, Khafre's pyramid sits higher and nearer the viewer, so it seems to loom over its larger neighbor. A good vantage point to compare them is from the air, or from the plateau's far edge.

At the top of Khafre's pyramid, a cap of the original Tura limestone casing is still intact, and it gives the best sense of what the original smooth faces looked like. At the bottom, the lowest courses of the casing were made of red granite from

Aswan. The interior is simpler than the Great Pyramid's. There are two entrances, both on the north face, one about 11 meters above the base and one at ground level, and the passages lead to a single burial chamber cut into the bedrock, which contains a granite sarcophagus sunk into the floor. The lid is broken. Giovanni Belzoni, the Italian circus strongman turned explorer, opened this pyramid in 1818 and wrote his name in the burial chamber, and his inscription can still be seen.

Khafre's valley temple and statues

Khafre's complex is the best preserved at Giza. His valley temple, at the foot of the causeway, is a masterpiece of Old Kingdom architecture. It is built of massive limestone blocks cased in red granite, with a floor of white alabaster. Inside is a T-shaped hall with square granite pillars, each a single block, and a total absence of decoration. The effect is solemn and stark. Some of the limestone blocks in its core weigh well over 100 tonnes, and the granite casing was cut with such accuracy that the joints are almost invisible.

In 1860, the French archaeologist Auguste Mariette found a well in the floor of the temple filled with broken statues. Among them was a life-sized seated statue of Khafre carved from a dark, very hard stone traditionally called diorite, now one of the stars of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. The king sits on a throne decorated with intertwined lotus and papyrus, which symbolize the unification of Egypt. Behind his head the falcon-god Horus spreads his wings protectively. Diorite is extremely hard, and the sculpture's detail and polish demonstrate the skill of Old

Kingdom sculptors. The temple originally held about twenty-three statues of the king.

The Sphinx

East of Khafre's valley temple, at the edge of the plateau, sits the Great Sphinx. It is about 73 meters long and 20 meters high, with a face about 4 meters wide. It is the largest monolithic statue in the world, and one of the oldest.

The Sphinx was carved from a knoll of limestone that the builders had left standing when they quarried stone for the neighboring pyramids. The knoll was uneven in quality. The harder layers at the head and the softer layers at the body explain why the head has survived well while the body has eroded badly. For centuries, the Sphinx was covered by drifting sand up to its shoulders, and it was periodically cleared. The body, which is a lion's, was later cased in stone blocks during various repairs, including by the Romans.

The face is generally believed to be that of Khafre. The evidence for this includes the Sphinx's position in his complex, the style of the face, and the fact that its temple is aligned with his valley temple. Some scholars have suggested Khufu or Djedefre as alternatives, but there is no strong evidence for that. A few writers have argued that the Sphinx is much older than the Fourth Dynasty. We will address that claim in Chapter 21.

The Sphinx's nose is missing, and many people believe that Napoleon's soldiers shot it off. This is a myth. Drawings made before Napoleon's expedition, including an illustration from 1737 by the Danish explorer Frederic Norden, already show the

Sphinx without a nose. The medieval Egyptian historian al- Maqrizi, writing in the fifteenth century, reported that a Sufi zealot named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr had damaged the face in 1378 because local peasants were making offerings to it. That is the likelier explanation.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "Napoleon's army shot the nose off the Sphinx." Fact:

Drawings made decades before 1798 show the nose already missing, and a fifteenth-century Egyptian historian blames a fourteenth-century religious zealot. The Sphinx's beard, incidentally, was a later addition, and pieces of it are in museums in London and Cairo.

A king who was also a lion

The Sphinx is a combination of a lion's body and a king's head, which was a long-standing symbol in Egypt. The lion stood for royal power, strength, and the vigilance of the sun, and the Sphinx guards the entrance to the royal necropolis. In later centuries, the Egyptians called it Hor-em-akhet, or Horus in the Horizon, which the Greeks rendered as Harmachis. Around 1400 BCE, a young prince named Thutmose, who would become Thutmose IV, fell asleep in the Sphinx's shadow and dreamed that the god promised him the kingship if he cleared away the sand. When he became king, he did, and recorded the story on a granite slab, the Dream Stele, which stands between the paws today.

The word "sphinx" itself is Greek. It was the name of a female monster in the Oedipus legend, a creature with a woman's head and lion's body that asked a riddle. The Greeks applied the name to the Egyptian statue, and the riddle story has become attached to it in popular memory, though it has no Egyptian origin.

Menkaure's pyramid

The third pyramid at Giza belongs to Menkaure, who ruled for somewhere between 18 and 28 years, depending on the source, and was probably the son of Khafre. His pyramid is much smaller than the others: about 104.6 meters on each side and about 65 meters high. Its volume is only about one-tenth that of the Great Pyramid. The decline in size is consistent with a pattern across the Fourth Dynasty, in which the pyramids reached a peak under Khufu and then got smaller, as the cost of the monument weighed on the economy, or as royal priorities changed.

What Menkaure's pyramid lacks in size, it makes up in materials. The lower sixteen courses were cased in red granite from Aswan, while the upper courses were cased in white Tura limestone. The contrast would have been beautiful. The granite casing was never finished. Many of the blocks still have their rough outer surfaces, with the final polishing left undone. That suggests Menkaure died before the project was complete, and his successor finished the pyramid and the temple in cheaper material, mudbrick. This tells us something about the speed of royal succession and the willingness of the next king to complete a predecessor's monument at less cost.

On the north face of the pyramid, there is a long vertical gash. It is the result of an attempt to dismantle the pyramid in 1196 CE, ordered by al-Aziz Uthman, the son of Saladin. His workers labored for months and found the stone too hard to remove. The project was abandoned after they had managed to strip only a part of the casing from one face. It is a vivid reminder of how much effort it took even to destroy a pyramid.

Inside, Menkaure's pyramid has a descending passage leading to a series of chambers, including a paneled antechamber and a burial chamber with a vaulted roof. In 1837, Howard Vyse found a wooden coffin lid and some human bones in the pyramid. The lid is now in the British Museum, and later study showed that the coffin and the remains belonged to a much later period, probably an intrusive burial. The original basalt sarcophagus was lost at sea off the coast of Spain in 1838 and never reached England.

Menkaure's triads

The best-known works of art from the pyramid age come from Menkaure's valley temple. When the American archaeologist George Reisner excavated it in 1908–1910, he found a series of beautiful slate statues known as triads. In each, the king stands between the goddess Hathor and a personification of one of Egypt's provinces. There is also a famous double statue, in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, of Menkaure and his queen, whose arm is around his waist. The statues are among the great works of Egyptian art, noted for their smooth, rounded forms and ideal proportions.

The queens' pyramids and the cemetery

The three Giza pyramids are each accompanied by smaller satellite pyramids. Khufu has three for queens and one for a cult, Khafre has one, and Menkaure has three for queens and one for a cult. Between and around them stretch the tombs of the nobles: large stone mastabas with decorated chapels, arranged in orderly streets. Officials held offices such as "overseer of the king's works," "royal scribe," or "inspector of priests," and they were buried near the king in hope of sharing in his eternity.

One of the most remarkable tombs belongs not to a king but to a queen. Khentkaus I, who lived at the end of the Fourth Dynasty, has a massive stepped tomb, cut from a natural rock outcrop, with a small adjoining town for her priests. Her titles include "Mother of two kings of Upper and Lower Egypt." She is a striking figure in the history of the period, though the details of her relationships remain a subject of discussion.

Shepseskaf: an end to the pyramid line

Menkaure's successor Shepseskaf did something unusual. He abandoned the pyramid form and built an enormous mastaba shaped like a sarcophagus at South Saqqara. It is known today as the Mastabat al-Fara'un, Pharaoh's Bench. Some historians read the change as a religious or political shift, a break from the sun-centered ideology of the pyramid. Others point out that his tomb was built with similar techniques and may have been a rare variant or a response to the limited resources of the time. In either case, the Fifth Dynasty restored the pyramid, and the next chapter takes up that story.

Who lived at Giza?

The Giza plateau was a workplace, as well as a necropolis. To the south of the plateau, beyond a huge stone wall called the Wall of the Crow, archaeologists have found the remains of a settlement known as Heit el-Ghurab, the "Lost City of the Pyramid Builders." It contained bakeries, breweries, barracks, workshops, and storage areas, together with the cemeteries of the workers. We will visit it in Chapter 13. The existence of this settlement, which dates from the time of Khafre and Menkaure, is among the most convincing proofs that the pyramids were built by organized Egyptian laborers.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Giza has three main pyramids: Khufu's (the largest), Khafre's (almost as tall, with surviving casing at its peak), and Menkaure's (much smaller, with granite lower courses). The Sphinx was carved from quarry bedrock, most likely in Khafre's reign. The smaller size of Menkaure's pyramid and the unfinished casing suggest that the great scale of Khufu's project could not be sustained. A thousand years later, kings were still restoring the plateau and worshipping its monuments.

CHAPTER 7

The Later Old Kingdom: Smaller Pyramids, Sacred Texts, and Collapse

From the sun-temple kings of the Fifth Dynasty to the end of the Old Kingdom.

After the Fourth Dynasty, the great pyramids were over. Egypt did not stop building pyramids, and in some ways the next two dynasties were its most productive in religious and artistic terms. But the monuments became smaller, the construction cheaper, and the emphasis shifted. What the later pyramids lost in size they made up in words. For the first time, the walls of the burial chambers were covered with writing.

A change of dynasty

The Fifth Dynasty began around 2494 BCE with Userkaf. Later Egyptian tradition, preserved in the Westcar Papyrus, told that the first three kings of the dynasty were triplets, sons of a priest of Ra and a woman named Rededjet, fathered by the sun god himself. The story is a legend, but it reflects something real: the priesthood of Ra at Heliopolis had become a rival center of power, and the new dynasty owed it a great deal.

Userkaf marked the change in two ways. He built his pyramid not at Giza but at Saqqara, close to Djoser's old complex.

And he built something new: a sun temple at Abusir, about 15 kilometers to the north. Six kings of the dynasty are known to have built sun temples, though only two have been found: Userkaf's and Niuserre's. These were open-air courtyards dominated by a squat stone obelisk on a base, with an altar facing the sky. They were dedicated entirely to Ra. The pyramid was no longer the only monument of a king's devotion to the sun.

The Abusir pyramids

The kings who followed Userkaf, beginning with Sahure, shifted the royal necropolis to Abusir, where they built a line of pyramids along the desert edge. They were much smaller than the Giza giants: around 80 meters per side and 50 meters high, with a volume of only a few percent of Khufu's.

They were also built differently. The Fourth Dynasty kings had used large blocks of good limestone throughout the core. The Fifth Dynasty builders built an outer shell of fine limestone around a core of small, rough stone, sand, and rubble, held in place by a framework of internal retaining walls. This was cheaper and faster but far less durable. Over the centuries, once the casing was stripped off, the rubble cores spilled out and the pyramids collapsed into heaps. That is why many Fifth Dynasty pyramids look like low, shapeless mounds today.

The decline in structural quality is a measure of how the state's priorities changed, but it should not be read as a failure of skill. The Fifth Dynasty builders concentrated their efforts on the temples, which were richly decorated. The mortuary temple of Sahure is one of the finest examples of Old Kingdom art. Its

walls carried reliefs of ships, foreign peoples, and offering bearers, and its columns were carved as palm trees. The artists were as good as ever.

The Abusir papyri

Abusir also gave us something almost priceless: papers. In the 1890s and again in the twentieth century, excavators found the remains of a temple archive in the funerary temples of kings Neferirkare and Neferefre. These Abusir papyri, written in hieratic script, are the oldest substantial group of administrative papyri from Egypt. They include duty rosters, inventories of temple property, delivery records, and accounts of offerings.

They reveal how a mortuary cult worked day to day. Priests were organized into five groups, each serving in rotation for a month at a time. Each group counted the temple's equipment, checked its seals, and made the offerings. Part-time priests, who held other jobs in the community, worked their rotation and then returned to civilian life. This is exactly the kind of system the state used for labor on the pyramids: rotation, recording, and accountability. Egypt ran on paperwork.

Unas and the Pyramid Texts

The last king of the Fifth Dynasty, Unas (c. 2375–2345 BCE), built a small pyramid at Saqqara, just beside Djoser's complex. It is only about 43 meters high, and from the outside it is a modest ruin. But when archaeologists entered it in 1881 they found something extraordinary. The walls of the burial chamber and the antechamber were covered with columns of hieroglyphs, painted blue-green, more than 200 spells in all. These are the Pyramid Texts, the oldest religious writings in Egypt and among the oldest known religious texts in the world.

The Pyramid Texts continued in the pyramids of the Sixth Dynasty kings Teti, Pepi I, Merenre, and Pepi II, and in some queens' pyramids. They are not the same in every pyramid. Each king's selection of spells differs, and over time the corpus grew to about 800 separate utterances. The spells include rituals for offerings, protective charms against snakes and enemies, hymns to the sun, and descriptions of the king's ascent. We will look at them in more detail in Chapter 17.

For scholars, the Pyramid Texts are crucial. They give us the language in which the Egyptians themselves explained what the pyramid was for. They also provide evidence of an extensive royal theology already in place by 2350 BCE. The Great Pyramid had no such texts, which is one of the reasons its purpose has been so debated. By the time of Unas, the builders were willing to say it out loud.

The Sixth Dynasty: Teti to Pepi II

The Sixth Dynasty (c. 2345–2181 BCE) began with Teti, who built his pyramid at Saqqara, north of Djoser's. Its surroundings became a prestige necropolis for his officials, including his vizier Mereruka, whose mastaba has 33 rooms and some of the most detailed relief scenes of daily life in the Old Kingdom: fishing, boat-building, hunting in the marshes, and the preparation of food.

Pepi I followed and built a pyramid at South Saqqara. He and his son Merenre presided over an expanding Egyptian presence in Nubia and the Sinai. A famous biographical inscription by an official named Weni, who served under Teti, Pepi I, and Merenre, describes in detail how he organized the quarrying and transport of stone for royal monuments, including a granite sarcophagus and its lid, and how he led a military campaign against Asiatic nomads. His text is one of the best surviving descriptions of how an Old Kingdom official managed stone, labor, and ships. It makes clear that it was a matter of state business, planned and carried out by trained men.

Pepi II succeeded to the throne as a child and, according to Egyptian tradition, reigned for more than 90 years. Modern scholars think the figure is exaggerated and that the real figure was about 64 years, though even that would be a record. His pyramid at South Saqqara is about 52 meters high and has a complex of fine reliefs and texts, and three small queens' pyramids.

Smaller pyramids, bigger state

If the pyramids got smaller after Khufu, how are we to understand the shift? Historians have proposed several explanations. • Cost and economy. The Great Pyramid had strained the

country's resources. Reducing the scale of subsequent pyramids freed resources for other purposes, such as temples, trade expeditions, and sun temples.

• Shift in ideology. The cult of Ra took center stage. The

pyramid became one part of a larger religious system that also included the sun temple.

• Changing power structure. Over time, provincial gover-

nors and high officials gained wealth and independence, and the king could no longer command the whole country in the way Khufu had.

• Learning. By using local rubble and small blocks, the

builders cut the cost and the effort. They may have decided that grand scale was unnecessary because the spells carved on the walls were enough.

KEY POINT

The Pyramid Texts changed the way pyramids communicate.

Fourth Dynasty pyramids are silent. Fifth and Sixth Dynasty pyramids have their purpose written on the walls. This is the single best written source for what the pyramid builders believed.

The end of the Old Kingdom

The Old Kingdom ended around 2181 BCE, and the causes have been debated for a century. A number of factors appear to have contributed.

First, the central government gradually lost power. Over generations, the offices of provincial governors became hereditary, and local rulers built impressive tombs in their own regions. The king had to pay for their loyalty with land and tax exemptions, and these concessions drained the treasury.

Second, there is evidence of climatic stress. Studies of ancient climate show that the late third millennium BCE was marked by a period of reduced rainfall across the Near East, sometimes called the 4.2 kiloyear event. Nile floods may have been low for several years in a row. Some Egyptian inscriptions of the period, including the autobiographies of nomarchs, mention famine and the efforts of local leaders to feed their people. The famous text known as the Admonitions of Ipuwer describes a world turned upside down, though it was written much later and may be a literary work, not a historical record.

Third, the length of Pepi II's reign may have contributed to a succession crisis. With a very old king and many heirs who died before him, the throne may have passed to a series of short-lived rulers, as the Egyptian king lists suggest.

Historians generally avoid a single explanation. The Old Kingdom's decline was probably a combination of political decentralization, economic strain, climate variability, and dynastic instability. Whatever the causes, the result was the First Inter-

mediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BCE), a time when Egypt had no strong central government and regional rulers competed for power.

What the late pyramids teach us

The later Old Kingdom shows that the Egyptians were not trapped in a single approach. They adapted. They experimented with different construction methods, changed the form of the monument, added texts, and reallocated resources according to their needs. They also continued to maintain the cults of their ancestors. Priests were still giving offerings to Khufu and Sneferu long after the kings who built them were dead. And they were collecting data, writing it down, and passing on knowledge.

The Great Pyramid thus appears not as an isolated marvel but as the highest point of a long process, a moment when the Egyptian state had the resources, the knowledge, and the motivation to do something enormous. Other kings did not have those exact conditions, and they did what they could with what they had.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

After Khufu, pyramids shrank and were built with rubble cores. The Fifth Dynasty added sun temples and moved the cemetery to Abusir. Unas (c. 2375–2345 BCE) is the first king to inscribe the Pyramid Texts, which tell us directly what the pyramids were for. The Old Kingdom ended around 2181 BCE through a mixture of political decentralization, climate stress, and succession problems.

Pyramids After the Old Kingdom: Revival, Decline, and the Nubian Kings

The Middle Kingdom's mudbrick pyramids, the last royal pyramid of Egypt, and the Sudanese pyramids that outnumber them all.

The Old Kingdom did not take the pyramid with it when it fell. After a century and a half of division, Egypt was reunited, and its new rulers turned to the pyramid again. They built differently, with new engineering ideas and new ways to defeat tomb robbers. Then, after about 1550 BCE, Egypt's kings stopped building them, but the form lived on. Hundreds of miles to the south, in Nubia, the pyramid acquired a second life that lasted nearly a thousand years longer than Egypt's own.

Reunification and a new capital

The First Intermediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BCE) was a time of regional rule. Power was held by local governors, and in the south, a line of kings based at Thebes eventually defeated their northern rivals. Around 2055 BCE, Mentuhotep II reunited the country. He built a remarkable temple-tomb at Deir el-Bahari, across the river from Thebes, with terraces and colonnades, possibly topped by a small pyramid-like structure. The design would later inspire Queen Hatshepsut's temple nearby.

Around 1985 BCE, a vizier named Amenemhat took the throne and founded the Twelfth Dynasty. He moved the capital to a new city, Itjtawy, "Seizer of the Two Lands," near the modern village of Lisht, south of Memphis. Next to it he built a pyramid. The Twelfth Dynasty is generally regarded as the high point of Egypt's Middle Kingdom, a period of strong government, public works, and literature.

A pyramid built from older pyramids

The pyramid of Amenemhat I at Lisht reveals something unexpected about the Middle Kingdom builders: their attitude toward the past. When excavators took the pyramid apart, they found that its core included hundreds of decorated blocks taken from the Old Kingdom pyramid complexes at Giza, Saqqara, and Abusir. Some bore the names of Khufu and Khafre. Fragments of relief from the causeway of Unas were also found.

Why would a king take stone from the monuments of earlier rulers? The simplest answer is convenience: the Old Kingdom

stone was already quarried and dressed, and the old pyramid sites were by then 600 years old and, in many cases, in disrepair. Another possibility is symbolic: by incorporating the stone of the great kings into his pyramid, Amenemhat linked himself to the glory of the past. A third possibility is that it was an act of piety toward earlier kings, since the blocks were placed, not discarded. These explanations are not mutually exclusive.

The new way to build: mud brick and hidden entrances

Middle Kingdom builders returned to the pyramid, but they changed the construction method. Instead of solid limestone throughout, many of the pyramids were built with a core of mud brick, supported by a framework of stone walls and covered in limestone casing. This was cheaper and faster, but, like the Fifth Dynasty's rubble cores, it left the pyramid vulnerable once the casing was stripped. Today, most Middle Kingdom pyramids are brown heaps of eroded brick.

The kings also devoted new attention to the problem of robbers. A tomb that looks like a mountain is an advertisement, and by the Middle Kingdom, everyone in Egypt knew what pyramids had held and how often they had been robbed. The architects responded with elaborate security.

• Hidden entrances. Instead of facing north on the pyramid's

face, as at Giza, entrances were moved to the south side, to the east, or even beneath the ground at some distance from the pyramid.

• False passages and dead ends. Corridors that led nowhere

were meant to confuse intruders.

• Massive blocking stones. Huge slabs of quartzite or gran-

ite, sometimes weighing tens of tonnes, were lowered into place after the burial.

• Trap chambers. Some designs included concealed shafts

and hollows.

At Lahun, the pyramid of Senusret II (c. 1880 BCE) was built around a natural spur of rock, which gave the structure a stable, solid core, and then completed with mud brick and a limestone casing. The entrance was hidden. It was not on the pyramid at all but down a shaft in the courtyard to the south, where a hidden stair led into a labyrinth of passages and chambers. At the heart of the structure, the burial chamber contained a pink granite sarcophagus. The robbers of antiquity found it anyway. When Flinders Petrie entered in 1889, he found the chamber looted but the sarcophagus still in place. Years later, in 1914, his colleague Guy Brunton found the tomb of a royal woman, the princess Sithathoriunet, nearby, still holding spectacular jewelry that the thieves had overlooked.

Near the pyramid, Petrie excavated a planned town, which he called Kahun, home to the priests and workers who served the pyramid. It was laid out in a grid, with a district of large houses and another of smaller ones, and the remains included papyri with accounts, letters, medical texts, and veterinary advice, as well as toys, tools, and household goods. It offers a rare glimpse of the daily life of the community around a pyramid.

The last great pyramid builder

Amenemhat III (c. 1860–1814 BCE) was one of the longestreigning and most prosperous kings of the Middle Kingdom, and he built two pyramids. The first, at Dahshur, is known as the Black Pyramid because its mud brick core has weathered to a dark color. It was built with ambition but ran into trouble. The weight of the pyramid caused the underground chambers to crack and the corridors to subside, and some of the passages bear signs of emergency repair. The king abandoned it as a burial place, though he may have kept it as a symbolic monument, and built a second pyramid at Hawara, in the Faiyum oasis.

The Hawara pyramid contained the most sophisticated security of any Egyptian pyramid. Its burial chamber was carved from a single enormous block of quartzite, weighing an estimated 110 tonnes, and was roofed with giant slabs lowered into place and sealed. The passages included sliding stone doors, false corridors, and a dead-end that returned to the entrance. Even so, thieves broke in during antiquity. Petrie opened the pyramid in 1889 after a lengthy effort and found the chambers plundered and flooded with groundwater. The burial chamber held two sarcophagi, both emptied by thieves.

The labyrinth

Adjacent to the Hawara pyramid, there once stood a gigantic mortuary temple that struck visitors with awe. Herodotus visited it around 450 BCE and described it as even more impressive than the pyramids: 3,000 rooms, half above ground and half below, arranged around twelve covered courts. Later Greek and Roman writers called it the Labyrinth, evidently comparing it to the mythical labyrinth of Crete.

Almost nothing remains of it. Quarrying in antiquity and later periods reduced the structure to a vast field of broken limestone chips. Petrie, and later scholars, traced the outline of its foundation, which covered an area of roughly 300 by 250 meters, or about the size of the entire Step Pyramid enclosure, in the 1880s. In recent years, a team using ground-penetrating radar has claimed to detect large buried structures beneath the site, but those findings need further investigation. As things stand, the Labyrinth is known mostly through the words of ancient writers.

The end of the royal pyramid in Egypt

The Twelfth Dynasty ended around 1800 BCE, and a succession of short-lived kings followed in the Thirteenth, who continued to build smaller pyramids. Then Egypt fragmented again, and a foreign dynasty of rulers from western Asia, the Hyksos, took control of the north. A line of native Egyptian kings at Thebes resisted them. Around 1550 BCE, Ahmose I drove out the Hyksos and reunified Egypt, beginning the New Kingdom.

Ahmose I built a pyramid at Abydos, with a temple and a cenotaph chapel, and it was the last royal pyramid in Egypt. After him, the kings of the New Kingdom chose a different kind of tomb. They had their burial chambers cut deep into the cliffs of a remote valley across the Nile from Thebes, the Valley of the Kings, and had their offering temples built separately along the river. The reasons are debated. The most common explanation is security: a hidden tomb is harder to find, and a hundred years of experience had shown that pyramids did not keep out robbers. A second is religious: the cult of Amun had grown in importance, and there was a new theology of the afterlife that emphasized the underground journey of the sun through the Duat.

The valley itself is dominated by a natural pyramid-shaped peak called al-Qurn, "the Horn," which many Egyptologists believe was a conscious choice: the kings were buried beneath a mountain that looked like a pyramid. The pyramid shape never completely vanished. It survived in small pyramids, often with steep sides, that capped the tombs of workmen at Deir el-Medina, the village that housed the artisans who built the royal tombs. The capstone of an obelisk was called a pyramidion, too, and the shape stayed a powerful symbol for the sun.

KEY POINT

The royal pyramid in Egypt lasted about 1,100 years, from Djoser (c. 2670 BCE) to Ahmose I (c. 1550 BCE). During that time, the form changed, from solid limestone to mud brick, and the security became more elaborate, but the idea of a monumental, sun-linked tomb stayed the same.

The pyramids of Nubia

South of Egypt, in the land called Kush, in what is now Sudan, another civilization had grown up along the Nile. For centuries it was alternately an Egyptian colony, a trading partner, and a rival. Around 750 BCE, a Kushite king named Piye marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. The Kushite kings ruled Egypt for about a century, until the Assyrians expelled them in 664 BCE.

The Kushites loved Egyptian culture. They worshipped Amun, wrote in hieroglyphs, and built temples in the Egyptian style. And they built pyramids. At El-Kurru and Nuri, near the Fourth Cataract, Kushite kings, including Taharqa, were buried beneath small, steep-sided pyramids with an underground burial chamber. After the Kushite capital moved south to Meroë, in the sixth century BCE, the kings and queens of the Meroitic kingdom continued the custom for another thousand years, until about 350 CE.

The result is a remarkable landscape. Archaeologists have counted more than 200 pyramids in Sudan, which is more than twice as many as survive in Egypt, though they are far smaller.

Typical Nubian pyramids are 6 to 30 meters high, built of sandstone blocks in stepped layers, and have a much steeper angle, perhaps 70 degrees. Each was accompanied by a small chapel on the east side, decorated with reliefs, where offerings were made. The Meroitic cemeteries, with their rows of pointed silhouettes, are among the most beautiful sights in Africa.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "Egypt has the most pyramids in the world." Fact: Sudan has more, probably over 200, though they are much smaller than Egypt's. Egypt has between about 118 and 138, depending on how one counts the smaller and ruined ones.

The Nubian pyramids suffered a famous act of destruction. In 1834, an Italian physician and treasure-hunter, Giuseppe Ferlini, demolished the top of a pyramid at Meroë, thought to be that of Queen Amanishakheto, and found a hoard of gold jewelry. He then proceeded to damage dozens of other pyramids, but he found nothing else. His jewelry was sold to museums in Berlin and Munich, where it remains. The episode is a harsh reminder of how archaeology looked in the nineteenth century.

Pyramids elsewhere in the world

Pyramids are not unique to Egypt and Nubia. The shape appears across the world, because a pyramid is one of the simplest ways to build a tall, stable structure from stacked material. A broad base and tapering sides need little more than gravity and stones.

• Mesopotamia. The ziggurats of ancient Iraq were stepped

temple towers built of mud brick, starting around 2100 BCE. They were platforms for temples, not tombs.

• Mesoamerica. From about 300 BCE onward, builders at

Teotihuacan, Tikal, Chichen Itza, and other sites erected stepped pyramids topped by temples. Most were platforms for ritual, but some, such as the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque, contain royal tombs. The tomb of King K'inich Janaab' Pakal, who died in 683 CE, was found inside it in 1952.

• China. Large pyramid-shaped mounds, built of rammed

earth, cover the burials of the early emperors. The tumulus of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor, near Xi'an, dates to about 210 BCE.

• Elsewhere. There are also stepped pyramids in the Canary

Islands, Sudan, and Indonesia.

These monuments differ in purpose, construction, and symbolism. There is no evidence that they are related to each other through cultural contact. The better explanation is independent invention. A mound is a natural way to mark a grave or a holy place, and a stepped mound is a natural way to make it higher.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

After the Old Kingdom, Middle Kingdom kings built pyramids with mud brick cores and elaborate defences against robbers, including hidden entrances and giant sealing stones. The last royal pyramid in Egypt was built by Ahmose I (c. 1550 BCE), after which kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings. The Kushite kings of Nubia then built more than 200 steep pyramids in Sudan over nearly a thousand years. Pyramids elsewhere in the world arose independently.

CHAPTER 9

Surveying and Planning: Squares, Levels, and True North

How the builders marked out a base the size of ten football fields and made it level, square, and aligned to the stars.

Before a single block was cut, someone had to decide where the pyramid would go and how it would sit on the ground. This stage is easy to overlook, because it leaves little visible trace, but it is one of the most impressive parts of the achievement. The Great Pyramid's base is nearly a perfect square, almost perfectly level, and almost perfectly aligned with the cardinal directions. Getting a monument of this size right at the start was essential, because every error in the base would be magnified as the pyramid rose.

The tools of the surveyor

Egyptian surveyors had a small kit of simple instruments, but they used them skillfully. Many of the tools are known from tomb paintings, models, and actual finds.

• The cubit rod. The basic unit of length was the royal cubit,

about 52.3 to 52.5 centimeters, divided into seven palms of four fingers each. Wooden and stone measuring rods, marked off in palms and fingers, have survived from the

New Kingdom, and similar ones were surely used in the Old Kingdom. Measurements were also made with knotted cords.

• The stretched cord. A rope, rubbed with chalk or ocher

and snapped against a surface, drew a straight line. A rope held between two stakes gave a straight edge. Ropes were so important to surveying that one of the king's ritual acts at the foundation of a temple was called "stretching the cord," and a Greek tradition called Egyptian surveyors "ropestretchers."

• The plumb bob. A weight hung on a string establishes a

true vertical. Egyptian plumb bobs of stone and metal are known.

• The set square and the A-frame level. A right angle can

be checked with a wooden set square. A level was made from an A-shaped frame with a plumb line hanging from the apex. When the line fell on a mark at the center of the crossbar, the feet were at the same height.

• The merkhet. This was an instrument for observing the

stars, consisting of a bar with a sighting slit and a plumb line. Examples survive from the Ptolemaic period, and the device may have been much older.

• Sighting rods and water. A level surface can be found with

water, simply because water finds its own level.

No tool on this list is surprising. All were available, in recognizable form, throughout the Egyptian Bronze Age, and none requires anything more than wood, string, stone, and metal.

Choosing and preparing the ground

The Great Pyramid sits on a limestone plateau, and the builders' first step was to prepare a firm, level platform. They did not level the entire site. Instead, they left a natural rise of bedrock in the middle, a small hill that they incorporated into the pyramid's core. The hill rises about seven meters at the center and is still visible inside the lower part of the structure. This saved effort, but it also meant that the builders had to level the ground around the rise.

How did they level an area of roughly 53,000 square meters to within a couple of centimeters? The most popular explanation is a water-leveling system. In this approach, the builders cut a grid of shallow channels in the bedrock, flooded them with water, and used the water surface as a reference. They then cut away the rock between the channels down to a common level, and the remaining ridges gave them the height of the platform. This method needs only water and a hoe, and it is accurate. Direct evidence at Giza is limited, since the channels would have been cut away as the work proceeded, but the method is simple, accurate, and consistent with the practice of using water as a reference in later Egyptian construction.

A second approach was to use many sighting rods and string levels across the site, checking one against another. Egyptians used long wooden "boning rods" in a kind of sight-and-line

method, which could have worked at this scale, though it would take longer.

Squaring the base

A square base needs four right angles and four equal sides. The most straightforward way to construct a right angle with ropes is to use a triangle whose sides are in the ratio 3:4:5, a so-called Pythagorean triple. A popular claim says that Egyptians used a rope with twelve equally spaced knots, forming a 3-4-5 triangle. The idea is appealing, but we have no Egyptian document that describes it. Greek writers mention it centuries later, and modern authors repeated it. It is a plausible method, but not proven.

Another way to find a right angle is to use the diagonals. If the two diagonals of a four-sided figure are equal in length, and the opposite sides are equal, it is a rectangle. If all four sides are equal as well, it is a square. Checking that two ropes stretched across the corners are the same length is simple. Surveyors can then adjust the corners until the diagonals match. It is an easy method, requiring no calculation.

The results speak for themselves. The side lengths of the Great Pyramid vary by only a few centimeters, and the corners deviate from true right angles by only a few seconds of arc. Whatever method the builders used, they were extremely careful.

Finding north

The most famous precision of the Great Pyramid is its orientation. The sides face the cardinal directions with an error of only about three arcminutes, or one-twentieth of a degree. How did the builders find true north without a compass? Two main answers have been proposed.

The sun method. Set a vertical pole, called a gnomon, on a flat, level surface. Mark the end of its shadow in the morning, and draw a circle around the pole with a radius equal to the shadow's length. In the afternoon, the shadow will reach the circle again, and the line between the two points the shadow touched will run east-west. A line at right angles to it is northsouth. This method was suggested by the Egyptologist I. E. S. Edwards in 1961 and developed by others. It works best around the equinoxes, when the sun's path is nearly a straight line, and it can produce an accuracy of about a tenth of a degree. In 2016, the engineer Glen Dash argued, on the basis of field tests at Giza, that a refined version of the method could account for the small error seen in the Great Pyramid.

The star method. In 2000, the Egyptologist Kate Spence proposed in the journal Nature that the builders used two stars in the northern sky: Kochab in the Little Bear and Mizar in the Big Dipper. At certain times, when the two stars were aligned vertically, they would form a plumb line pointing to the north celestial pole. Because of the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, called precession, the alignment would shift over the centuries, and Spence showed that the small errors in the orientation of Old

Kingdom pyramids seem to correlate with their dates in a way that matches the movement of these stars. Her hypothesis would let us date the pyramids to within a decade or two. Other researchers have challenged it, pointing to uncertainties in the dating, the practical difficulty of making observations, and the possibility that the correlation is coincidental.

KEY POINT

Neither the sun method nor the star method has been proven.

Both are workable with simple tools, and both are consistent with the accuracy seen. It is possible that Egyptian surveyors used more than one approach, and that they tested the result with a second method.

The accuracy in context

Three arcminutes is a very small angle. A good way to appreciate it is to convert it into distance. If you were to stand at one corner of the Great Pyramid and sight along a side, 230 meters long, an error of three arcminutes would shift the far end sideways by about 20 centimeters.

WORKED EXAMPLE

How big is a three-arcminute error? One degree equals 60 arcminutes, so 3 arcminutes is 0.05 degrees. The tangent of 0.05° is about 0.00087. Multiply by the 230-meter side: 230 × 0.00087 ≈ 0.20 meters. In other words, over the length of one side, the pyramid's alignment error amounts to about the length of a hand.

That is an extraordinary achievement for a pre-industrial culture. It is also not magic. A careful team with a gnomon, a cord, and enough time could achieve it. What the result shows is a deep investment in craftsmanship, a repeated cycle of measurement and correction, and probably a team that included several experienced surveyors.

The mystery of the drift

The orientation of other pyramids is less perfect. The pyramids of Meidum and Dahshur are a little further from true north. The pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure show larger errors than Khufu's. The Great Pyramid seems to be the most accurate of all. This pattern raises an interesting question: why was the orientation of Khufu's pyramid better than those of both his predecessors and his successors? Put another way, did the care taken over the orientation rise and then fall within a few decades?

A plausible answer is that Khufu's builders had access to an unusually capable surveyor, or invested extra care because the project was so important. Another is that by the later Fourth Dynasty, the orientation was no longer treated as a priority. This is speculation, and we do not know.

Planning on paper

No architectural plan of a pyramid has survived. Egyptians did not leave behind a blueprint of the Great Pyramid, and we cannot be sure they drew one. But we do have indications that Egyptian builders used drawings.

• Sketches on limestone flakes. At the Step Pyramid, archae-

ologists found a flake of limestone with a curve drawn on it and numerical measurements, thought to be a plan for the curved roof of a chamber. Similar sketches were used by later builders.

• Grid-based drawings. Egyptian artists used a square grid

to proportion figures and, probably, architectural elements. Squared grids appear on unfinished tomb walls.

• Guidelines on the stone. At Meidum and Giza, lines were

drawn on the surface of casing blocks to mark the intended slope. In the Great Pyramid, red ocher marks of various kinds can still be seen.

• Models. Small models, like those used in later times for

temples, may have been used to explain designs to the work crews.

A more surprising source of information is that the builders appear to have changed their plans several times, as we have seen in the successive chambers of the Great Pyramid. This implies that the design was not fixed in advance. It was developed, adjusted, and tested as the work went on. That is another sign of a human process.

The foundation ritual

Surveying was also ritual. In Egyptian temples, from the earliest period, the foundation of a new building began with a ceremony called stretching the cord. A king, often accompanied by the goddess of writing and measurement, Seshat, drove stakes into the ground and stretched a cord between them to mark the corners. Scenes of the ceremony survive in temples. We do not have direct evidence of such a ceremony at the Great Pyramid, but it is likely that it was performed, given how consistently the rite appears in later periods.

This reminds us that for the Egyptians, practical and religious acts were not separate. Aligning the pyramid with the heavens was both a surveying problem and a way of locating the king in the cosmos.

Why the planning mattered

The precision of the base had real structural consequences. A pyramid built on an uneven foundation can tilt or crack, as the Bent Pyramid shows. A pyramid built with slightly different slopes on its four sides will not meet at a point. A pyramid with a base that is not square will have faces that twist. The Great Pyramid's faces meet in a point to within a few centimeters, and the structure has stood for 4,500 years with no major structural failure. The care taken with the base paid off.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The builders used simple tools: cubit rods, cords, plumb bobs, A-frame levels, set squares, and water. The base was leveled by cutting channels filled with water and a central knoll was left as core. North was probably found by the sun's shadow (Edwards, Dash) or two circumpolar stars (Spence); both are plausible and neither is proven. The result, a square base with a 3-arcminute orientation error, is explained by careful craftsmanship, not exotic knowledge.

The Giza quarry

Archaeologists have mapped the quarries on the plateau and found that most of the stone for the Great Pyramid came from just south and southwest of the site. A vast quarry, partly shaped like a bowl, lies only a few hundred meters from the pyramid. It is a good example of efficient planning. By taking stone from nearby, the builders cut their transport distance to a minimum. The quarry also supplied the bedrock rise that the builders left as the pyramid's core.

At the quarry, we can still see how the work was done. The blocks were cut from the rock face in horizontal layers, working from the top down. Quarrymen first cut narrow trenches, about the width of a man's arm, around the sides of a block, marking out a shape. They then undercut the block from below, probably by tunneling beneath it with small chisels. When the base was cut through, the block was levered free. Some partially detached blocks, still attached to the bedrock, are visible in the Giza quarries today, frozen in the middle of the process.

The stone itself is nummulitic limestone, formed in the Eocene, about 40 to 50 million years ago, from the shells of tiny marine creatures. It is full of fossil nummulites, small coinshaped shells, which the Greeks called "lentils." The local limestone is relatively soft, a hardness of about 3 on the Mohs scale, which is about the same as copper. That makes it practical to cut with copper tools.

The tool kit

The materials available to Old Kingdom workers were few: stone, wood, copper, and fiber. Iron was unknown, and bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, would not be common in Egypt until some centuries later. The main tools were these.

• Copper chisels and picks. Copper is soft, but it can be

• Stone hammers and pounders. The hardest tool the Egyp-

• Copper saws with abrasive sand. A copper blade is too

soft to cut hard stone, but with a sharp quartz sand carried in the cut, it works as an abrasive. The saw moves the sand, and the sand does the cutting. Tool marks on granite sarcophagi and statues show the kerfs from this process.

• Drills. Tubular drills, probably made of copper or reed,

and to engrave harder stones.

and checking.
