Myth: "You can't cut granite with copper tools, so the Egyptians must have used advanced technology." Fact: Copper alone cannot cut granite, and the Egyptians knew it. They used the abrasive-sand method for cutting and dolerite pounders for shaping. The marks are still on the stones, and the quarries contain the tools. Modern experiments have reproduced the process, though it is slow: a few centimeters per day.

Quarrying granite at Aswan

Granite was the most demanding material. The red granite used for the King's Chamber and its ceiling beams was quarried at Aswan, on the First Cataract. The quarries are still there. They include a spectacular and famous object: the Unfinished Obelisk, which was cut from the rock but cracked during the work and abandoned. If it had been completed, it would have measured about 42 meters and weighed about 1,200 tonnes. It was probably carved in the New Kingdom, long after the pyramids, but the marks around it reveal the method.

To remove a granite block, workers first identified a suitable section and marked the outline. They then pounded a trench around it with dolerite balls, working the stone down to the required depth. In the trench they could insert wooden wedges and use levers. To detach the block from below, they hammered out a series of slots in the base and drove in wedges, splitting the stone along a plane. The dust was cleared away by hand. Experiments have shown that a team of workers can pound a trench with dolerite at a rate of a few centimeters in a day, depending on the hardness of the rock.

Considering the scale of the Great Pyramid, the amount of granite is small: the walls and ceiling beams of the King's Chamber, the five relieving chambers above it, the sarcophagus, the plugs, and the lining of the antechamber. Even so, it comes to some thousands of tonnes, by most estimates. Each piece was cut and transported 800 kilometers. The effort of transporting

these loads on the river would be daunting, as we will see in Chapter 11.

Tura: the white stone

The fine white limestone that sheathed the Great Pyramid came from quarries at Tura and Maasara, on the east bank of the Nile, about 13 to 15 kilometers upstream of Giza. The stone there is of exceptional quality: fine-grained, pale, and so uniform that it can be cut and polished into smooth faces with narrow joints. The quarries are still partly visible. They consist of long underground galleries, worked inward along the best layers, with pillars of rock left to support the roof.

An inscription from the Fourth Dynasty records that stone was brought from Tura and loaded on boats for Giza. We know the details of one such shipment because of the logbook of the inspector Merer, which was found in 2013 and which we will read in the next chapter.

Marks, codes, and a paperwork system

The workers who cut and moved the stone left their marks on it. On many of the blocks in the Great Pyramid, especially in hidden places, there are red-painted marks of several kinds.

• Gang names. Teams of workers had names that expressed

pride in their work, such as "The Friends of Khufu," found in the relieving chambers. At Menkaure's pyramid, a gang called "The Drunkards of Menkaure" is known.

• Dates and counts. Quarry marks sometimes record regnal

years, months, and days. They show that the work was done on a schedule and that it was recorded.

• Position marks. Lines, arrows, and numbers show where a

block was to be placed in the course.

Marks of this kind exist at the Great Pyramid, and they indicate that work crews were organized into named teams, that each team took responsibility for specific sections, and that supervisors tracked production. They also show that there was friendly rivalry between the teams, and that the workers took pride in being part of a royal enterprise.

Dressing and fitting

At the quarry, blocks were roughly shaped, which cut the weight and made them easier to move. At the pyramid, they were further dressed. For the interior masonry, a fairly rough fit was acceptable, and gaps were filled with gypsum mortar and chips of stone. The mortar did not act as glue. Rather, it filled the spaces between blocks, provided a smooth bed on which to slide each block into place, and spread the load.

The outer casing was another matter. The Tura limestone casing blocks were cut to fit each other with astonishing precision. The joints between casing stones were so thin, around half a millimeter, that a knife blade cannot be inserted. Each stone was cut to the specific slope of the pyramid face, and the surfaces were dressed with copper chisels, stone rubbers, and fine sand. The finishing was done after the blocks were in place,

working from the top down, so that the surface was smooth and continuous.

The fit of the casing stones, and the fact that they were dressed to a common plane while in place, is the reason that the pyramid looked, from a distance, like a single polished surface.

The size of the blocks

The common idea that the Great Pyramid is built entirely of enormous blocks is wrong. Most blocks are modest. Typical core blocks weigh about 1.5 to 2.5 tonnes, and many are smaller. The blocks in the lower courses are larger and thicker, up to about 1.5 meters tall, and the courses diminish in height as the pyramid rises, to about half a meter near the top. This arrangement makes sense for the builders: the heavy blocks are at the bottom, where they have the shortest route and the most stable footing, and the lighter blocks are at the top, where they have to be raised the highest.

There are exceptions. The granite beams over the King's Chamber, each of which weighs between about 25 and 80 tonnes, are the heaviest. The sarcophagus weighs about three tonnes. The plugs in the Ascending Passage weigh several tonnes each. And the Tura casing stones, which were thick wedges, weighed up to about 15 tonnes. But these were a minor portion of the total.

How many quarrymen?

How big was the quarry crew? Estimating this is difficult, but we can set bounds. If the Great Pyramid took 20 years and required 2.3 million blocks, the rate was about 115,000 blocks per year. A skilled team of quarrymen, working with copper tools on soft limestone, could probably produce a rough block in a day or two. So the quarry required perhaps a few thousand workers, on top of those transporting, lifting, and laying the stone. The figure fits well with the estimates of a total workforce of 20,000 to 30,000 that archaeologists derive from the size of the workers' settlement.

WORKED EXAMPLE

A rough quarry estimate. Suppose each quarry worker produced one rough block every three days, working 300 days a year, which is about 100 blocks a year. To supply 115,000 blocks a year, you need about 1,150 workers. Add a factor of 2 to 3 for the work of cutting the trench, clearing debris, repairing tools, and so on, and the figure becomes 2,500 to 3,500 quarry workers. This is a reasonable fraction of a total workforce of about 20,000.

The question of tools

It is fair to ask why more copper tools have not been found at Giza. After all, we would expect thousands. The answer is simple: copper was valuable and recycled. Worn or broken tools were melted down and recast. This is also the reason that few of the pyramid builders' tools survive. When a tool was too blunt to use, it went back to the smelter. The tools that do survive are mostly from unusual circumstances, such as a tool left in a sealed tomb or lost in a crevice.

What the quarries tell us

The quarries are the best answer to a question that is often asked: how can we be sure that the builders were Egyptians using the tools of their time? The answer is that the evidence is there. We have the quarry faces, the trenches, the half-cut blocks, the abandoned obelisk, the dolerite pounders, the copper tools, the grooves from saws, the quarry marks, the paintings of stone-working scenes in tombs, and the written records of expeditions. Taken together, they form a consistent story. There is no gap that needs to be filled by anything exotic.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The Great Pyramid's core is local Giza limestone. The casing is white limestone from Tura. The granite came from Aswan, 800 km away, and was shaped by pounding with dolerite balls and cutting with sand-fed copper saws. Copper chisels, wooden wedges, and levers handled the limestone. The blocks were mostly modest, about 2.5 tonnes. Quarry marks, tools, and half-finished blocks show a well-organized human operation.

CHAPTER 11

Moving Stone: Sledges, Wet Sand, Boats, and a Logbook

How millions of blocks, and a few giant ones, reached the Giza plateau, and the diary of a man who helped move them.

Cutting stone is only half the problem. The other half is moving it. A block of limestone weighing 2.5 tonnes does not roll, slide, or float on its own. It has to be hauled, often over long distances, on ground that offers no hard roads. For the Great Pyramid's 2.3 million blocks, and for its few hundred heavy granite pieces, the builders needed a system of transport as carefully organized as the quarrying itself. We now know a good deal about how it worked, thanks to a handful of discoveries made within living memory.

The problem of the sledge

The Egyptians did not use the wheel to haul heavy loads. Wheeled vehicles, in the form of chariots, did not reach Egypt until about 1600 BCE, and heavy carts were not used for monument construction. Instead, builders used the sledge, a wooden platform with runners, pulled by ropes. Sledges survive from the Egyptian past. Several from the Middle Kingdom, built of cedar or sycamore with sturdy cross-pieces and curved runners, were found at Dahshur. Tomb paintings show them in use, loaded with statues, shrines, and stone blocks.

A sledge on ordinary desert sand works poorly. Dry sand piles up in front of the runners like a small wave, and the sledge has to climb over it. The resistance is high, and haulers tire quickly. A well-known scene suggests that Egyptians had found a remedy.

The painting that shows how

In a tomb at Deir el-Bersha, in Middle Egypt, belonging to a nobleman named Djehutihotep (about 1850 BCE), a painted relief shows the transport of a colossal statue of the owner. The statue sits on a sledge, and 172 men haul it on four ropes, in four rows. Above, the inscription says that the statue was cut from alabaster and stood about 13 cubits tall, or about 6.8 meters. The scene contains a small detail that has fascinated researchers: a man standing at the front of the sledge, on a platform, pouring liquid from a jar onto the ground ahead.

For years, scholars interpreted this as a ritual act, a libation. But in 2014, a team of physicists at the University of Amsterdam, led by Daniel Bonn, tested the idea. Their experiment, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, measured the force required to drag a loaded sledge across sand with different amounts of water. They found that on dry sand, the sledge piled up a heap in front of it and the force climbed. On slightly damp sand, the water created capillary bridges between the sand grains, giving the surface extra stiffness, and the heap did not form. At the right level of moisture, about two to five percent water by volume, the force required fell by about half.

KEY POINT

The Amsterdam experiment shows that wetting the sand in front of a sledge can reduce the pulling force by half. This was within the reach of any team of Egyptian workers with jars and water. It means a task that needed 40 haulers might need only 20.

The paper also noted that too much water is as bad as too little: the sand becomes soupy and the advantage is lost. A skilled worker, pouring the water at the front, would have to judge the amount. That the figure in the tomb is doing exactly this, in a scene about 4,000 years old, is remarkable. It does not prove that the same technique was used at Giza, since the tomb is 700 years later. But the technique is simple, the materials are cheap, and nothing suggests it was a recent invention.

Hauling on roads and rails

Egyptians did not simply drag stones across the desert. At Giza, they built haul roads, graded paths that led from the quarries to the pyramid. Some were paved or lined with stone and mud plaster. The best-preserved example is at the basalt quarry of Widan el-Faras, in the Faiyum, where a stone-paved road of about 11 kilometers leads to an ancient harbor on the shore of a lake in the Faiyum. This is the oldest known paved road in the world.

Another invention was the use of wooden rails or sleepers. A line of planks laid across the path under a sledge can reduce friction, and wooden sleepers have been found in a few places. Rollers are sometimes proposed, but they are not well documented for monument-building, and they perform poorly on soft sand.

WORKED EXAMPLE

How many people to pull a block? Take a 2.5-tonne block, which weighs about 24,500 newtons. On wet sand, a coefficient of friction of about 0.25 is reasonable, so the pulling force is 0.25 × 24,500 ≈ 6,100 N. If an adult can pull steadily with about 200 N for hours, you need around 30 people. On a ramp with a 1-in-8 slope (about 7 degrees), the extra force needed to lift the block is about 24,500 × 0.12 ≈ 3,000 N, bringing the total to about 9,000 N, or around 45 people. These numbers are rough, but they show why the Egyptians used gangs of 20 to 40 haulers.

The river road

The Nile was the main transport artery. To carry stone and supplies, the Egyptians built large boats, and tomb reliefs show cargo vessels carrying blocks, granite columns, and obelisks. The best evidence from the pyramid age comes from the causeway of King Unas, about 200 years after Khufu, where reliefs show boats carrying huge granite palm columns from Aswan to Saqqara. Weni, the official we met in Chapter 7, boasted that he had a fleet of cargo and towing boats built from acacia wood in a single year to fetch granite from Elephantine.

The seasons were crucial. During the inundation, from July to October, the Nile flooded the fields and spread across the plain. Boats could travel much closer to the edge of the desert, and at Giza, they could bring stone to a harbor near the plateau's foot. Granite blocks from Aswan, loaded onto boats in the summer, could drift north on the current and be unloaded at Giza. The ships were steered by oars and carried by the river's flow, and they could return upstream with the prevailing north wind filling their sails.

The river was not just a way to move cargo, but also a way to move people. This has implications for the labor force, as we will see: when the fields were flooded, farmers had no work to do on the land, and they could be sent to the project.

The harbor at Giza

The Giza plateau has no natural port, but the builders made one. Archaeologists have found evidence of a basin, canals, and harbor facilities near the base of the plateau, connected to the Nile by channels. Recent geological work has suggested that a nowvanished branch of the Nile, which scientists call the Ahramat Branch, once ran along the western edge of the floodplain, close to the pyramids. A study published in 2024 by Eman Ghoneim of the University of North Carolina Wilmington used satellite radar, sediment cores, and other data to trace this ancient channel for about 64 kilometers and showed that it passed very close to 31 pyramids, including Giza. Its existence helps to explain why so many pyramids are on the edge of the desert. A waterway at the base of the plateau would have made delivering stone much easier. We return to this study in Chapter 22.

The valley temple of Khufu, at the end of the causeway, would have stood beside this harbor, and the causeway itself ran from it to the pyramid, a distance of several hundred meters.

Merer's logbook

In 2013, a French-Egyptian team led by the Egyptologist Pierre Tallet of the Sorbonne, working at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient port on the Red Sea coast, found something extraordinary. In a man-made gallery sealed by a stone, they found about 30 rolls of papyrus, many in fragments, dating to the reign of Khufu. They are the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. Most are administrative records of the harbor, but a group of them are the personal log of an inspector named Merer.

Merer was an official, a "sab," in charge of a team of about 40 men. Their job was to haul and ship stone for Khufu's pyramid. His logbook, written in hieratic script on papyrus, records day-by-day entries over several months. The entries are dated to year 26 or 27 of Khufu's reign, in the final years of the pyramid's construction.

The entries tell a clear story. Merer and his crew sailed to the quarries at Tura, on the east bank of the Nile, where they loaded boats with blocks of white limestone for the pyramid's casing. They then sailed down to Giza, a trip that took about a day each way, and unloaded the blocks at a harbor basin that the logbook calls She Akhet-Khufu, "the Lake of the Horizon of Khufu," which appears to have been connected by a canal to the Nile. A typical sequence reads, in paraphrase: Day 1: the crew spent the day hauling stone at Tura, and spent the night at Tura. Day 2: they loaded the boats and sailed. Day 3: they unloaded at the Lake of Khufu. Day 4: they returned. A round trip took about four days, and Merer's crew repeated this round trip many times.

KEY POINT

The log shows the Great Pyramid's casing stones moving by boat from Tura to a harbor at Giza, with a named official, a crew size, a schedule, and a destination. It is a direct written record of the construction process from someone who took part in it.

The logbook also names the official in charge of the harbor. He was Ankhhaf, a half-brother of the king who held a senior post at the pyramid's harbor and is named in connection with the arrival of the stone. The logbook gives a human face to the project: a regular crew, with regular hours, a boss, and a payroll.

Merer's papyri are not the only finds at Wadi al-Jarf. The site is a harbor, built about 4,600 years ago, with a stone jetty, anchors, ropes, and storage galleries holding dozens of large jars. The port was used as the starting point for expeditions to Sinai, where the Egyptians mined copper and turquoise. It tells us that Khufu's government was running naval and mining expeditions at the same time as the pyramid project. It also gives the physical evidence: an Egyptian harbor, run by Egyptian officials, on the shore of an Egyptian sea.

The ropes

Hauling on this scale required rope, and lots of it. Egyptian ropes were made of papyrus, halfa grass, palm fiber, and flax, twisted by hand in a long process, and they survive from many Egyptian contexts, including harbor stores and the boat pits at Giza, where the cedar planks of Khufu's ship were lashed together with rope. Rope-making was an industry in itself, and the expertise to make strong ropes was widely shared. In the tomb scenes of haulers, the ropes are drawn as thick as a man's wrist.

The granite problem

Granite from Aswan posed the toughest transport challenge. A single ceiling beam for the King's Chamber, weighing perhaps 50 tonnes, needed to be dragged from the quarry to the Nile, loaded on a boat, and floated for about 800 kilometers. At Giza, it was unloaded at the harbor and dragged from the harbor, along the causeway and up a ramp, to the pyramid.

The ships had to be big. Egyptians knew how to build them. The Khufu ship, the cedar vessel found next to the pyramid, is 43.6 meters long and built with great sophistication. It was built from planks sewn together with rope, with no nails, and has a flat hull with a shallow draft. Whether it was used for ceremonies on the river or only for the afterlife is debated, but its design shows the high level of Egyptian shipbuilding. Boats of that size, with a reinforced bottom and sturdy cross beams, could carry loads of many tonnes.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "The Egyptians could not have moved 50-tonne blocks without modern machinery." Fact: Egyptians moved even larger loads. The colossal statue in the tomb of Djehutihotep has been estimated at about 58 tonnes, and the painting shows it hauled by 172 men. Obelisks weighing more than 300 tonnes were later shipped by barge and hauled by large teams of men. The pyramid builders' loads were well within their capacity.

The logistics

The transport system was supported by a larger network. Cargo needed unloading, supplies needed to get to the haulers, and workers needed food and water. Workers, in turn, needed tools, rope, sledges, and replacement planks. The Egyptians managed this by a combination of centralized planning, local administration, and written record-keeping. It is the paper trail that makes the project work: Merer's logbook is a small part of it.

The scale of the logistics is almost as impressive as the lifting. We are not just talking about a single transport route but a regional network that took in Tura, Aswan, the Faiyum, and the Red Sea, as well as the Nile and the road network. Every day, blocks of stone, loads of grain, jars of beer, and bundles of rope were arriving at Giza. It was the largest construction logistics operation of its time, and it was run on papyrus and muscle.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Heavy blocks were hauled on wooden sledges, with water poured on the sand to halve the friction (Djehutihotep's tomb painting; Amsterdam experiment, 2014). Stone came by river, with the flood bringing boats close to Giza. Merer's logbook (Wadi al- Jarf, found 2013) records a crew hauling Tura limestone to Giza in the 26th–27th year of Khufu. Egyptian ships and ropes were big and sophisticated enough to move the heaviest loads.

Raising the Blocks: Ramps, Levers, and the Great Debate

The question that engineers and Egyptologists still argue about: how did the stone get to the top?

If you ask a group of people how the Great Pyramid was built, most will say the same thing: ramps. They are right, but the word hides a long and lively argument. Everyone agrees that ramps were used. What nobody has proven is exactly what kind, how many, where they ran, and what they were made of. In this chapter we look at the problem, the main proposals, and the evidence that has recently begun to settle some questions.

Where is the work?

The first thing to understand is that the work of raising stone is not evenly distributed. A pyramid is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so most of its volume lies near the base. This means that most of the blocks never had to be lifted very high.

For a pyramid, the fraction of volume lying below a given height is easy to calculate. If H is the total height and h the height of interest, the volume below h is 1 − (1 − h / H )³ of the total.

More than half the stone is below 37 meters, and nearly 90 percent is below 73 meters. Only about 2 percent of the pyramid's blocks have to rise above the 110-meter mark. That changes the question. Moving blocks up to the first 40 or 50 meters is a large job, but moving them to the top is a small one. A system good enough for the lower half of the pyramid does most of the work.

The straight ramp

The simplest idea is a single ramp, built of rubble, brick, and mud, leaning against one face of the pyramid and growing higher as the pyramid grows. This is the picture many people have in mind, and it is supported by one thing: ramps are known to have been used in Egypt. Remains of construction ramps have been found at the pyramid of Senusret I at Lisht, at Meidum, and at many temple sites. Tomb scenes show ramps used to raise stones and bricks, and a New Kingdom scribal text, Papyrus Anastasi I, mentions the dimensions of a ramp for a colossal statue in the form of a mathematical problem.

The straight ramp has a problem, however. A ramp must keep a gentle slope or the haulers cannot pull the sledge up it. At a slope of 1 in 10, a ramp that reaches the top of the Great Pyramid would be nearly 1.5 kilometers long. Its volume would be a

large fraction of the pyramid itself, and it would need to be rebuilt, higher and longer, as the pyramid grew. Allowing for its width, it would need a large fraction of the pyramid's own volume, perhaps half or more. At Giza, there is no sign of the remains of such a monstrous ramp, which would have left a huge amount of rubble.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Size of a straight ramp. A ramp to a height of 146 meters at a slope of 1 in 10 would be 1,460 meters long. If it is 10 meters wide, its volume is about ½ × 1,460 × 146 × 10 ≈ 1.07 million cubic meters, around 40 percent of the pyramid's volume. A steeper slope of 1 in 5 would halve the length to 730 meters but roughly double the part of the hauling force that goes into lifting each block.

A straight ramp could work for the lower levels. After that, it becomes unwieldy. Some experts think the builders used a straight ramp for the first third or half of the pyramid and then switched to another method for the upper part.

The zigzag ramp

To get around the problem of length, some proposals have the ramp running back and forth up the face of the pyramid, in a zigzag. This design would use less material than a straight ramp, since the ramp is carried by the pyramid's own slope. Several scholars have proposed versions of this, in which the ramps run up the sides of the pyramid on temporary platforms.

The zigzag has its difficulties as well. At the turns, the haulers must pull the sledge around a sharp bend, which is awkward with large blocks. A ramp lying against the pyramid's face would cover the casing stones and make it difficult to level and dress them as the pyramid rose. And the evidence for it is slight.

The spiral ramp

Another idea is a spiral ramp, wrapping around the pyramid like a mountain road. It has the advantage of using the pyramid's own sides for support, and it is a familiar image from old illustrations. The problem is the corners. As the ramp passes around each corner, it would cover the edge of the pyramid, making it impossible for the surveyors to check the alignment of the corners with their instruments. Since the pyramid is so precisely aligned, it seems hard to imagine that the builders would risk blocking their sightlines. Some suggest the ramp could have been dismantled periodically to check the corners, but that adds work.

The internal ramp

In 2007, a French architect named Jean-Pierre Houdin proposed a different solution, with a book by Bob Brier and Houdin to follow in 2008. His idea was a combination: a straight external ramp to a height of about 43 meters, where the first third of the pyramid is complete, and from there, a spiral ramp built inside the pyramid itself. The internal ramp would run just inside the outer wall, making turns at the corners, and would be left in place as part of the structure. Houdin argued that the corners, where the ramp turns, could be seen as a small notch visible in the pyramid's northeast edge at a height of about 90 meters.

The theory is clever and has attracted a lot of attention. In 1986 and 1987, microgravity surveys by a French team found regions of different density inside the pyramid, which some have interpreted as consistent with an internal spiral, though other interpretations exist. More recent scans, including those of the ScanPyramids project, have found anomalies, but no confirmed spiral corridor has yet been identified. Many Egyptologists remain skeptical. Others find it plausible as part of the system. At present, the internal ramp theory is an interesting hypothesis, not an established fact.

The Hatnub evidence

The most important recent discovery bearing on this debate was made not at Giza but about 300 kilometers to the south, at the quarry of Hatnub, the source of Egyptian alabaster. Starting in 2012, a team led by Yannis Gourdon and Roland Enmarch of the French and British institutes excavated an extraordinary system there. It included a ramp with a steep slope of about 20 percent, flanked on each side by a staircase. On the ramp and next to it were numerous post holes, carefully cut into the rock in a regular pattern. The structure dates to the reign of Khufu, according to inscriptions at the quarry.

The excavators reasoned that the system was used to haul alabaster blocks up out of the quarry pit. Workers would have fastened ropes to wooden posts set in the holes and used them to pull a heavy sledge up the ramp. The posts acted as anchors, allowing the haulers on the stairs at each side to share the effort and to hold the load if it slipped. A sledge pulled by ropes tied to posts could climb a steeper slope than a simple team on a flat ramp, and the staircases gave the workers a stable footing.

KEY POINT

The Hatnub ramp was built at the same time as the Great Pyramid, by the same administration, and it used a steep slope with posts and ropes to lift heavy blocks. This is the first direct evidence of how Khufu's engineers moved heavy stone uphill. If the same system were used on the pyramid, a ramp with a slope of 20 percent would be only 730 meters long, and a series of smaller steep ramps would be even easier.

The Hatnub finds show that the Egyptians were capable of using steep ramps, anchored by posts and ropes, rather than depending on gentle slopes. This supports the idea of a system of shorter, steeper ramps used together with levers and other methods, though it does not tell us which of the ramp layouts was used at Giza.

Levers and rockers

Ramps are only part of the answer. At each stage, workers needed to move blocks sideways and to set them accurately in place. The tool for this was the lever, and it is widely accepted that wooden levers and wedges were used to nudge blocks into their final position. Wooden cradle rockers, curved timbers on which a block could be rocked from side to side and then lifted a little at a time, have been proposed as a means of raising blocks up a short step. A few objects interpreted as rockers have been found in Egyptian contexts, but whether they were used on the pyramids is disputed.

The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt around 450 BCE, said that the pyramid was built in steps, and that when the first level was complete, the stones were raised to the next by machines made of short timbers. He did not describe them. It is possible that he heard a garbled report about levers, rockers, or small ramps, and the tradition has endured.

There were no cranes or pulleys. The pulley does not appear in Egypt until much later, in the Greek and Roman periods. The Egyptians relied on ramps, ropes, levers, and muscle, and these were sufficient.

The granite beams

The hardest lifting job was the granite beams over the King's Chamber. The beams weigh between about 25 and 80 tonnes and had to be placed at a height of about 50 to 60 meters. How did the builders do it?

One answer is that a ramp of rubble, mud, and stone was built to the required height, and the beams were hauled up with sledges and rope teams, as at Hatnub, anchored by posts. Once the beams were in place, the chamber could be completed. Another is that the beams were hauled up the Grand Gallery, but the gallery is only about two meters wide at the base, and the beams are too large. A more likely answer is that they were placed during construction, before the upper courses of the pyramid were laid. The relieving chambers above them, which took the weight, were then built on top. The granite sarcophagus, which is too big to fit up the Ascending Passage, was almost certainly placed in the chamber at the same time, before the roof went on.

The placing of the capstone at the top was simple in comparison. It was the last block, a small one, and was lifted by the same methods used for the other blocks.

Combining ideas

Faced with a choice among ramp theories, many modern researchers suggest that more than one method was used. A sensible combination is:

• A long, low ramp (or ramps) from the quarry to the pyra-

mid base, for the hauling of the bulk blocks.

• A broad, straight ramp against one face for the lower part

of the pyramid.

• Steeper, shorter ramps or zigzag ramps for the upper lev-

els, perhaps with post-and-rope assistance as at Hatnub. • Levers and rockers for final positioning, and possibly to

move blocks onto the next course at the top.

The advantage of this blended approach is that it matches the changing geometry of the pyramid. At the bottom, the course is wide and the blocks are large, so a broad ramp is used. At the top, the course is narrow, and the blocks are smaller, so a lighter system will do.

What remains to be found

It may be a surprise that the question of how the Great Pyramid's blocks were raised is not fully settled. The reason is that ramps are temporary structures, made of rubble and brick, which were removed or left to erode once the work was done. The signs left behind are subtle: post holes, bedrock cuttings, small deposits of rubble, and marks on the pyramid's own surface. Archaeologists are still looking.

Despite this uncertainty, nobody has found a feature of the pyramid that could not have been made with ramps, ropes, sledges, and levers. The builders had the means, they had the evidence for their methods in other places, and they had the time. The exact form of the ramp is a puzzle of detail, not a gap in the case that humans built it.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Most of the pyramid's volume is in its lower half, so the lifting work is concentrated near the base. A single straight ramp is too large for the full height. Zigzag, spiral, and internal ramps have each been proposed, and none is proven. The Hatnub quarry (dated to Khufu) shows steep, post-anchored ramps in use, a strong clue. Most researchers think a combination of methods was used. Levers placed the blocks. There were no cranes or pulleys.

The Workforce: Who Really Built the Pyramids

Not slaves, not aliens: a rotating, fed, housed, and honored labor force, and the town they lived in.

Few questions about the pyramids have a more popular answer than "who built them?" For generations, the standard answer was slaves, driven by overseers with whips. That image was shaped by ancient writers, by Biblical stories, and by Hollywood. It has proven remarkably durable. It is also, as far as the archaeological evidence can tell, wrong. The people who built the pyramids were Egyptians, and the physical evidence of where they lived, what they ate, how they were buried, and how they were cared for shows a workforce that was organized, supplied, and in many respects respected.

Where the slave story came from

The notion of enslaved pyramid builders goes back to the Greek historian Herodotus, who wrote around 450 BCE, about two thousand years after the Great Pyramid was built. He reported that Cheops forced all the Egyptians to work for him, in gangs of 100,000 men who worked for three months at a time, for twenty years. He described them as suffering under a tyrant. His account is the oldest surviving description of the pyramid's construction by an outsider, and it was based on what Egyptian priests and guides told him. It has to be treated with care. The numbers are too large, the tone is that of a Greek moralist, and he was writing a long time after the fact.

A second source of the idea was the Bible. The Book of Exodus describes the Hebrews laboring under a Pharaoh, making bricks and building store cities. This is sometimes linked to the pyramids in popular memory. But the text mentions store cities, Pithom and Ramesses, and the setting, if it was historical, would belong to the New Kingdom, more than a thousand years after the Great Pyramid. The stories have no connection with Giza. Yet through centuries of retelling, and with the boost of twentieth-century films, they merged into a single mental picture.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "The pyramids were built by tens of thousands of slaves." Fact: There is no archaeological evidence for slave labor on the pyramids. The evidence points to a force of Egyptian laborers, some permanent and many rotating in on a labor-service basis, who were fed, housed, buried with honor, and given medical care. Slavery existed in ancient Egypt, mostly in households and mostly involving foreign captives, but it is not documented as the basis of pyramid construction.

The discovery of the workers' cemetery

The first real challenge to the slave theory came in 1990, near the southern edge of the Giza plateau. According to a popular story, a tourist's horse stumbled on a mudbrick tomb. Whatever the truth of that anecdote, the Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass and his team investigated and found a large cemetery that had been hidden under the sand. Over the years, the excavations uncovered several hundred tombs, in two main cemeteries, an upper one on the slope of the plateau and a lower one beside it. Many of them contained intact skeletons.

The tombs were modest, built of mud brick and local stone, but they were real tombs, with a burial chamber and often a small superstructure. Some of the upper tombs were built in the shape of small pyramids or stepped structures. Burials were placed in the traditional position, curled on one side, with the head to the west. Pottery jars, bread, and beer were left for the deceased. Some contained jewelry, such as simple beads. A few

of the larger tombs had inscriptions naming the owners, with titles connected to the work crews.

A person who was a slave, with no standing, would not have been given a tomb within sight of the royal tombs. These people were buried at Giza close to the king whose pyramid they built, in the manner of Egyptians of their rank, and equipped to take food and drink with them to the afterlife. This is how a respected laborer was buried.

What the bones show

The skeletons are a lasting record of working lives. Osteologists who examined them found clear evidence of hard physical labor: arthritis in the spine, knees, and hips, compressed vertebrae, and worn joints. Many of the men and women had stress injuries. These match the demands of heavy hauling and lifting.

But there is also evidence of care. Many skeletons show healed fractures, including broken legs and arms that had set well, which means the injured person received treatment and was allowed to recover. In some cases, bones show signs of surgery. A few individuals had survived amputations, one of a lower leg, with healing around the cut, which implies skilled surgical treatment and long recovery. A pattern of this kind is not what would be expected for slave labor, where an injured worker might simply be discarded. It reflects a system in which there was a medical service, and the workforce was valued.

The cemeteries also contain the graves of women and of children. This has been taken as evidence that the labor force included families, or that the settlements included women who

worked in bakeries, breweries, and workshops. The relative sparseness of the tombs of babies might suggest that families lived elsewhere, but the evidence is not conclusive.

The Lost City of the Pyramid Builders

If the dead are one half of the evidence, the other half is the living quarters. In 1988, the American Egyptologist Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass began excavating an area south of the Sphinx, beyond a huge stone barrier known as the Wall of the Crow. Over the next several decades, Lehner's team, known as Ancient Egypt Research Associates (AERA), uncovered what they called the Lost City of the Pyramid Builders, officially known as Heit el-Ghurab, "the Wall of the Crow."

The settlement dates to the reigns of Khafre and Menkaure, a generation or two after Khufu, but it is generally accepted as representative of the system. It was a planned community of about seven hectares, filled with streets, courtyards, houses, workshops, and storehouses.

The excavations revealed several distinct areas.

• Bakeries. Large installations, with rows of ovens and thou-

sands of bell-shaped bread molds, indicate mass production of bread. The bakeries were on a scale that could feed thousands of people.

• Breweries. Vats and jars show that beer, a key part of the

Egyptian diet and a source of calories, was brewed on site. • Fish and meat. Excavators found large deposits of fish

bones, and of cattle, sheep, and goat bones. A study of the

bones concluded that the workers ate a good deal of beef, which was a high-status food. It also found evidence that cattle and sheep were brought in on the hoof from farms in the Delta and elsewhere, a sign of a large supply network. • Barracks. A series of long, narrow buildings, called the

Galleries, each with a wide platform, seem to have been dormitories for the rotating laborers. They are estimated to have housed between about 1,600 and 2,000 workers at a time.

• Houses. Streets of smaller homes, probably for the perma-

nent staff of overseers, craftsmen, and their families, and a district of larger houses for officials.

• Workshops. Remains of copper working, flint tool making,

sculpture, wood working, and other crafts.

KEY POINT

The Lost City shows a settlement built for pyramid construction, with food production on an industrial scale, accommodation for thousands, a hierarchy of housing, and workshops. The workers were housed, fed, and supplied. Nothing about it suggests a population of captives.

How the labor was organized

The evidence of the Giza workmen's marks and of later documents shows that the workforce was divided into a hierarchy of units, a sort of military-style organization. Tentatively, the structure looked something like this.

• The crew or gang, the largest unit, with a name. Names

found in the pyramid include "Friends of Khufu" and, at Menkaure's pyramid, "The Drunkards of Menkaure." A gang, according to Lehner's reconstruction, might have numbered in the range of 1,000 to 2,000.

• The phyle, a subdivision of a gang, of a couple of hundred

men.

• Divisions of about 20 men, each with a leader. Merer's log-

book shows a team of about 40 men led by an inspector.

Each unit had an overseer and a scribe who kept records. The names show a sense of pride and rivalry. A gang might compete to place stones faster than another.

Not all workers were equally skilled. There were different categories. A permanent core of craftsmen and overseers stayed on site year-round. These included stonemasons, carpenters, surveyors, scribes, copper workers, and rope makers. A much larger group of laborers did the heavy hauling and lifting, and rotated in for periods of weeks or months. The latter were drawn from villages and towns across Egypt and may have been part of a labor obligation to the state, known as a corvée. They worked for the king for part of the year, in return for rations and, in effect, as part of their tax. It was a system that was demanding, but not enslavement.

How big was the workforce?

Estimates vary. Herodotus's 100,000 is regarded as too high. Modern estimates, derived from the size of the workers' town, the food needed, the number of blocks to move, and the capacity of the quarries, settle on a total workforce of about 20,000 to 30,000 people at the peak. Lehner and others have suggested that a core of several thousand permanent workers was supplemented by a larger number of rotating laborers. The total is considerable but it is a small proportion of Egypt's population at the time, estimated at between 1 and 2 million. That would mean 1 to 2 percent of the population was engaged in building the pyramid at any given time.

The number needs to be put in perspective. Many more people were involved indirectly: farmers and herders who produced the food, boat builders, rope makers, potters, and the families who supported the workers. A pyramid project was a national economic undertaking.

Pay, food, and the beer ration

Pyramid workers were paid in kind, in the way most Egyptians were: with rations of bread, beer, and other goods, plus clothing and oil. Later records from the workers' village at Deir el-Medina, about 1,000 years after the Great Pyramid, show that rations were calculated in numbers of loaves and jars of beer, with the bread and beer an essential part of the diet. Egyptian beer was not much like a modern lager. It was a thick, nutritious, low-alcohol drink made from barley, drunk through a straw. It provided carbohydrates, vitamins, and safe hydration.

The food needs of the workforce were considerable. A modern estimate suggests that feeding 20,000 workers would require about 20 tonnes of grain a day. We return to this calculation in Chapter 14.

Why people worked

Why would tens of thousands of people leave their villages and spend months hauling stone? There are several possible explanations.

First, it was an obligation. Egyptian farmers owed labor service to the state, as part of their taxes. This was an old and deeply rooted institution.

Second, it was an opportunity. The work included regular meals, medical care, housing, and, for skilled workers, status. In a hard agricultural world, regular food could be an inducement. The inundation season, when the fields were flooded, meant farmers had no other work.

Third, it was a religious duty. Building a pyramid for the god-king was, for the Egyptians, an act of devotion and a contribution to the maintenance of the world order. A worker who helped to bring the king safely into the afterlife might hope to share some of his benefits. Many of the workers' tombs were built next to the king's tomb for just that reason.

Fourth, it was a source of pride. The gang names and the tombs show it. People took pride in their work and in the group to which they belonged.

None of this means that the work was voluntary or pleasant. A labor draft is a labor draft, and the work was hard and dangerous, and some people died. But it was part of an accepted social system, not a regime of chains.

Strikes and complaints

Direct evidence from the pyramid age on workers' complaints is scarce, but later records show that Egyptian workers were capable of organized protest. The earliest recorded strike in history took place around 1157 BCE, in the reign of Ramesses III, when the workers of the royal tomb village at Deir el-Medina laid down their tools and sat down outside the mortuary temples of earlier kings, because their grain rations were late. The strike worked, at least temporarily. The incident is recorded on a papyrus, the Turin Strike Papyrus, and it shows that workers on royal tombs had expectations and the power to enforce them. A state that depended on skilled labor could not afford to treat it as disposable.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The pyramids were built by Egyptian workers, a mix of permanent skilled staff and rotating laborers, totaling perhaps 20,000–30,000 at the peak. The workers' town (Heit el-Ghurab) had bakeries, breweries, barracks, and workshops, and the workers' cemeteries show proper burials, healed injuries, and evidence of medical care. The slave story comes from Herodotus and later tradition, not from archaeology.

CHAPTER 14

Energy and Effort: The Numbers Behind the Pyramid

How much work did it take, where did the energy come from, and what do the numbers tell us?

When people ask about the energy behind the pyramids, they are often hoping for something mysterious. The real answer is both less exotic and more impressive. The energy was human: muscle, fueled by bread, beer, fish, and beef, delivered through a vast organization. When we put numbers on it, we find that the pyramid fits comfortably within what a large preindustrial society could do. It also becomes clear where the effort actually went, and the answer is not where most people expect.

This chapter works through the arithmetic step by step. Where a figure is an estimate, we say so. The aim is not to prove a single exact number but to show the scale, so that the claims in later chapters about "lost energy technologies" can be measured against reality.

Step 1: How much does it weigh?

The Great Pyramid has a volume of about 2.6 million cubic meters. Limestone has a density of about 2,200 to 2,700 kilograms per cubic meter, depending on type, and the pyramid also contains voids and mortar. A commonly used figure for the total mass is about 5.9 million tonnes, or 5.9 billion kilograms. If we divide by the 2.3 million blocks, we get an average of about 2.5 tonnes per block, which agrees with the typical block weight seen in the masonry.

Step 2: How much energy to lift it?

Raising a mass against gravity takes energy equal to the mass times the gravitational acceleration times the height. Because the pyramid is wider at the bottom, the average block did not have to be lifted all the way to the top. The center of mass of a pyramid is one quarter of the way up, so the average lift height is about one quarter of the pyramid's height: 146.6 divided by 4, or about 36.7 meters.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Lifting energy. E = m × g × h = 5.9 × 10⁹ kg × 9.81 m/s² × 36.7 m ≈ 2.1 × 10¹² joules. In more familiar units, that is about 590,000 kilowatt-hours, or 590 megawatt-hours.

To put this number in context: 590 megawatt-hours is what a single one-megawatt power station produces in about 24 days. It is the electrical energy used by about 55 average American

homes in a year. In terms of fuel, it is roughly the energy in 60,000 liters of gasoline, or a couple of tanker trucks.

That sounds small, and it is. A modern engineer would say that the useful work done in raising the stone was modest. This is the figure sometimes quoted to claim that the pyramid "needed" some special source of power. It does not.

Step 3: How many calories does that take?

Human muscle is not very efficient. The body converts food energy into mechanical work at about 20 to 25 percent efficiency; the rest becomes heat. If we use 20 percent, the food energy needed to supply the 2.1 × 10¹² joules of lifting work is five times as much: about 1.06 × 10¹³ joules. A food calorie (kilocalorie) is 4,184 joules, so that equals about 2.5 billion kilocalories.

A working adult in a heavy job might need about 3,500 kilocalories per day. If a workforce of 20,000 people ate that much, the group would consume 70 million kilocalories per day. So the lifting work alone, in energy terms, corresponds to about 36 days of food for such a workforce.

KEY POINT

The energy needed simply to lift the stone is equal to about five weeks of food for a 20,000-person workforce. The pyramid was not hard because of the lifting energy. It was hard because of everything else.

Step 4: What was the rest of the effort?

The lifting energy is only a small part of the story. A human being can do about 75 to 100 watts of useful mechanical work over a long working day. Let us take 75 watts, a reasonable figure for sustained labor, and assume an 8-hour workday. A single worker delivers 600 watt-hours, or 0.6 kilowatt-hours, per day. A workforce of 20,000 delivers 12,000 kilowatt-hours, or 12 megawatt-hours, per day.

Over the 20 years of construction, assuming 300 working days a year, the total work output of the workforce would be about 6,000 days times 12 megawatt-hours, or 72,000 megawatt-hours. Compare that with the 590 megawatt-hours needed to lift the stone: the lifting was less than one percent of the total labor capacity of the workforce.

Where did the other 99 percent go? Several places.

• Quarrying. Cutting 2.3 million blocks out of rock by hand,

with copper tools and pounders, is slow. Every cubic meter of stone removed takes many hours of labor.

• Dressing. Shaping blocks so that they fit, and dressing the

outer casing to a polished face, was labor-intensive, particularly the casing.

• Hauling on the level. Pulling blocks across sand and up the

ramps, against friction, takes far more energy than the lifting itself, as we calculate below.

• Boats and rope. Building, loading, rowing, and unloading

ships, and making rope.

• Building and removing ramps. The ramps themselves

were enormous heaps of material that had to be built, raised, and then taken away.

• Support work. Brewing, baking, farming, carrying water,

making tools, keeping records, and managing the settlement.

• Idle time and rest. Even the best-organized workforce has

downtime, sick days, and festivals.

Step 5: The cost of friction

To see how friction dominates, we need to calculate the work done in dragging blocks. Take the average block, 2.5 tonnes, dragged across level wet sand at a friction coefficient of about 0.25. The force is 0.25 × 2,500 × 9.81, or about 6,100 newtons. Work equals force times distance. If the average block was dragged 500 meters on the level between the quarry, the harbor, and the foot of the pyramid, the energy is 6,100 N × 500 m, or about 3 million joules per block.

For 2.3 million blocks, the total is about 7 × 10¹² joules. That is more than three times the lifting energy. If we add the work of dragging blocks up ramps, where friction and lifting are combined and the sledge has to travel a longer distance than the vertical rise, the total frictional work grows again.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Friction versus lifting. Lifting: 2.1 × 10¹² J. Hauling 500 meters on the level at a friction coefficient of 0.25: 2.3 × 10⁶ blocks × 3.1 × 10⁶ J ≈ 7.0 × 10¹² J. Hauling up ramps at a 1-in-8 slope adds friction over the ramp length, perhaps another 3 to 5 × 10¹² J. Total hauling energy is therefore several times the lifting energy. If the sand was dry, with a friction coefficient of about 0.5, the hauling energy would double. Wetting the sand saved about half of it.

This calculation shows why wetting the sand mattered so much. The saving of several trillion joules, achieved with a few jars of water, is one of the most cost-effective innovations in the history of construction. It also shows why the Egyptians built harbors near the pyramid and why they chose a quarry next door: every extra 100 meters of hauling added hundreds of billions of joules.

Step 6: Feeding the workforce

The work had to be paid for in food. At 3,500 kilocalories per person per day, a workforce of 20,000 needs about 70 million kilocalories per day. Barley, the main cereal, contains about 3,300 kilocalories per kilogram (as flour or grain). That means about 21 tonnes of grain per day, or about 7,700 tonnes a year. Of course, the Egyptian diet was not all barley. Some of the calories came from emmer wheat bread, beer, fish, meat, vegetables, and fruit. But the order of magnitude is what matters.

Over the 20 years of the project, the workforce would consume about 155,000 tonnes of grain, or the equivalent. This

sounds enormous, but it needs to be seen against the productivity of the Nile Valley. Egyptian farmland in a good year could produce on the order of a tonne of grain per hectare, and the cultivated area of the Nile Valley and Delta was very large. The pyramid's food needs were well within the capacity of the country. The workers' food also did not come from nowhere: much of it would have been eaten at home had the workers not been drafted. The state's added cost was the extra food for the specialist and permanent workers, and the logistics of moving it.

The Giza settlement shows the process: bakeries with bread molds by the thousand, breweries, fish processing, and animal pens. The economics worked because Egypt had a taxation system that collected grain and a transport network, the Nile, that moved it cheaply.
