The totals do not match exactly, since most of the work in quarrying and dressing is hard to quantify. But the broad picture is clear. The labor force of 20,000 had enough capacity to do the work, with plenty of margin for every kind of inefficiency. A workforce of 5,000 would have been too small. A workforce of 100,000 would not have been needed. A figure in the range of 20,000 to 30,000, which is what archaeologists have estimated from the settlement and the logistics, matches the physics.

Comparisons

Sometimes it helps to compare the Great Pyramid with modern projects.

• The Hoover Dam used about 3.3 million cubic meters of

concrete, comparable to the pyramid's volume, and took about five years, with a workforce of up to 5,000 and heavy machinery.

• The Great Pyramid took about 20 years with muscle, ropes,

copper, and wood.

• A modern construction crane lifts a block of 2.5 tonnes to a

height of 100 meters in about a minute, using a few tens of kilowatts. A work gang of Egyptians took several hours to bring the same block up the pyramid.

The comparison is not to belittle the Egyptians but to show that the task was big, and that the time and workforce the Egyptians used were reasonable for their technology.

What the energy numbers do not say

It is also worth being clear about the limits of these calculations. • They do not prove how the pyramid was built. They only

show that a human workforce with simple technology had enough power to do it. The method has to be established by other evidence, such as the quarries, the tools, the logbooks, and the workers' town.

• They are not precise. Changing the friction coefficient, the

average haul distance, or the efficiency can shift the totals by a factor of two or more.

• They do not include the labor of the people who produced

the food and materials. A fuller account would add the farmers, herders, and boat crews.

Nonetheless, the basic conclusion is robust. The pyramid does not require any energy source other than human muscle, animal power, the river, and the sun. There is no energy deficit to be explained.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "No ancient civilization had enough power to build the pyramids, so they must have used another energy source." Fact: The mechanical work of lifting the Great Pyramid is about 590 megawatt-hours, less than 1 percent of the work that a 20,000-person workforce could do in 20 years. The big costs were friction, quarrying, and logistics, all of which the Egyptians managed with muscle power and good organization.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Lifting the Great Pyramid takes about 2 × 10¹² joules, or 590 MWh, equal to about 5 weeks of food for a 20,000-person crew. The real costs were friction, quarrying, dressing, and logistics, together amounting to more than 99 percent of the labor capacity. Wetting sand halved hauling effort. Feeding the workers needed about 21 tonnes of grain a day, well within Egypt's means. The numbers match archaeological estimates for the workforce size.

CHAPTER 15

Inside the Great Pyramid: Shafts, Voids, and Hidden Doors

What is known about the interior's mysteries, from the star shafts to the cosmic-ray discoveries of the last decade.

Chapter 5 gave a tour of the Great Pyramid's main passages and chambers. This chapter takes up the parts that have generated the most speculation: the narrow shafts, the doors in the Queen's Chamber, the relieving chambers, and the new voids revealed by modern scanning. This is the frontier of pyramid research, and it is a place where careful science and enthusiastic speculation often meet.

The four shafts

The Great Pyramid has four narrow shafts, two leading out of the King's Chamber and two from the Queen's Chamber. They are roughly 20 centimeters across, square or nearly so, and they rise at angles through the masonry. They are unique among Old Kingdom pyramids, and nothing like them has been found elsewhere.

The King's Chamber shafts emerge at the pyramid's north and south faces. The northern one rises at about 31 degrees at first, then bends to avoid the Grand Gallery and continues at

about 32 degrees. The southern one rises at about 45 degrees. Both reach the outer surface of the pyramid, though the openings are now at a height that is not accessible without scaffolding. Their openings inside the chamber were noted by nineteenth-century visitors, and in the 1990s the shafts were explored with robots. A small fan was installed in the southern shaft in 1992 to circulate air in the chamber for visitors.

The Queen's Chamber shafts also run north and south, rising at about 39 degrees, but they never reach the surface. At their lower ends, the builders left the last few centimeters of stone in the chamber wall in place, so the shafts were invisible until Waynman Dixon and his team found them in 1872. Both were explored with robots, and each stops at a limestone slab or door.

The shafts are the subject of debate, and the debate has produced a number of ideas.

• Ventilation. An early assumption was that these were air

shafts, to ventilate the chambers. But the Queen's Chamber shafts were sealed and the chamber was never meant to be used by living people. This idea is generally rejected.

• Star alignment. In the 1960s, the astronomer Virginia

Trimble and the engineer Alexander Badawy noted that the shafts from the King's Chamber seem to have pointed at particular stars at the time of construction. Their analysis suggested that the southern King's Chamber shaft pointed at Orion's Belt (Al-Nitak), which was linked to Osiris, and the Queen's Chamber southern shaft pointed at Sirius, linked to Isis. The northern shaft of the King's Chamber was thought

to point to the region of the northern stars, including Thuban, the pole star of the time, or alternatively to the circumpolar stars. The northern Queen's Chamber shaft was thought to point to Kochab. This idea has been very popular.

• Ritual function. Another suggestion is that the shafts are

symbolic "passages" for the king's spirit, or ba, to leave the pyramid and join the stars. This reading fits the Pyramid Texts, which speak of the king ascending to the sky. In this view, the shafts need not be aimed at any specific star, only at the sky in general.

KEY POINT

The star-alignment theory is attractive, but it has weaknesses.

The shafts bend, the dating is uncertain, and the shafts at the Queen's Chamber were not open to the sky, so no one could see a star down them. It is possible that the builders aimed them toward general regions of the sky. The ritual interpretation does not require that stars be seen.

The Queen's Chamber doors

The Queen's Chamber shafts have been explored three times with robots, and each time produced a new surprise.

In 1993, the German engineer Rudolf Gantenbrink sent a small tracked robot called Upuaut 2 up the southern shaft. About 65 meters along, the robot found a small slab of limestone blocking the shaft, with two copper fittings that look like

handles. This was the first "door." The finding made headlines worldwide, and gave rise to expectations of a hidden chamber behind it.

In 2002, a National Geographic team led by Zahi Hawass sent a more advanced robot, the Pyramid Rover, to the same spot. It drilled a small hole through the first slab and pushed a camera through. Behind the slab was a small empty space, and then a second slab, similar to the first. The second slab had no visible handles. The 2002 televised event was dramatic, but the result was inconclusive.

In 2011, an international team that included the roboticist Rob Richardson sent a more refined robot called Djedi with a flexible fiber-optic camera that could be threaded through the hole. The camera was able to look around the corner and into the space between the slabs. It also looked at the back of the first door and saw red painted marks, written in what look like hieratic or masons' marks, on the back of the first slab. It also showed that the space beyond the first door is a small cavity. The second door was not breached.

Some interpretation has been attempted, but there is no scholarly consensus. The most common view is that the doors are symbolic: a representation of a gate through which the king's spirit would pass. Some propose that the slab is a stopper, set in place to close the shaft and perhaps hide a small chamber. In the absence of more evidence, the question stays open. Researchers have proposed new robot missions, but the permit system is slow.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "A hidden chamber full of treasure has been found behind the doors in the Queen's Chamber shafts." Fact: Behind the first door is a small empty cavity and a second door. No chamber has been entered, and no one has seen anything behind the second door.

The relieving chambers and Vyse

Above the King's Chamber there are five relieving chambers, between the ceiling beams and the apex of the structure. The lowest is called Davison's Chamber, after Nathaniel Davison, a British consul who found it in 1765 by crawling through a hole above the Grand Gallery. The other four were opened in 1837 by Colonel Howard Vyse and his engineer John Perring, who used gunpowder to blast his way upward through the ceiling stones. He was looking for hidden treasure and burial chambers. He found none.

What he did find were graffiti painted in red ocher on the stones of the topmost chambers, in places where no one ever expected them to be seen. They include the cartouches of Khufu, the names of work gangs, and various marks. Because these chambers had been sealed since construction, the graffiti are authentic marks from the time of building, and they are the best evidence for the pyramid's date.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: "Vyse forged the Khufu cartouches inside the pyramid." Fact: This claim was popularized by the author Zecharia Sitchin in 1980. But the paint inscriptions run across the joints between blocks and in places that Vyse could not have reached. Some are upside down or on the hidden faces of blocks that were placed before the chambers were formed. They match the style of Fourth Dynasty writing and gang names. Forgery would have required a level of Old Kingdom scholarship that did not exist in 1837, since hieroglyphs had been deciphered only in 1822. The marks are accepted as genuine by Egyptologists.

The subterranean chamber and the well

Beneath the pyramid, the unfinished Subterranean Chamber is a rough, irregular cavity cut in the bedrock, with a pit in the floor and a short dead-end passage. Its purpose is unclear. Some suggest that it was an early burial chamber, abandoned when the plan changed. Others suggest it was a symbolic tomb of Osiris. Its roughness suggests it was not completed.

Another feature is the Well Shaft, a narrow, irregular shaft connecting the lower end of the Grand Gallery to the Descending Passage. It is thought to have been an escape route for workmen who sealed the Ascending Passage's granite plugs. After lowering the plugs, the workers could have exited by the shaft, rather than being trapped inside. That is an engineering explanation, and is generally accepted.

ScanPyramids: using particles to see inside

For two centuries, explorers entered the Great Pyramid with ropes and candles. In the twenty-first century, they use particles from outer space. In 2015, an international project called Scan- Pyramids, involving Egyptian, French, and Japanese researchers, began using non-invasive technologies to look inside the pyramids without drilling. The methods included:

• Muon tomography. Muons are particles created when cos-

mic rays strike the upper atmosphere. They rain down in huge numbers and can pass through hundreds of meters of rock. Detectors placed inside or around the pyramid record how many muons arrive from each direction. Where there is a void, more muons arrive; where there is dense rock, fewer. Over weeks and months of exposure, a detector builds up an image of density, like a cosmic X-ray.

• Infrared thermography. Thermal cameras can detect small

temperature differences on the surface, which may point to hidden structures.

• Ground-penetrating radar and micro-gravimetry. These

detect differences in density and electrical properties.

The first results appeared quickly. In 2016, the team found a thermal anomaly on the east face of the Great Pyramid, in the stones at the base. In 2017, they announced a much bigger discovery, which they published in the journal Nature: a large void in the pyramid, above the Grand Gallery.

The Big Void

The Big Void, announced in November 2017, is a cavity at least 30 meters long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery. It lies above the Grand Gallery, at about the same slope, and it was detected by three independent muon detection techniques, using different detector types in different locations. It was the first major discovery inside the Great Pyramid since the nineteenth century.

What is it? No one knows. Scientists have made several suggestions.

• A second gallery, possibly a construction feature, built to re-

lieve the weight on the Grand Gallery.

• A building-ramp remnant or an internal construction space.

• A chamber, empty or filled with something.

The void has not been entered. In 2023, the team announced a further step: they inserted a small endoscope through a joint in the pyramid's masonry, and imaged the interior of another structure, discussed below. The Big Void remains unexplored, and its meaning is still being debated.

KEY POINT

The Big Void shows that even after 4,500 years, the Great Pyramid still holds surprises. But the discovery of a void does not imply a hidden treasure room or burial chamber. Large pyramids contain many structural voids, such as relieving chambers and construction spaces.

The north-face corridor

The 2016 scans also detected a void behind the pyramid's north face, above the original entrance, at the place where large gabled stones form a chevron structure. In 2023, the team drilled a tiny hole, about six millimeters wide, through a joint between the stones, and inserted a flexible endoscope. The camera revealed a corridor, about nine meters long and about two meters wide, with a gabled ceiling, behind the chevron stones. The walls were roughly finished. It is a sealed passage that was not known to exist.

The team's interpretation was that the corridor was built to relieve the load on the entrance passage, which sits beneath the chevron. It runs along the same plane. It is a structural feature, not a burial chamber. It could also be an access route to something else. At the end of the corridor, a large block was seen, which may conceal a continuation.

The corridor is considered a clear example of the way new technology can add detail to the pyramid's design without damaging the monument. It also raises a question: if there is a corridor that has been invisible for 4,500 years, what else is there?

Reading the interior

The interior of the Great Pyramid is a record of a design in flux. The plans seem to have changed as the work went on. The Subterranean Chamber, the Queen's Chamber, and the King's Chamber, with their different degrees of finish, show the building plan being revised upward. The shafts, the relieving chambers, and the Grand Gallery are all adapted to weight management. The newly discovered voids are consistent with an elaborate set of structural and perhaps ritual features. None of them requires an explanation beyond ancient Egyptian engineering and belief.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The Great Pyramid's shafts probably served a ritual purpose, possibly linked to stars. Robots have found small doors at the end of the Queen's Chamber shafts, but nothing beyond the second door has been seen. The relieving chambers contain authentic Fourth Dynasty graffiti, including Khufu's name. In 2017, ScanPyramids found the Big Void above the Grand Gallery, and in 2023, a corridor behind the north face. Neither has been entered, and neither implies a treasure room.

Interlude: A Day on the Plateau

An imagined reconstruction of one working day during the building of the Great Pyramid, with every detail tied to the evidence.

Before we turn from how the pyramids were built to what they meant, it is worth pausing to put the evidence together into a picture. This interlude is a work of reconstruction. The characters in it are invented, apart from one, Merer, the boat foreman whose logbook has survived. The day itself is imagined. But each detail is drawn from something archaeologists have found, and at the end of the chapter a table shows where each one comes from. Think of it as a way of testing the evidence: if the pieces fit together into a believable day, we are probably on the right track.

Before dawn

It is the season of the inundation. The Nile is high, and the fields of the valley are under water, glinting like a long, flat mirror in the faint light. On the desert edge, on the ridge above, the great pyramid is a pale mass against the stars, with its lowest courses sheathed in white and its upper steps still raw. Below the plateau, in the long low streets of the workers' town, the first smoke is rising.

Nakht, a baker, has been awake since the middle of the night. He tends a row of ovens at the edge of the settlement, where clay molds shaped like tall bells are stacked in the embers. He fills each with dough, a mixture of emmer wheat flour and water, and lets the bread bake in the heat. By the time the sky turns grey, there are hundreds of loaves, flat on one side and round on the other, with a dense, slightly sour crumb. Beside the bakery is the brewery, where Nakht's cousin stirs vats of mashed barley and bread dough, which will ferment into beer. It is a thick, nourishing, low-alcohol drink, closer to a liquid meal than to the beer of today. Neither product is a luxury. Together they make up the main part of a worker's pay.

Farther down the street, a butcher is already at work. A steer has been brought in from the royal estates in the Delta, and the meat will be divided among the work gangs. The town's refuse heaps, which archaeologists would one day dig through, are full of the bones of cattle, sheep, and goats, along with the remains of fish from the Nile. The workers of the pyramid eat better than the average farmer of the valley.

The gang assembles

As the light grows, men begin to gather in the lanes between the long galleries where they sleep. These are the work gangs. Each has a name, and the name is a point of pride: the men of one crew call themselves "Friends of Khufu," another "Followers of Khufu," or by a more playful name. The gang is divided into smaller parties, each with its own leader and its own mark, which will be painted on the blocks it moves. The marks are practical, so that the supervisors can tell which crew did what. They are also a way of claiming credit.

The foreman of this gang is called Senu. He is not a farmer but a permanent member of the project's staff, a skilled man who has been on the plateau for years. Most of the men in his gang are different: they are farmers from the villages of the Delta and the Nile valley, called up for a period of service during the weeks when their fields lie under water. They have come with their rations of bread and beer, and with bundles of clothing. They will work here for a stretch of months and then go home to plant their fields as the flood recedes. Others will take their places. The system gives the state a huge labor force and gives the farmers a task for the idle season, and in a society that has no money, labor is a form of tax.

Senu counts his men, and a scribe beside him enters the numbers on a sheet of papyrus. Each worker will receive a ration at the end of the day. The scribe's list is the foundation of the project: it tells the granaries how much grain to release, and it tells the overseers who is present.

At the quarry

The plateau itself is the quarry for the main body of the pyramid. A short walk from the base of the monument, a long gash has been cut into the rock, and there the stonecutters are at work. They are skilled men who have spent years learning to read the grain of the limestone. One of them, a veteran named Ipi, uses a copper chisel and a wooden mallet to cut a channel around a block. He works slowly and carefully, tapping, checking, tapping again. Then he drives wooden wedges into slots at the base of the block and wets them with water. As the wood swells, the stone cracks along the line he has prepared. A team of men, using wooden levers, edge it free.

The block weighs about two and a half tonnes. It is not a perfect cube. It is a rough, squarish mass, with edges that will be trimmed at the building site to fit its neighbors. Ipi paints a mark on its side with red ochre: the name of his gang and a number that will tell the masons where it belongs.

Copper chisels dull quickly, and a boy runs back and forth between the quarry and a nearby workshop, where a smith sharpens them, hammers them back into shape, and sometimes casts new ones. At the edge of the quarry lies a heap of limestone chips, a kind of waste that will be used to level the courses of the pyramid or to fill the spaces between blocks.

Dragging the stone

Once a block has been cut, it is levered onto a wooden sledge, a simple runner-based frame made from imported cedar or from local timber, and lashed in place with ropes. A team of a dozen or two men takes hold of the ropes. In front of the sledge, a man crouches with a jar of water and pours a thin stream onto the sand. The sand darkens. It will pack more firmly, and the sledge will glide more easily. Modern experiments have shown that sand wetted to the right degree can halve the force needed to pull a sledge. A scene in a tomb painting from a later period, in which a man pours water in front of a giant statue on a sledge, shows that the Egyptians knew the trick.

The men chant to keep time. A foreman walks beside them, calling out directions. Ahead of them runs a prepared track of packed gravel and mud, which has been laid with care, and in places lined with wooden beams. At the foot of the pyramid, the track turns into a ramp. The ramp is made of rubble, mud brick, and clay, and it climbs against the side of the monument. As the pyramid rises, the ramp is extended.

A short distance away, at a different quarry, a different gang is moving a different kind of block. These are the casing stones, which will form the smooth outer surface of the pyramid. They are cut from the fine white limestone of Tura, across the river, and they arrive by boat. Each is carefully dressed on its face and its sides, so that it will fit snugly against its neighbors, with a joint no wider than a fingernail.

The boat from Tura

By mid-morning, a fleet of boats approaches the harbor at the foot of the plateau. At the head of one of them stands a man with a roll of papyrus in his hand: Merer, an inspector in charge of a crew of about forty men. He has been traveling with his boat for several days, loading limestone at Tura and delivering it to the harbor at Giza, then returning for another load. He keeps a daily record of the journey, noting when his crew sets out, where they spend the night, and when they arrive. Some of the entries are dry and brief. Others mention the name of the high official who oversees the harbor, a royal prince, and the name of the monument for which the stone is intended: Akhet-Khufu, "the Horizon of Khufu."

Merer and his crew tie up the boats at the edge of the basin. The stones are unloaded onto sledges, and another scribe checks the delivery against a list. Merer receives his rations and an acknowledgment. His boats will head back across the river by afternoon, rowing against the current of the flood or sailing with the north wind behind them. It is a routine job, and Merer does not know that his log will survive for four and a half thousand years in a sealed gallery beside the Red Sea, or that his words will be the key to understanding how this monument was built.

The noon heat

By noon the sun is fierce, and the stone is hot to the touch. The work slows. In the shade of a long, low shed, men sit with their backs against the wall and share bread and beer. Some eat onions and a little dried fish. An overseer walks through, speaking to the foremen. The day's work is on schedule.

One of Ipi's apprentices has cut his hand on a flake of stone, and a medic dresses the wound with honey, linen, and a poultice. The skeletons from the workers' cemeteries show that injuries were common, including broken bones, crushed limbs, and the wear of heavy labor, and some of those injuries healed, a sign that the injured received treatment and time to recover. The project has a small medical staff, and a man who cannot work is taken care of. That is not charity: a worker lost is a skill lost.

At the edge of the shed, a priest of Khufu's cult offers a few words and a libation to the god of the workers. The pyramid is a sacred project as well as a practical one. Everyone who works on it takes part in the king's passage to eternity, and the king is a god. The labor is a service as well as a duty.

At the pyramid

In the afternoon, the masons are at the foot of the monument. Here the blocks are set. A gang of men on the lower courses guides each stone into position with levers and wooden rockers, nudging it a few fingers at a time. A mason checks the line with a taut cord, a plumb bob, and a wooden set-square. A thin layer of gypsum mortar, made from burnt and ground gypsum, is spread between the blocks to act as a lubricant while the stone is shifted, and as a filler once it is in place. Higher up, men work on the ramp, hauling the stones to the upper levels.

On the rising structure, the builders have marked the center lines and the corners with ink and chisel. The base was laid out in the earliest stage with great care, using the stars or the shadows of the sun to find true north, and a network of channels filled with water to establish a level. The accuracy they achieved is such that even today, nearly forty-six centuries later, the four sides of the pyramid still point nearly exactly to the compass points.

In one of the chambers inside, a team is setting the last of the stones that will form the roof of a room. Here and there, on the blocks that will soon be hidden forever, they paint the names of their gangs. The paint will survive undisturbed in the dark for thousands of years, until a nineteenth-century explorer, with a crowbar and gunpowder, breaks into the space and reads them.

The end of the day

As the sun sinks, the work stops. The gangs return to the town in the long evening light, tired and covered in dust. The ovens are lit again. At the doors of the galleries, the rations are handed out: loaves of bread, jugs of beer, meat, onions, perhaps a few figs or dates. The men eat and talk. Some play a board game, in a corner of a courtyard, with pieces of clay or stone. A few of them go to a small chapel, where they leave a loaf of bread for the spirit of a colleague who died of a fall some weeks before and is buried in the cemetery on the hill above the town.

That cemetery lies in the shadow of the pyramid itself. The tombs of the workers are small but carefully built, of mud brick and stone, some with a little pyramid shape on top, with a chamber below. Inside are jars of beer and loaves of bread, set beside the body for the journey to the next life. A few of the tombs carry inscriptions naming the owner and his title. The people who built the pyramid were permitted, in a modest way, to share in the same hope that the king enjoyed. They were buried within sight of his monument, as members of his household.

Night falls. Across the settlement, the lamps are lit, and the smell of baking bread and woodsmoke drifts over the roofs. On the plateau above, the half-built pyramid is a silhouette against the stars. It will take another decade of days like this one to finish it.

The Pyramid Complex: Temples, Causeways, Boats, and Priests

The pyramid was the center of a machine for eternity, and a town that kept it running for centuries.

When people picture a pyramid, they usually picture a lone triangle in the sand. Egyptians would not have recognized the picture. For them, the pyramid was one part of a complex, a set of buildings with different functions that together formed the royal tomb. The complex reached from the desert plateau to the edge of the farmland, and it was supported by a community that lived and worked beside it. Understanding the complex is the best way to understand what the pyramid was for.

The standard plan

By the time of the Fourth Dynasty, a standard layout had developed. It is clearest at Giza, in the complexes of Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure, and it was repeated, with variations, for the next several centuries. The parts, in order from the river to the burial, were as follows.

Not every complex had every feature, and some elements are missing from some sites. But the general logic was consistent, and the overall plan stayed fairly stable for a thousand years.

The valley temple

The valley temple stood at the bottom of the causeway, close to the edge of the cultivated land and the harbor. It was the formal entrance. When the king died, his body was brought by boat to the valley temple, where it underwent final rites of purification before the funeral procession. The building was also the start of the daily ritual cycle: offerings were presented there and carried up the causeway to the pyramid.

The best-preserved valley temple is Khafre's, built of massive limestone blocks cased in red granite, with a floor of alabaster. We saw in Chapter 6 how its pillared hall once held about twenty-three statues of the king. Other valley temples have been lost or are buried under modern buildings. Khufu's valley temple, for example, is thought to lie under the village of Nazlet el-Sissan, at the foot of the plateau, and has been only partly investigated.

The causeway

The causeway was a long ramp, running for hundreds of meters from the valley temple up the plateau to the pyramid. In Khufu's case, it was about 700 meters long, and in Unas's, 750. The causeways were often roofed and walled, giving them the appearance of a long corridor, with a narrow slit in the roof to let in light. The walls were covered in painted relief carvings.

The Fifth Dynasty causeway of Unas at Saqqara preserves some of the most informative reliefs. They show scenes of the transport of granite columns by boat, of craftsmen at work, of

foreign trade expeditions, and, famously, of people suffering from hunger. This last scene, which shows emaciated figures, has been interpreted as a reference to famine in the region. It is rare to find such a depiction of hardship in a royal monument, and it indicates that artists of this period could depict harsher realities.

The causeway also served the logistics of construction. While the pyramid was being built, the causeway may have been used as a haul road. Some researchers think that it was partly a ramp, serving first for construction and then, after the pyramid was complete, as the processional way.

The mortuary temple

On the east side of the pyramid, facing the rising sun, stood the mortuary temple. It was the place where, day by day, the king's spirit was fed. In the earliest pyramids of the Fourth Dynasty, the temple was a modest structure, but by the Fifth Dynasty, it had developed into an elaborate building, with an entrance hall, a pillared courtyard, five niches for statues of the king, storerooms, and an inner sanctuary with a false door facing the pyramid.

The false door was a carved panel that represented a door between the world of the living and the realm of the dead. The king's ka was thought to pass through it to receive offerings of food, drink, linen, and incense. Offerings were laid on a stone altar in front of the door. The reliefs on the temple walls depict processions of estates bringing produce, rituals, and scenes of the king with the gods.

Khufu's mortuary temple has almost entirely disappeared. What remains is a basalt pavement, 4,600 years old, one of the earliest uses of this stone in monumental architecture. The basalt came from a quarry at Widan el-Faras, and its transport, noted in the last chapter, was a considerable effort. The scale of the black pavement, still visible on the east side of the pyramid, gives a sense of how much expense was lavished on the temple.

The boat pits

Around the Great Pyramid, five rock-cut pits were found. Three were along the east side and two along the south. Some were originally covered with limestone slabs. Those on the south side were opened in 1954 and 1987, as described in Chapter 5, and they contained the disassembled boats of cedar wood. The pits on the east side were empty.

The purpose of the boats is debated. A traditional view is that these were "solar boats," intended for the king's voyage with the sun god through the heavens, an idea that fits the Pyramid Texts, which describe the dead king sailing with Ra. Another is that they were boats actually used in the funeral, carrying the body of the king from the capital to the valley temple, and then buried afterward, as the king's ships for eternity. Evidence from the first ship supports this second idea in part: examination showed signs of wear and traces of water, suggesting that it had been used, and the ropes found with it were worn. It may have been both. A boat used in the funeral procession was then buried as a vehicle for the afterlife. Boat pits have also been found at the pyramids of Khafre, Djedefre, and others.

The cult pyramid and queens' pyramids

Beside each Giza pyramid stands a small subsidiary pyramid. Egyptologists call it a satellite pyramid or cult pyramid. Khufu's stands at the southeastern corner. It has a short passage and a small chamber, but no burial. Its purpose is still debated. Theories include a tomb for the king's ka, a symbolic southern tomb that balanced the main northern tomb, or a place for ritual, such as for the reburial of the king's ritual regalia.

The pyramids of the queens, three in Khufu's case, stand in a row to the east. They housed the burial of royal women. It is thought that the three belong to important wives or mothers of Khufu, but we do not know who they were. In one of them, G1-a, excavators found a shaft containing the empty sarcophagus and funerary equipment of Queen Hetepheres I, which we met in Chapter 5, though it was in a shaft some distance away. Another small tomb is identified as the tomb of Meresankh III, a granddaughter of Khufu, whose tomb, decorated with colored reliefs and a row of statues of women, was found nearby in the 1920s.

Who served the pyramid?

A pyramid complex needed staff. Every day, offerings had to be prepared and presented, the buildings cleaned, supplies delivered, and records kept. The staff were organized into a cult, with priests and attendants, and supported by endowments.

Priests held titles such as hem-netjer, "servant of the god," and wab, "pure one." Most were part-time, working in rotating

groups, and most also held jobs outside the temple. The Abusir papyri give detailed rosters of duty, and show that priests were organized into five groups, each serving one month in turn. A priest might work one month in five, and spend the rest of the year in other occupations, such as farming, trade, or administration. They were paid in the goods that passed through the temple: bread, beer, meat, and linen.

The system was an elegant solution. Once the king died, the offerings placed before his statues were not wasted. After the gods and the dead king had received their share, in a ritual sense, the food was passed on to the priests and officials. This is called the reversion of offerings. It meant that the temple served as a distribution center, and the staff could live from the produce of the king's estates.

It is a remarkable document, which shows that the king's cult was still active 300 years after his death.

These towns show that a pyramid complex was not a dead monument but an institution that lasted. In some cases, they lasted for centuries, and a king who had died hundreds of years before was still being served. The state had committed itself, in a legal sense, to supporting the royal cult, and it recorded the obligation in endowments of land and tax exemptions.

The cemetery of the court

The pyramid complex was also the center of a larger necropolis. Around the Great Pyramid, the tombs of princes, officials, and priests were laid out in orderly rows, called the Eastern Field, Western Field, and Southern Field. The mastabas were close to the king, in the hope of sharing in his afterlife. Many of the tombs have decorated chapels that tell us about the titles and duties of the people buried there: overseers of the king's works, scribes, priests, physicians, and craftsmen.

The idea of burying one's most important officials near the king was part of the way that the royal court operated. In life, they served him, and in death, they would continue to serve. At Giza, the plan of the cemetery reflects the hierarchy of the living court. The highest-ranking people were closest to the pyramid.

KEY POINT

The pyramid complex was a place of continuing ritual. The king was not simply buried and forgotten. Offerings were made every day, by priests who lived nearby, for as long as the cult lasted. In some cases, the cult of a king survived for more than a thousand years.

What the complex tells us about purpose

Taken together, the elements of the complex give strong evidence for the purpose of the pyramid. A monument that was only a landmark or an observatory would not need a harbor, a causeway, a temple with a false door, an altar, storerooms, and priests. A building that was a power plant or a machine would not need statues of the king, offering lists, and a cult that fed his spirit. The complex only makes sense as a system for the burial and eternal maintenance of a dead king.

The absence of a body in the Great Pyramid does not alter that conclusion. The Egyptians built the system as a whole, and the Great Pyramid, with its harbor, temples, boat pits, queens' pyramids, and cemetery, was built as part of it.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

A pyramid was one part of a complex that included a valley temple, causeway, mortuary temple, cult pyramid, and often boat pits. It was staffed by part-time priests and supported by endowments and pyramid towns. Royal decrees show that cults continued for centuries. The complex is strong evidence that the pyramid was a tomb, and that the king's spirit was supported by daily offerings.
