Burial and the Afterlife: Mummies, Spells, and the King's Journey

What the Egyptians did with a dead king, what they believed would happen next, and why no one has found Khufu.

If the pyramid was a machine for eternity, what did it do to the person inside? To answer that, we need to look at the Egyptians' own descriptions of the process. They are among the oldest texts about the afterlife in the world, written on the walls of the pyramids themselves. We can combine them with evidence from tombs, mummies, and later texts to reconstruct, with some caution, what happened to a king at his death.

From death to burial: the funeral

When a king died, his body was taken to the embalmers. The Egyptian word for the process, which we call mummification, has a rich vocabulary, and the practice changed over time. By the New Kingdom, the full process took seventy days. In the Old Kingdom, the practice was less developed, but already included removing the internal organs, drying the body with natron, a natural salt from desert lakes, and wrapping it in linen.

The evidence for early mummification is slim. The earliest known sign that organs were removed from a royal body comes

from the tomb of Queen Hetepheres I, Khufu's mother, where a chest held her internal organs, preserved in a solution of natron. This dates to about 2600 BCE. The chest is the oldest known evidence of evisceration for a royal burial. For the first pyramid-age kings, most of what we know about mummification comes from the later periods, which are better preserved.

The body of the king was then taken in a procession, probably by boat, from the royal residence to the valley temple at Giza. There it was purified, and the final rituals were performed in a special tent. A procession went up the causeway to the pyramid, with priests, mourners, and officials, carrying the body, burial goods, and statues. In the burial chamber, the body was placed in the stone sarcophagus, and the lid, if there was one, was closed.

One of the key rituals was the Opening of the Mouth, a ceremony performed on the mummy and on the statues of the king by priests using special tools, including an adze and a ritual implement shaped like a snake's tail. It was meant to restore the senses and abilities of the dead king, allowing him to breathe, eat, speak, and see in the afterlife. We know it from later periods in detail, and we know that its origins go back to the Old Kingdom. After the ritual, the burial chamber was sealed, the passages were closed by heavy stone plugs, and the funeral party left.

What went into the tomb

The grave goods of an Old Kingdom king are poorly known because every one of the royal burial chambers was robbed. But the tomb of Hetepheres gives a sample. When the American archaeologist George Reisner found it in 1925, in a deep shaft near the Great Pyramid, it contained gilded furniture: a bed with a headrest, a carrying chair, a canopy frame covered in gold leaf, boxes, and bracelets of silver inlaid with turquoise, carnelian, and lapis lazuli. The furniture had collapsed because the wooden parts had rotted, but the gold sheathing and inlays were intact. It took Reisner's team years to reconstruct the pieces. The set shows the quality of what a queen, and probably a king, took into the tomb.

A king would have been buried with similar objects on a larger scale: furniture, jewelry, statues, weapons, tools, ritual objects, and vast quantities of food and drink. Stone vessels, in the tens of thousands, filled the galleries of the Step Pyramid. The idea was to provide the dead king with everything he needed in the afterlife, and to provide him with the symbols of his status. In some cases, objects were also placed in boat pits, as we have seen.

Another feature was the canopic equipment: containers for the internal organs. The embalmers removed the stomach, liver, lungs, and intestines and stored them in four jars or compartments, each protected by a guardian deity. Hetepheres's chest has four compartments. In later periods, the jars had lids in the shape of the heads of the four sons of Horus.

The Pyramid Texts

The most important evidence for royal afterlife beliefs comes from the Pyramid Texts, mentioned in Chapter 7. They were carved on the walls of the burial chambers and corridors of the pyramids from Unas (about 2350 BCE) onward. The first complete set, in the pyramid of Unas, has about 283 spells. When all of the pyramids are counted, there are around 800 different spells, called utterances, though no single pyramid has them all.

The spells are not a continuous story. They are a collection of ritual speeches, recited by priests at the burial and presumably during the continuing cult. They have several kinds of content.

• Offering ritual. Spells that accompany the presentation of

food and drink, with lists of items: bread, beer, meat, fowl, fruit, incense, linen.

• Protection. Charms against snakes, scorpions, and hostile

spirits that might threaten the king.

• Resurrection. Spells that reassemble the king's body, iden-

tify each limb with a god, and call on him to rise.

• Ascent. Spells that describe the king's journey to the sky.

He climbs a ladder or stairway, crosses the heavens by boat, or flies as a bird, a falcon, or a beetle. He is welcomed by the gods and takes his place among the stars.

• Identification. Spells that identify the king with a god: with

Osiris, with Horus, or with Ra.

The language is archaic, compressed, and hard to translate. It is sometimes lyrical and sometimes violent. One of the most famous sections, called the Cannibal Hymn, found in the pyramid of Unas, describes the king as a hunter who captures and eats the gods, absorbing their powers into his own body. It is an unusual passage and has been interpreted as a metaphor for taking on divine energy. This and other spells show an older, more archaic layer of religious thought than the later, more familiar ideas of the afterlife.

KEY POINT

The Pyramid Texts do not describe the pyramid as a power plant, a machine, or an astronomical instrument. They describe it as the place where the king is resurrected and from which he ascends to join the gods. This is the Egyptians' own explanation, written in stone, two and a half thousand years before the Greeks first described the pyramids.

The journey

The picture that emerges is of a journey in several stages. First, the king's body is purified, reassembled, and animated. His ka, the life-force, is nourished by offerings, and his ba, the personality, is freed to move. Then the king rises. He may do this by ascending the sun's rays, by flying as a bird, or by climbing a stairway built for him. In the sky, he meets Ra and joins the sun god's boat, traveling across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. He also joins the imperishable stars, the circumpolar stars that never set, taking his place among the eternal.

At the same time, he is identified with Osiris, the dead god, and he rules the land of the dead. These overlapping paths were not seen as contradictory. For the Egyptians, the afterlife was multi-layered, and the king might exist in several forms.

In the New Kingdom, these ideas expanded to include the Book of the Dead, with its famous scene of the weighing of the heart against the feather of Maat. That judgment scene does not appear in the Pyramid Texts. In the Old Kingdom, the afterlife was primarily a royal matter. Over the course of the First Intermediate Period, the ideas spread to nobles and ordinary people, and a set of spells called the Coffin Texts was written on coffins. This process, sometimes called the democratization of the afterlife, made the promise of eternal life available to everyone who could afford a coffin. Later, it could be purchased on a papyrus roll.

Where is Khufu?

All of this brings us to the problem mentioned in the preface. No body has been found in any Fourth Dynasty pyramid. The sarcophagus in the Great Pyramid is empty, with no lid. The Red Pyramid had fragments of a body, and Menkaure's pyramid held bones of a later date. For Khufu, we have nothing. Has the king vanished?

There are several possibilities, and the most likely is the simplest: the burial was robbed. The Egyptians' own records show that tomb robbery was a problem from the Old Kingdom. In the chaos of the First Intermediate Period, around 2181 BCE, many royal tombs may have been plundered. A thief who found a

mummy of a king wrapped in linen and gold amulets would strip the body, destroy it, or discard it.

A second possibility is that the priests moved the body. We know the Egyptians did this in later periods. In the New Kingdom, when the tombs of the Valley of the Kings were robbed, priests collected the mummies of the kings and hid them in a few safe places. In 1881, a cache of more than 40 royal mummies, including Ramesses II, Seti I, and Thutmose III, was found in a hidden tomb at Deir el-Bahari. Perhaps something similar happened to Khufu, and his mummy was reburied elsewhere, and perhaps lost.

A third possibility is that the Great Pyramid was not the actual burial place of the king, and that his body was buried elsewhere, with the pyramid as a symbolic monument. This idea has long been popular, but there is no evidence for it. The sarcophagus, the sealed passages, the granite plugs, the burial-sized chamber, the funerary complex, and the fact that every other pyramid-age king was buried in his pyramid all point in the opposite direction.

KEY POINT

The absence of Khufu's body is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Thieves, priests, and time all work against the survival of a 4,500-year-old burial. Most Egyptologists consider the Great Pyramid to have been Khufu's tomb, plundered long ago.

The afterlife and the pyramid's design

The ideas in the Pyramid Texts help to explain some of the design features of the Great Pyramid. The use of granite, a hard, dark stone, for the burial chamber, may have been linked with the king's eternal body and the imperishable stars. The orientation of the pyramid to the cardinal directions reflected the cosmos. The corbelled Grand Gallery may have represented the primeval hill or the heavenly path. The narrow shafts may have been paths for the king's ba, or soul, to leave the pyramid. And the sloping sides, as the Texts say, were a stairway to heaven. All the features are open to debate, but they are all consistent with the idea of a resurrection machine, not a machine in the physical sense but a symbolic and ritual one.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Royal bodies were mummified, placed in stone sarcophagi, and buried with goods, though no Fourth Dynasty royal burial has survived intact. The Pyramid Texts (from Unas, c. 2350 BCE) contain about 800 spells for offerings, protection, resurrection, and ascent. They describe the pyramid as the king's route to the sky and the underworld. Khufu's body was likely lost through robbery or removal, as with other royal mummies.

CHAPTER 18

Robbers, Restorers, and Rediscovery

Four and a half thousand years of visitors: thieves, tourists, scholars, and the people who finally learned to read the stones.

A pyramid built to last forever has, in practice, spent most of its life being visited. Within a few centuries of its completion, thieves found the way in. Within a thousand years, Egyptians themselves were repairing and studying the monuments. Greeks and Romans came as tourists, medieval builders stripped them for stone, and European explorers measured them, blasted into them, and carried pieces home. This chapter follows that long history, because it explains both what has been lost and how we know what we do.

Why the pyramids were robbed

Tomb robbery was not a modern invention. As soon as a king was buried with gold, jewelry, and fine furniture, he became a target. For the Egyptians, such crimes were not only theft but sacrilege, an attack on the king's afterlife, and the penalties were severe. But the temptation was great, and the knowledge needed to commit the crime was widely available. Workers, priests, and officials all knew where the treasure was and how to get in.

Pyramids were designed with this in mind. The sealed entrances, granite plugs, false passages, and heavy sarcophagus

lids were all intended to stop thieves. But even the best security failed when people had time. Most of the pyramids of the Old Kingdom appear to have been entered and plundered by the end of the Old Kingdom or in the First Intermediate Period. The Egyptians themselves seem to have known it. Later texts speak of tombs being laid bare and the dead being cast out, though these passages are literary and hard to use as evidence.

The robbery trials

Our best evidence for how tomb robbery worked comes from a later period. In about 1110 BCE, during the reign of Ramesses IX, Thebes was shaken by accusations that royal tombs on the west bank had been plundered. A commission of officials was sent to inspect the tombs, and the findings were recorded on papyri, such as the Abbott Papyrus and the Amherst Papyrus, now in the British Museum.

The commission inspected the tombs of the kings of the Seventeenth Dynasty, who had been buried in small brick pyramids at Dra Abu el-Naga. Some were found intact. One, the pyramid of King Sobekemsaf, was found to have been broken into. The thieves had confessed, giving a detailed account of how they tunneled into the pyramid, found the burial chamber, took the gold from the mummies, and burned the coffins. The confessions were obtained under torture, and some of the accused were later executed.

The papyri show that robbery was often an inside job, involving people who worked in the necropolis and could easily gain access. They also show corruption among officials. They

are valuable evidence that the problem of security was permanent, and that no design could solve it. The solution adopted by the priests of the Twenty-First Dynasty was to take the royal mummies out of their tombs and re-hide them in secret caches.

The prince who was the first Egyptologist

The Egyptians were conscious of their own past. About 1,000 years after the Great Pyramid was built, a New Kingdom prince named Khaemwaset, a son of Ramesses II, took the title of High Priest of Ptah at Memphis. He took an interest in the old monuments of the Memphite necropolis. He inspected the pyramids of Giza, Abusir, and Saqqara, found them in ruins, and ordered repairs. He had inscriptions carved on the pyramids of Unas, Userkaf, and others, stating that he had restored them and recording the name of the king to whom each belonged.

Khaemwaset is sometimes called the first Egyptologist, and the title seems fair. He was motivated by piety and by dynastic pride, wanting to show his father's devotion to the ancestors. He did not know as much about the pyramids as we do, but he understood that they belonged to ancient kings, and he took pains to record their names. His inscription on the pyramid of Unas is one of the oldest known acts of monument preservation.

Later in Egyptian history, the Twenty-Sixth Dynasty (c. 664–525 BCE), known as the Saite Period, consciously revived Old Kingdom art and religion, restoring cults and monuments. At Giza, a chapel was built near the Sphinx, and the cult of Khufu and Khafre was revived. People of the Late Period saw

the Great Pyramid as the work of a great ancestor, and honored him.

The Greeks and Romans

By the time the Greeks arrived, the pyramids were ancient. Herodotus visited around 450 BCE. His account, written in Book II of his Histories, is the first detailed description by an outsider. He described the Great Pyramid, giving its dimensions, and said that it was built by "Cheops" using forced labor. He also gave details that cannot be verified, such as an inscription on the pyramid that recorded the sum paid for radishes, onions, and garlic for the workers. He was told things by local guides, some of which were garbled, and his account should be read as a record of what people said in his time.

The pyramids became part of the Greek list of the Seven Wonders of the World. The list appeared in the second century BCE in a poem by Antipater of Sidon, and it included the Great Pyramid of Giza first. Of those wonders, it is the only one that has survived.

Later Greek and Roman writers visited and wrote about them. Diodorus Siculus, who visited around 60 BCE, gave the names of the builders and the story that they were not buried in the pyramids. Strabo, around 25 BCE, wrote that the Great Pyramid had a stone that could be moved, a hinged door that opened to a passage inside the pyramid. His description fits the original north entrance. Pliny the Elder wrote in the first century CE that the pyramids were useless displays of royal wealth. The Roman emperor Hadrian visited in 130 CE. Visitors

scratched their names on the stones, and some of these graffiti survive, in Greek and Latin. The Great Pyramid has been a tourist attraction for more than two thousand years.

The caliph's tunnel

By the Middle Ages, the entrance to the Great Pyramid had been lost. Its location was hidden by debris and by the pyramid's own casing. According to a tradition recorded by later Arab historians, in about 820 CE, the caliph Abdullah al-Ma'mun decided to enter the pyramid in search of treasure and knowledge. He had his workmen tunnel into the north face by heating the stone with fire, pouring on vinegar to crack it, and hammering with battering rams. After days of work, they heard something fall inside. It was a stone that had been hidden in the wall of a passage, and it revealed the Ascending Passage. The workmen, blocked by the granite plugs, tunneled around them and reached the upper chambers.

Inside, according to the story, they found an empty sarcophagus. A famous legend claims that the caliph's men salted the pyramid with just enough gold to cover the cost of the excavation, so that the caliph would not be embarrassed. This is a later embellishment, and we cannot say how much of the story is true. What is certain is that someone cut the tunnel, called the Robbers' Tunnel, through the masonry at about this time. It is still the way visitors enter the pyramid today.

Stripped for stone

During the Middle Ages, Cairo grew into a major city, and it needed stone. The pyramids' fine Tura limestone casings were a convenient source. Beginning in the tenth and eleventh centuries, and especially after an earthquake in 1303 that loosened the stones, builders dismantled the casing and reused it in mosques, palaces, and city walls. This is why the pyramids are now stepped, with the rough core exposed, and why some of the stones in the old city of Cairo bear traces of Fourth Dynasty cutting.

The Giza complex also lost its smaller monuments. The queens' pyramids, mortuary temples, and causeways were quarried heavily. In 1196, as we saw, the son of Saladin tried to demolish Menkaure's pyramid and gave up. In the nineteenth century, the Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali considered dismantling the pyramids for the stone to build the barrages on the Nile, but his engineers advised that it would cost more than quarrying new stone. The pyramids survived, partly because they were too big to destroy.

European travelers and early science

After the Renaissance, European scholars rediscovered the pyramids. In 1638–39, the English astronomer John Greaves traveled to Egypt, measured the Great Pyramid, and published Pyramidographia in 1646. He was one of the first to use scientific methods. A century later, in 1737, the Danish captain Frederic Norden made detailed drawings, including of the Sphinx without a nose, and in the 1760s, Nathaniel Davison found the chamber above the King's Chamber that bears his name.

In 1798, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt with an army and with a team of 167 scholars and artists, known as the savants. They surveyed the Giza plateau and other sites and produced the monumental Description de l'Égypte, published from 1809 to 1829. According to a report, before the Battle of the Pyramids, Napoleon told his soldiers that forty centuries looked down on them from the top of the pyramids. The line is probably an embellishment, but it captures the awe of the age. The savants also found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, which would allow Jean-François Champollion to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822, a key to everything that followed.

The age of explorers

In the early nineteenth century, a series of colorful figures explored the pyramids. The Genoese captain Giovanni Battista Caviglia cleared the Sphinx of sand in 1817 and explored the Great Pyramid's passages and the Well Shaft. The Italian Giovanni Belzoni, a strongman at a circus before he became an explorer, found the entrance to the pyramid of Khafre in 1818. The British officer Howard Vyse and engineer John Perring spent 1836–37 at Giza, using gunpowder and drills to find hidden chambers, as we have seen. They made a great deal of useful measurement but did much damage.

In the 1840s, the German scholar Karl Richard Lepsius led a Prussian expedition that mapped 67 pyramids along the Nile, creating a numbered list that scholars still use. The French archaeologist Auguste Mariette, who founded the Egyptian Antiquities Service in 1858, found Khafre's statues in 1860.

The age of scientific excavation

Modern archaeology of the pyramids begins with the British archaeologist Sir William Matthew Flinders Petrie, who surveyed Giza in 1880–82 and published The Pyramids and Temples of Gizeh in 1883. His measurements, made with great care, became the foundation for all later work. He also brought a principle that changed archaeology: pay attention to everything, including potsherds and everyday objects, not just treasures. He later excavated the pyramids of Meidum, Lahun, and Hawara.

In the early twentieth century, the American Egyptologist George Reisner led the Harvard–Boston expedition to Giza, from 1902 to 1942. He and his teams recorded and excavated the cemeteries, the queens' pyramids, and Menkaure's valley temple, and discovered the tomb of Hetepheres in 1925. The expedition's records, photographs, and field notes are still the basis of Giza research. The German scholar Ludwig Borchardt excavated the Fifth Dynasty pyramids at Abusir from 1902 to 1908, and the Egyptian archaeologists Selim Hassan and Ahmed Fakhry worked at Giza and Dahshur in the 1930s and 1950s. In 1954, Kamal el-Mallakh found Khufu's boat. The French architect Jean-Philippe Lauer worked for seven decades at Saqqara.

The modern era

Since the 1980s, research has changed in character. Mark Lehner, Zahi Hawass, and their teams have uncovered the workers' town and cemeteries, giving an unprecedented view of the people who built the pyramids. Pierre Tallet 's discovery of the Wadi al-Jarf papyri in 2013 gave us Merer's diary. Yannis Gourdon and Roland Enmarch found the ramp system at Hatnub. And since 2015, the ScanPyramids team has used cosmic rays, thermal imaging, and endoscopes to look inside the great monuments without harming them. The next chapters describe other sides of the modern study of the pyramids, including the myths that surround them.

KEY POINT

The history of pyramid research shows a steady shift from treasure-hunting to science, and from a few adventurers to teams of specialists. Each step, from the Rosetta Stone, to Petrie's careful measuring, to the muon detectors of today, has added evidence and eroded speculation.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

Pyramids were plundered from antiquity; Egyptian records of robbery trials survive. Prince Khaemwaset restored pyramids about 1250 BCE. Greek and Roman tourists wrote about them. Medieval Cairo stripped the casing. Explorers from Greaves to Vyse measured and sometimes damaged them. Petrie, Reisner, Lehner, Hawass, Tallet, and ScanPyramids transformed the study into a science.

PART 5

Myths, Mysteries, and Modern Science

Fair hearings for popular claims, and a look at the real frontier

CHAPTER 19

Machines, Chemicals, and the "Power Plant" Theory

Was the Great Pyramid a lost machine? What the claim says, where it came from, and how it holds up against the evidence.

Almost everyone who has looked at the Great Pyramid has felt the same pull. The thing is so large, so regular, and so precisely made that it does not feel like a tomb. It feels like equipment. A tomb is something you hide a body in. This looks like something that was supposed to do something.

That feeling is the seed of a family of ideas that treat the pyramids as machines: power plants, pumps, resonators, water-lifting devices, or generators of some unnamed force. This chapter takes those ideas seriously enough to describe them accurately, trace where they came from, and test them. Some are plain wrong. One, which looks like a machine theory at first glance, is an interesting engineering proposal about construction. And one piece of modern physics, which is often cited in support of the machine theories, turns out to say something much more modest than its popularizers claim.

Why machine theories feel natural

It helps to understand why these ideas are so persuasive before we try to answer them. Three things push people toward them.

The first is precision. As we saw in Chapter 9, the Great Pyramid's base is level to within a couple of centimeters over an area of more than five hectares, and its sides are aligned to the cardinal directions to within a small fraction of a degree. Precision on this scale is something modern readers associate with machine tools and lasers. It is natural to ask whether people with copper chisels could have achieved it, and if they could not, what else could have.

The second is the modern habit of reading old objects as technology. We live in a world where nearly every large structure has a function beyond itself: a dam holds back water, a tower broadcasts, a plant makes electricity. A giant structure that seems to do nothing invites a modern viewer to look for the hidden function.

The third is a quiet one. The people who built the pyramids left no engineering manuals. They left tomb inscriptions, offering lists, work-gang graffiti, and the logbook of a boat foreman, but no document saying "here is how we made the base level." The gap invites speculation. Silence in the record becomes a blank screen onto which each age projects its own technology.

None of this makes the machine theories correct. But it explains why they keep returning, and why a reader who has felt drawn to them is in good company.

The Giza Power Plant

The best-known machine theory was set out by the American engineer and machinist Christopher Dunn, who published a book in 1998 titled The Giza Power Plant: Technologies of Ancient Egypt. Dunn had spent his career working in precision manufacturing. He had been impressed by the accuracy of Egyptian stone-work, and he had read the measurements of the nineteenth-century archaeologist Flinders Petrie, who surveyed Giza in the early 1880s and reported extremely fine work on some granite objects. Dunn argued that such accuracy implied machine tools, and he went on to propose that the Great Pyramid as a whole was a machine.

Stated briefly, and as fairly as possible, the proposal goes like this.

1. The Great Pyramid was built to be a power plant, not a

tomb. Its purpose was to generate and transmit energy of some kind.

2. Water flowed into the pyramid from underground channels.

In the Queen's Chamber, Dunn proposed, two chemicals were combined: zinc, and hydrochloric acid (which he suggested might be made on site from other materials). The reaction between them produces hydrogen gas.

3. The hydrogen rose through the narrow shafts that run from

the Queen's Chamber. The shafts were not for stars or souls; they were pipes.

4. In the King's Chamber, which is lined with granite, the hy-

drogen was ignited or otherwise interacted with a vibrating

system. Sound waves, produced in part by the flow of gas and in part by the natural vibrations of the Earth, made the granite resonate. Granite contains quartz, and quartz is piezoelectric, meaning it generates electricity when squeezed or vibrated.

5. The result, Dunn said, was a resonant system that converted

the Earth's vibrations into microwave energy, which was then beamed out through the shafts or conducted away.

There are elements of real science in this chain. Hydrogen can be made from zinc and hydrochloric acid, which is a standard classroom demonstration. Quartz is piezoelectric. Rooms do resonate. A reader with a technical background can follow each link and say, yes, that is something that exists.

The trouble is that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and nearly every link in this one breaks when tested against the record.

Testing the claims, one by one

Let us go through the main points in order.

There is no physical trace of the apparatus. If a chemical plant had operated in the Great Pyramid, there would be pipes, tanks, vessels, pumps, valves, or at least the places where they were fixed. There would be corrosion, residue, scorched surfaces, and a great deal of chemical contamination. Hydrochloric acid is highly corrosive. Hydrogen is explosive. Over a long operating life, the chambers would show it. Instead, the interior shows plain, dry limestone and granite, carved graffiti from the

work gangs, and the scars of nineteenth-century explorers' crowbars and gunpowder. No archaeologist, chemist, or geologist who has studied the interior has reported any trace of reaction products, metallic residues, or the mounting points of any equipment.

The salt deposits do not point to a reaction. Dunn and others have cited the crystalline salt crust on the walls of the Queen's Chamber as evidence that something chemical went on there. Salt crusts are real, and visitors can see them. But they are common in limestone chambers in the Egyptian desert, and the explanation is ordinary. Rock in contact with moisture slowly dissolves trace minerals, and when the water evaporates at the surface the salts are left behind. This is the same process that attacks the stones of many tombs and temples in Egypt. Salt deposits of this kind are found in rooms of other pyramids, and in tombs that were never anything but tombs.

The shafts do not behave like pipes. Chapter 15 described the narrow shafts that rise from the King's Chamber and the Queen's Chamber. The King's Chamber shafts reach the outer faces of the pyramid, though the openings are not where one might expect for ventilation. The Queen's Chamber shafts, by contrast, do not begin at the chamber floor; they start some distance above it inside the masonry, and their inner ends were never opened until modern times. Robots sent up the southern one in 1993 and 2002, and again in 2011, found small limestone slabs, with copper fittings, blocking the way. A pipe that is sealed with a stone slab at one end and closed off in the masonry

at the other is not carrying gas. Whatever the purpose of these shafts, it was ritual or symbolic, not plumbing.

No source of zinc or hydrochloric acid has been found in

Old Kingdom Egypt. The metal that Dunn's reaction required, zinc in a pure form, does not seem to have been produced anywhere in the ancient world until a very late period. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, is known in later antiquity, but pure metallic zinc is difficult to produce because it boils at a temperature close to the one needed to smelt it, and it was a centuries-later achievement. Hydrochloric acid, for its part, is generally credited to alchemists of the early medieval Islamic world. There is no evidence for either substance in the Egyptian Old Kingdom, not as finished products, not as raw materials, not in residues in any tool or vessel.

The energy does not add up. This is the deepest problem, and it does not even require any archaeology. A chemical reaction can only release the energy that was stored in its ingredients. When zinc dissolves in acid and makes hydrogen, the energy that eventually comes out as heat, or as a flame, came from the zinc and the acid. But zinc, in its metallic form, was itself produced by smelting ore, which takes at least as much energy as you can get back by reacting it. In other words, a plant that runs on zinc and acid is a way of storing and releasing energy that had to be put in first. It is a battery, not a generator. It cannot be a net source of power.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Suppose you wanted to get one megajoule of heat from burning hydrogen. Burning one mole of hydrogen (two grams) releases about 286 kilojoules, so you would need about 3.5 moles, or about 7 grams of hydrogen. Making that hydrogen from zinc would consume about 3.5 moles of zinc, or roughly 230 grams. To refine that much zinc from ore takes more energy than you get back from the hydrogen, and the acid has to be made as well. So you would be spending far more energy to produce the zinc than you would ever recover. This is why nobody today makes power by dissolving zinc in acid.

Resonance is not generation. Dunn's central idea is that vibrations in the granite generate electricity. But resonance, the tendency of a structure to vibrate strongly at certain frequencies, does not create energy; it can only amplify energy that is already being supplied. A bell rings loudly if you strike it, but the ring is made from the energy of the blow. For the King's Chamber to act as a generator, there would have to be a strong, constant source of vibration feeding it. The Earth's ambient seismic noise is tiny. The proposed gas flow would have to supply the rest, and we have just seen that there is no gas.

The piezoelectric argument fails for a specific reason.

Quartz is indeed piezoelectric, and granite contains quartz. But the grains of quartz in granite are oriented randomly. When the rock is squeezed, each grain generates a small voltage, but the voltages point in all directions and largely cancel each other out. This is the reason why a block of granite is not a battery, and

why industrial piezoelectric devices are made from single crystals or carefully aligned ceramics, not from rocks.

There is no consumer. Finally, a power plant exists to supply something. The Great Pyramid is not connected to anything. There are no cables, no transmission towers, no remains of any apparatus anywhere on the Giza plateau that could have used the power. There is no wire, no lamp, no motor, no sign of any electrical or mechanical load. All the evidence points the other way: around the pyramid there are temples, boat pits, cemeteries, and a workers' town.

What the Egyptians themselves said and did

Set against all this is a body of evidence that points, consistently, in a different direction. The pyramid stands at the head of a complex whose parts make sense as a royal tomb and a cult center. The causeway leads down to a valley temple on the edge of the old harbor. The mortuary temple at the pyramid's foot held statues of the king and a place for offerings. Boat pits flanking the pyramid held full-size cedar boats, one of which, the Khufu ship, has been reassembled and conserved. Around the pyramid are the cemeteries of Khufu's relatives and officials, with their tomb chapels carrying inscriptions that name him. A priesthood served his cult for centuries. Chapter 16 described all of this.

Moreover, the builders themselves wrote their messages in the stone. In the sealed relieving chambers above the King's Chamber, work gangs painted names such as "Friends of Khufu" and the king's own name in red ochre on the blocks, with quarry marks. Nobody going into a machine room scribbles

gang names on the walls before it is sealed for good. But a crew finishing a building, who want their work to be credited, does exactly that.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: The Great Pyramid has no connection to burial because no mummy was found. Fact: The absence of a body in the chamber is real, but it is not unusual. Almost every large pyramid was robbed in antiquity, and the Great Pyramid was found open and empty when it was entered in the ninth century CE. Absence of the king does not make a power plant. What the Great Pyramid lacks is a body, not a funerary purpose; what it does not lack is everything else, including a sarcophagus, a complex of temples and boats, and a surrounding cemetery.

The physics paper everyone cites

Supporters of machine theories sometimes cite a scientific study published in 2018 in the Journal of Applied Physics. A team of physicists from Russia and Germany, with ties to ITMO University in Saint Petersburg and the Laser Zentrum in Hannover, modeled how the Great Pyramid, treated as a block of limestone of that shape, would respond to radio waves. Their calculations suggested that at certain wavelengths, between about 200 and 600 meters, the pyramid would resonate, and that under those conditions energy would concentrate in the internal chambers and beneath the base.

Headlines at the time said that the Great Pyramid "can focus electromagnetic energy." That is accurate as far as it goes, but it

needs context. The study was a computer model of a shape. The authors used it as a way to design tiny particles that could produce similar effects at optical wavelengths, with the aim of building better nanosensors and solar cells. They did not claim that the Egyptians knew about resonance, that the pyramid was designed for it, or that any of it had anything to do with ancient purpose. Their model also rested on assumptions, for example that the pyramid is a uniform block of limestone with no unknown cavities. Any large object of a given size and shape has resonances. A football stadium does. A church does. A mountain does. Finding that a pyramid-shaped body interacts with long radio waves says nothing about why anyone built it.

KEY POINT

A resonance is a property of a shape. It tells you what a structure would do if you drove it with the right wave. It does not tell you that anyone ever did, or that anyone built the structure in order to do it.

A different kind of machine: the hydraulic lift

Not every machine idea in the pyramid literature is mystical. In August 2024, a research team led by the French engineer Xavier Landreau, of the private research institute Paleotechnic in Paris, published a paper in the open-access journal PLOS ONE proposing that the builders of Egypt's first pyramid, the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, raised stones with a hydraulic lift.

The proposal is specific and ingenious. Landreau's team pointed to the large vertical shaft on the north side of the pyramid's complex and to a system of channels and basins, including a huge walled enclosure called the Gisr el-Mudir and a dry moat around the complex. They suggested that seasonal floodwater was collected and fed into the shaft, where it raised a floating platform carrying building stones; when the water was drained, the platform dropped to the bottom, and the cycle repeated. A wooden float and ropes over pulleys balanced the platform. The idea is that water, not muscle, did the heavy lifting.

The proposal drew much attention, and it also drew sharp criticism from specialists. Archaeologist Oren Siegel of the University of Toronto argued that the enclosure could not have held enough rainwater to run such a system, and suggested it was an early experiment in stone enclosures. Egyptologist Kamil Kuraszkiewicz of the University of Warsaw pointed out that no ancient Egyptian text mentions the lake the model requires, and that Djoser's stones, which average about 300 kilograms, are light enough that human labor would have been simpler than building a hydraulic device. Other researchers said they were unconvinced.

The hydraulic proposal is useful to compare with the powerplant theory because it shows what a testable machine theory looks like. It was published in a peer-reviewed journal, it makes specific claims about specific places, and it can be checked against the excavated landscape and against the texts. Its critics were able to answer it with specific objections. Whether it

stands or falls, it sits squarely inside the mainstream argument about how Egyptians built. It also does not make the pyramid a power plant; it treats the pyramid as a monument and the lift, if it existed, as a construction tool.

The valid core: the Egyptians were good with water and chemistry

There is a grain of truth in the machine theories that is worth rescuing. The Egyptians were extremely capable practical chemists and hydraulic engineers, but they used these skills for other purposes. They made faience, a glazed ceramic, and Egyptian blue, the world's first synthetic pigment. They refined gold and worked copper. They made plaster and gypsum mortar by burning and grinding gypsum. They used natron, a natural salt mixture from desert lakes, to dry bodies for mummification. They dug canals, built harbors, and managed floods. As we saw in Chapter 11, they probably used water to wet the sand ahead of heavy sledges. They had hydraulic skill. They did not have, and did not need, a chemical power plant.

When we say that the Egyptians built the Great Pyramid with copper tools and rope, we are not saying that they were primitive. We are saying that they were very good at the things they actually did, and that they applied their cleverness to organization, geometry, and material handling, not to the kind of energy technology we associate with the industrial age.

How to judge a machine theory

The power-plant theory gives us a useful checklist that applies to any claim that an ancient monument was a lost machine. You can ask:

1. What is the machine supposed to do? A real machine has

an input and an output. Where does the energy come in, and where does it go?

2. Where are the parts? Machines leave hardware, wear,

residues, and repair marks.

3. Where are the raw materials? If the theory needs zinc,

acid, copper wire, or lenses, where were they found and in what quantities?

4. Does the energy balance work? No process creates energy

from nothing.

5. What does the simplest explanation say? If the building

was demonstrably a tomb complex, with a tomb chamber, a sarcophagus, a funerary temple, boat pits, and a cemetery, a machine theory has to explain why all that is there.

6. What would count against the theory? A good theory

states in advance what evidence would refute it. If no discovery could ever count against a claim, it is not a scientific claim.

The Giza Power Plant fails the first five checks. It also fails the sixth, because each time a missing piece is pointed out, the answer is that the evidence must have been removed. A theory that explains away every gap with "it was taken away" cannot be

tested, and is no longer in competition with an explanation that fits the evidence we do have.

Chapter summary

The Great Pyramid's precision and size make it tempting to see it as a machine. The best-known version of that idea, the Giza Power Plant, rests on a chain of real scientific facts (hydrogen from zinc and acid, piezoelectric quartz, resonant rooms) that do not connect when set against the evidence: no apparatus, no residue, no zinc or hydrochloric acid in the Old Kingdom, shafts that were sealed, no way to get net energy from chemistry, and no consumer for the output. A 2018 physics study of the pyramid's radio resonance is a model of a shape, not a claim about ancient purpose. A 2024 proposal of a hydraulic lift at the Step Pyramid is a serious and testable engineering hypothesis about construction, which many specialists doubt. What the Egyptians did have was extraordinary organizational skill, practical chemistry for pigments, plaster and mummification, and a mastery of water and stone.

CHAPTER 20

Ancient Astronauts and "Impossible" Imagery

Where the alien-technology idea came from, what its supporters point to, and what Egyptologists say about each piece of evidence.

If you search the internet for the pyramids, a large share of what you find says that they were built or assisted by beings from elsewhere in the universe. The claim is common enough that it deserves a fair, careful chapter. Many readers of this book will have met it first on television, in a documentary, or in a viral video, and will want to know what is behind it.

This chapter does four things. It describes where the "ancient astronaut" idea came from. It lays out the specific pieces of imagery that are usually cited from Egypt. It examines each one. And it considers what the idea says, often without meaning to, about the people who actually built the monuments.

A short history of an idea

The notion that ancient wonders were made by visitors from space is far younger than the wonders themselves. Earlier writers of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries sometimes speculated about contact with other worlds, but the idea in its modern form took shape in the 1960s. In 1960, two French writers, Louis Pauwels and Jacques Bergier, published The Morning of the Magicians, a bestselling mix of history, science, and occult speculation that floated the notion of vanished civilizations and cosmic visitors. Then, in 1968, a Swiss hotel manager named Erich von Däniken published Chariots of the Gods?, which presented the idea to a mass audience. The book sold in the millions and was followed by many others and by a television franchise.

Von Däniken's argument rested on a pattern that is easy to recognize. He would point to a monument, a carving, or a myth, say that it was too advanced, too strange, or too precise for the people credited with it, and offer extraterrestrial contact as the simplest explanation. The Great Pyramid was an obvious candidate. Over the following decades, other writers expanded the theme, and in the twenty-first century a long-running cable television series brought a version of it to a wide audience.

It is worth noting that critics who checked von Däniken's sources, including a well-known television investigation in the late 1970s, documented numerous errors and misrepresentations in his books. That does not settle the matter by itself, since a claim can be wrong or right regardless of the track record of its

proponent, but it helps explain why professional historians and archaeologists have not treated the ancient-astronaut idea as a serious competitor to ordinary explanation.

The argument in outline

The case for alien involvement in Egypt, as its supporters make it, usually has four parts.

1. The pyramids are too big and too precise. The Great

Pyramid's size, its alignment, and its smooth finish are said to exceed what ancient people could have done.

2. Egyptian stonework includes "impossible" objects. Fine

granite vessels, huge stone boxes, and precisely cut blocks are cited as evidence of advanced tools.

3. Egyptian art shows technology. A handful of carvings and

objects are said to depict aircraft, light bulbs, or other machines.

4. Egyptian art shows non-human beings. Elongated heads,

animal-headed gods, and star-linked deities are read as depictions of visitors.

The first of these was dealt with in Parts Three and Four of this book. We have the quarries, the tools, the ramps, the workers' town, the bakeries, the cemeteries, and the logbook of Merer. It was not necessary to assume anything but human beings. In what follows we will concentrate on the other three.

Case one: the Abydos "helicopter"

The most famous piece of "evidence" is a set of carved hieroglyphs on a beam in the temple of Seti I at Abydos, in southern Egypt. Seti I was a king of the Nineteenth Dynasty, who reigned around 1290 to 1279 BCE, more than twelve hundred years after the Great Pyramid. In photographs, one section of the carving looks strikingly like a helicopter, with what could be a submarine, a jet, and other shapes beside it. Variations of the image have spread across the internet since the late twentieth century, and many people have seen it.

The explanation is mundane, and it is something that anyone who has studied Egyptian inscriptions will recognize. The carving was made twice. A first inscription, giving a set of the king's titles, was cut into the stone. After the death of Seti I, his son Ramesses II completed and usurped parts of the temple. The older text was filled in with plaster, and a new inscription with different titles was cut into the plaster. Over the centuries, the plaster eroded and fell away, and the older carving came back to light underneath, overlapping with the newer one. The "helicopter" is what you get when two different sets of hieroglyphs occupy the same space, with some of the signs of one running into the signs of the other. When the two layers are traced separately, each resolves into ordinary hieroglyphic signs, reading as phrases about the king.

This type of overlap is called a palimpsest, a word for a surface that has been written on more than once. Egyptians re-used and re-carved inscriptions constantly, because kings liked to

claim the work of their predecessors. Egyptologists see such overlaps all the time. The Abydos example only looks mysterious because it has been photographed at a flattering angle, in good light, and cropped.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: The Abydos carvings show a helicopter, a submarine, and a jet. Fact: They are overlapping hieroglyphs from two different inscriptions, one carved over a plaster repair of the other. When the layers are separated, each reads as a normal royal title.

Case two: the Dendera "light bulbs"

In the great temple of Hathor at Dendera, about sixty kilometers north of Luxor, are underground chambers called the crypts. On the walls are reliefs that show a large oval object shaped a little like a long bulb, in which a wavy line rises like a filament. A figure with raised arms stands behind it, and a pillar supports it. To some viewers it looks like a light bulb connected to a cable. The comparison has been made for more than a century, and it appears in books and videos that claim Egypt had electric light.

Egyptologists read the same scene differently, and their reading rests on the inscriptions around it. The wavy line is a snake, rising from a lotus flower. The oval is the lotus, or a container called a hen, which may stand for the womb of the sky goddess Nut. The snake is a manifestation of a god, and the whole scene is connected to Egyptian creation myths, in which a god

emerged from the primeval waters on a lotus. The pillar is a djed, a symbol of stability that is common in Egyptian art. The captions around the scenes describe the sacred statues of the gods that were kept in the crypts, and the rituals through which they were revived in the light of the sun on the temple roof.

There are two further points. First, the Dendera temple as it stands today is a late building, constructed in the Ptolemaic and early Roman periods, about two thousand years ago. That is roughly twenty-five centuries after the Great Pyramid. If these reliefs were evidence of lost pyramid-age technology, the technology would have to have survived the whole long gap without leaving anything else. Second, there is no hardware. No bulb, no wire, no filament, no battery, no generator, and no lamp socket has ever been found in any Egyptian site. The ancient Egyptians have left us thousands of oil lamps, which are small bowls of oil with a wick, and many tomb scenes showing people using them.

The "no soot" argument

A related claim is that Egyptian tomb ceilings, decorated with fine paintings in deep passages far from daylight, show no soot from torches or lamps. How, the argument goes, did artists work underground without leaving soot unless they had electric light?

The question has a number of plausible answers, and it is worth noting that a claim about what is absent is only as good as the survey behind it. Egyptians used oil lamps, and the lamps could be made to burn cleanly by using good oil and trimmed wicks, and some researchers have proposed that salt was added to reduce smoke. Mirrors of polished metal could bounce sun-

light into passages in relays. And soot marks have in fact been noted in a number of tombs. Researchers have also pointed out that artists often worked in tombs that were open to the outside and decorated the burial chambers last, when the work was small and the lamps could be few. The absence of soot, where it is absent, is far from demonstrating an alternative technology, and the absence of any physical evidence for the technology (no bulbs, no wires) is a much stronger fact.

Case three: the Saqqara bird

In 1898, in the tomb of a man named Pa-di-Imen at Saqqara, excavators found a small wooden figure that is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. It is a bird, carved from sycamore wood, with outstretched wings and a pointed beak. It has a wingspan of about eighteen centimeters and weighs less than forty grams. It dates to around 200 BCE, the Ptolemaic period.

In 1969, an Egyptian physician and researcher named Khalil Messiha proposed that the figure is a model of a glider, and that the ancient Egyptians must therefore have understood aerodynamics. The idea was taken up in books and documentaries. It looks, to a viewer, rather like a model airplane: the body is slim, the wings are long, and the shape is simple.

The objections are straightforward. The bird, as it survives, has no vertical tail fin, which a real glider needs for stability. Enthusiasts who build copies add one. A 2023 computational study of its aerodynamics by researchers at the Institute of Aerospace Technology in Bremen found that the object has a poor glide performance, is unstable in pitch, and would roll uncon-

trollably in flight. An aviation historian had earlier called it far too heavy and unstable to fly. The object seems to have been a decorative or ritual piece. Egyptians carved many bird figures, and birds were closely associated with gods, especially the falcon. Other suggestions include a child's toy, a weather vane, or an ornament for the prow of a ceremonial boat. In any case, an object that dates to two thousand years after the pyramids and cannot actually fly tells us nothing about how pyramids were built.

Case four: elongated heads and "strange" beings

Some of the images used in the alien argument are not machines but people. The most common example is the art of the Amarna period, around 1350 BCE, under the pharaoh Akhenaten. In the reliefs and statues of this reign, the royal family is shown with long faces, narrow, stretched skulls, thin limbs, swollen bellies, and broad hips. Popular writers have suggested that this reflects an alien lineage.

Scholars of Egyptian art have long recognized that Amarna style was a deliberate artistic revolution. Akhenaten broke with Egyptian tradition by promoting the worship of the sun disk, the Aten, over the old gods, and his artists developed a new, expressive style that exaggerated the human form. The style is found not only on the king and queen but on ordinary officials, courtiers, and even the sculptors' own workshop pieces, and it softens in the later years of the reign. Some modern writers have suggested the king had a medical condition. A 2010 study led by

Egyptian researchers, which examined the mummies of the royal family using DNA and imaging, concluded that there was no evidence of the genetic disorder some had proposed, though the study itself has been debated. The best-supported view is that the elongated forms were a stylistic choice with religious meaning, an artistic way of expressing the king's special role as the intermediary of the sun.

Akhenaten, we should note, lived well over a thousand years after the Great Pyramid. His art tells us about Amarna theology. It tells us nothing about who built Giza.

The same reasoning applies to Egyptian gods with animal heads, such as Anubis, Thoth, Horus, and Sekhmet. The Egyptians combined human bodies with animal heads to express the qualities of a deity: the keen sight of the falcon, the watchfulness of the jackal, the fierceness of the lioness. These were symbolic images, and the Egyptians themselves wrote at length about what they meant.

Case five: "impossible" stonework

A fifth line of argument holds that some Egyptian stone objects are so finely made that modern machine tools would be required. The cited examples include thin-walled stone vases, which are sometimes described as lathe-turned, and the huge granite boxes in the underground galleries of the Serapeum at Saqqara, which weigh many tonnes and have very flat surfaces.

Egyptologists have answered these claims in some detail, using three kinds of evidence.

• Tools and workshops. Excavations have turned up

stoneworking tools: copper chisels, dolerite pounders, flint blades, bow drills, and the abrasive materials, such as quartz sand, used in cutting and polishing. They have found workshops where vessels were made, and tomb paintings that show craftsmen working on stone vases.

• Unfinished pieces. Abandoned and half-finished objects

show the stages of the work: roughing out, hollowing, grinding, polishing. The unfinished obelisk at Aswan, abandoned in its quarry after it cracked, preserves the marks of the pounding stones used to cut it.

• Replication. Modern stonemasons and archaeologists have

reproduced Egyptian techniques, drilling and grinding hard stone with copper tools and sand, and have made vessels of a similar quality. The work is slow, but it can be done.

Precision work in hard stone is a mark of skill and patience, not of machinery. The Egyptians had centuries to refine their methods, and a craft tradition in which fathers taught sons.

KEY POINT

Almost every "impossible" object in Egyptian archaeology turns out to be made of a hard material by a long, laborious, but entirely traceable process. What looks impossible is usually just slow.

The deeper problem: what the idea leaves out

Beyond the cases, there is a further, more serious objection to the ancient-astronaut argument. It has to do with what the idea does to the people it claims to explain.

Think about what the argument is really saying. It says: the achievement is so great that the people credited with it must not have done it. That is a claim about the people, and it deserves to be examined. It assumes that a society of farmers, craftsmen, and scribes, working for a few generations, could not have de-

veloped the geometry, the organization, and the stonecraft to build monuments, even though we have their tools, their villages, their written records, their failed attempts, and their own graffiti. It treats the evidence of their work as irrelevant.

Archaeologists and historians have pointed out that ancient-astronaut claims tend to be applied far more to ancient cultures outside Europe, such as the Egyptians, the Maya, the Inca, and the builders of Easter Island, than to the Greeks and Romans, whose monuments are not generally said to need extraterrestrial help. Critics see in this pattern a quiet assumption that some peoples were less capable than others. Whether or not any individual writer intends it, the effect is to take credit from the actual builders.

There is also a logical problem. The ancient-astronaut explanation is an argument from ignorance: we cannot immediately see how this was done, therefore it must have been done in a way we cannot see. But the more we learn, the less room that leaves. In the 1960s, it was truly unclear how the pyramids were organized. Since then, archaeologists have found the workers' town, their cemeteries, the quarries, the harbor, the papyri, and the tools. Each discovery has made the human explanation stronger and the extraterrestrial one more redundant.

Finally, the idea fails a basic test of explanation. If aliens had built the pyramids, we would expect to see something that the ancient Egyptians could not have made: an alloy beyond their reach, an electronic component, a tool that does not fit into any known tradition. Instead, we find things that fit squarely into what we know of the Bronze Age: copper, stone, wood, rope,

and mud brick. We find mistakes, repairs, and changes of plan. We find the collapse at Meidum, the changed angle at the Bent Pyramid, and the successful third attempt at Dahshur. Superior beings, with advanced technology, would not need a century of trial and error.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: If we cannot explain exactly how something was done, aliens must have done it. Fact: "We do not know exactly how" is a very common situation in history, and it has always been resolved, when it was resolved, by finding more human evidence. Gaps in knowledge are gaps in knowledge. They are not evidence for a particular alternative.

Respecting the question

It would be a mistake to treat everyone who is drawn to these ideas as foolish. The longing behind them is a natural one. People want the past to be full of mystery. They want to feel the strangeness of the pyramids, and the sense that those monuments are older and bigger than ordinary life. That feeling is real, and it is a good one.

The honest answer is that the strangeness is real, but the explanation is human. A group of people, with no machines, took on the biggest construction project in history and finished it, and they did it so well that it is still standing. They organized food for tens of thousands, trained crews, ran quarries, ran boats, and kept records. The evidence for this is richer and more specific

than the evidence for any alternative. The truth, once you know it, is not a smaller story. It is a bigger one, because it is about us.

Chapter summary

The ancient-astronaut idea took its modern form in the 1960s and has been applied to the Great Pyramid and to a handful of Egyptian images. Examined individually, each claimed piece of evidence has a straightforward explanation: the Abydos "helicopter" is an overlapping inscription, the Dendera "bulbs" are a lotus and snake in a creation scene, the Saqqara bird is a small bird figure that cannot fly, Amarna art is a religious style, and "impossible" stonework is the product of known tools and techniques. The idea also fails on logic and evidence, since it rests on arguments from ignorance and finds none of the hardware that outside technology would leave behind. And it takes credit away from the real builders.
