CHAPTER 21

Star Maps, Secret Numbers, and "Pyramid Power"

The Orion correlation, the pi and golden-ratio claims, the pyramid inch, the razor-blade sharpener, and a lost civilization: what each says and how it holds up.

The previous two chapters dealt with machines and with visitors from space. This one deals with a third family of ideas, which is in some ways the most human. These are the claims that the Great Pyramid encodes something: a map of the sky, a table of cosmic constants, a prophecy, or a mysterious energy that works on objects placed inside a pyramid shape. Some of these ideas contain real observations, and one of them, the possible alignment of the narrow shafts with particular stars, remains an open question among scholars. Others have been tested many times and found empty.

We will take them in order, beginning with the one that has the best claim to be taken seriously.

The Orion Correlation

In 1994, a construction engineer and writer named Robert Bauval, who was born in Alexandria and raised in Egypt, published a book called The Orion Mystery. His central idea, now known as the Orion Correlation Theory, is that the layout of the three great pyramids at Giza reproduces on the ground the pattern of the three stars of Orion's Belt in the sky.

The argument runs like this. The three pyramids of Giza, those of Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure, are not in a straight line. The third, Menkaure's, which is the smallest, is offset slightly to the east from the diagonal line formed by the first two. The three stars of Orion's Belt, called Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka, show a similar pattern: the smallest and faintest, Mintaka, is offset slightly from the line through the other two. Bauval proposed that the pyramids were placed so as to mirror those stars, with the Nile standing in for the Milky Way.

There is a real basis for connecting Orion with Egyptian royal burial. The Egyptians identified the constellation of Orion with Sah, a god associated with Osiris, the god of the dead and the afterlife. The Pyramid Texts, which we met in Chapter 17, say that the dead king ascends to the sky and becomes a star in the company of Orion. In addition, as Chapter 15 mentioned, in the 1960s the astronomer Virginia Trimble and the engineer Alexander Badawy noticed that the southern shaft of the King's Chamber seems to have pointed toward the region of Orion's Belt at the time of construction, while a shaft in the Queen's

Chamber may have pointed toward Sirius, which the Egyptians associated with Isis. Bauval built on those suggestions.

So the Orion Correlation has a few legs of real material to stand on. The trouble is that each of them is weaker than it first looks.

The match between the pyramids and the stars is loose.

To make the pyramids match the Belt, you have to turn the map upside down, or otherwise rotate or flip it, because, in the natural orientation, north on the ground does not correspond to north on the star map. The stars of Orion's Belt run diagonally across the sky, with a slight bend. The pyramids also run diagonally, with a slight bend. But a bend is a bend: with three points and a few degrees of freedom, there are very few ways to place three dots that cannot be matched to some three-star group in the sky. When one tries the match carefully, the angles and relative distances are only approximately similar, and the match depends on which way you orient the sky and the ground.

The other pyramids do not fit. Egypt has dozens of pyramids. At Abu Rawash, a few kilometers north of Giza, stand the ruins of the pyramid of Djedefre, Khufu's son. At Zawyet elAryan, Abusir, Saqqara, Dahshur, and Meidum there are many more. The Orion Correlation concentrates on three pyramids and ignores the others. Bauval suggested that a larger map of the Nile Valley might fit the entire constellation, but this extension requires choosing which pyramids to include and which to leave out. A pattern that holds only for the points that are picked is not a strong pattern.

The three pyramids were not built as a single design. As we saw in Chapters 5 and 6, the Giza pyramids were built by three different kings over about eighty years. Khufu's pyramid was placed first, on a good site, and the later pyramids were placed with reference to it and to the terrain. Khafre's pyramid was placed on higher ground to the southwest, and Menkaure's farther southwest still. The arrangement is easily explained by available space and the slope of the plateau. The idea that three different kings, in three different reigns, followed a single predetermined star map requires a continuity of plan across generations for which there is no evidence.

The Egyptians did not leave any such map. We have a large body of Egyptian astronomical material, including star clocks, ceiling paintings of the sky, and lists of constellations and decans. None of them refers to a pyramid layout as a star map. The Egyptians who built pyramids in the Fourth Dynasty were most concerned with the circumpolar stars, the "imperishable ones" that never set below the horizon, because those were the stars that symbolized eternal life. The orientation of the Great Pyramid to the cardinal directions, to north in particular, fits that concern. The Orion Belt idea is much less central to the evidence than it first appears.

The dating does not line up easily. Part of Bauval's theory depended on a particular date in the sky: he argued that Orion's position in about 10,500 BCE matched the layout of the pyramids. In later versions of the argument, the pyramids were said to have been planned much earlier than the traditional date. But the evidence of dating, including the papyri of Merer, which are

dated to Khufu's reign, the workers' town, and radiocarbon work on short-lived organic material, puts the Great Pyramid squarely in the reign of Khufu, in the twenty-sixth century BCE. (Early radiocarbon tests on mortar gave dates a few centuries too old, an effect usually blamed on old wood burned to make the mortar, and not on an older pyramid.)

KEY POINT

It is true that the Egyptians linked Orion with the dead king's afterlife. It is not shown that the Giza pyramids were laid out as a map of Orion's Belt. The first claim is in Egyptian texts. The second is a modern proposal that has not been supported by the evidence.

The question of the shafts is a separate one, and it remains open. It is entirely possible that the builders aimed the King's Chamber shafts at stars that were important to them, in order to guide the king's soul. Several scholars have suggested alignments of this sort, and they are consistent with Egyptian religion. The difficulty is that the shafts are not perfectly straight, the stars' positions are only roughly known across the centuries, and the Queen's Chamber shafts have never been explored beyond the small stone doors. The question will be settled, if at all, by more exploration, not by a theory of the layout of the pyramids.

The Sphinx, the Younger Dryas, and a "lost civilization"

A related idea has to do with the claim that the monuments of Giza are much older than they appear to be, perhaps by thousands of years, and were built or begun by a civilization that has vanished from the record.

The best-known proponent of this idea is the British writer Graham Hancock, whose 1995 book Fingerprints of the Gods became an international bestseller, and who has continued to write and present on the subject, including in a streaming television series in 2022. Hancock has argued that a lost advanced civilization existed during the last ice age and was destroyed in a catastrophe around 12,000 years ago, a period geologists call the Younger Dryas, and that its surviving members passed on knowledge to later cultures, including Egypt.

A related piece of the argument concerns the Great Sphinx. In the early 1990s, the geologist Robert Schoch of Boston University examined the Sphinx and its enclosure and argued that the pattern of weathering on the walls, with deep, rounded, vertical fissures, looked like the result of long-term rainfall rather than wind and sand. Since the climate of Giza has been very dry for the whole of the historic period, he suggested, the Sphinx must date from a much earlier, wetter time, thousands of years before the traditional date.

It would be unfair to dismiss the Sphinx question as stupid. It was posed by a trained geologist, and it received serious atten-

tion. Still, the great majority of Egyptologists and geologists who have examined it have not accepted it, for several reasons. • The weathering has other explanations. Limestone

weathers differently depending on the quality of the layers. The soft, shaley layers of the Sphinx's body erode quickly, while the harder layers resist. Salt crystallization, dew and humidity, and wind erosion all produce the type of rounded profile seen at the Sphinx. Similar weathering is seen on other monuments of known age at Giza.

• The Sphinx is tied to the surrounding monuments. The

enclosure around the Sphinx is the quarry from which the blocks of the nearby Sphinx Temple and Valley Temple were cut. Those temples are in the architectural style of the Fourth Dynasty and are connected to the causeway of Khafre's pyramid. The Sphinx sits on the axis of that complex. Archaeologists therefore date it to the reign of Khafre, around 2500 BCE.

• There is no sign of a people who could have done it. If a

society capable of carving and moving enormous blocks existed in Egypt in the tenth millennium BCE, it would have left evidence in the form of settlements, tools, food remains, burials, and rubbish. The archaeology of Egypt in that period shows hunter-gatherers and early herders, with no evidence of a society with the necessary resources and organization. In contrast, for the pyramid age we have all of these things in abundance.

• The hypothesis is not needed. The chain of development,

from Djoser's step pyramid to Sneferu's experiments to Khufu's masterpiece, shows the builders learning. A civilization that had inherited the knowledge of a lost master culture would not have needed that.

In 2022 a streaming series presenting Hancock's ideas drew public criticism from archaeologists and from professional organizations, including the Society for American Archaeology, who said that it misrepresented the evidence and downplayed the accomplishments of known peoples. Hancock has rejected that criticism and says that his work calls for a more open search of the evidence. Readers are encouraged to read both sides. But it is fair to say that the proposal has not persuaded the specialists in the field, and that no physical evidence of the lost civilization it describes has been presented that has survived independent examination.

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: Giza was built by a civilization that vanished 12,000 years ago. Fact: There is no archaeological evidence for such a civilization in Egypt, and the pyramids, temples, and workers' town at Giza have been dated to the twenty-sixth century BCE by several independent methods.

Is the Great Pyramid a table of cosmic constants?

The second family of ideas concerns numbers. The Great Pyramid has famous proportions, and for nearly two centuries writers have found in them mathematical "secrets."

Pi

In 1859, a London publisher named John Taylor published a book, The Great Pyramid: Why Was It Built, and Who Built It?, in which he noticed that the perimeter of the Great Pyramid's base, divided by twice its height, comes out very close to the number pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. Taylor proposed that the builders had known pi and had deliberately designed the pyramid to represent a circle and a square at once. The idea has been repeated ever since.

The observation is correct, as far as the arithmetic goes. With a base of 440 cubits on each side and a height of 280 cubits, the perimeter is 1,760 cubits, which divided by twice the height, 560, gives 3.1428..., a value that matches the fraction 22/7. That is about 0.04 percent above pi. It is a striking coincidence.

But there is a simple reason for it, and the reason has to do with the seked, the Egyptian measure of slope that we met in Chapter 5. The builders chose a slope of 5½ palms per cubit, which works out to a rise of 14 for a run of 11. It is easy to measure out with ropes and to repeat in practice. A pyramid with a 14-to-11 slope necessarily has a perimeter-to-height ratio of 44 to 7, or 6.2857, and 22/7 is just the half of that. In other words, the builders were not trying to represent pi; they chose a practi-

cal, repeatable slope, and the pi-like ratio is a consequence of that choice. As the Egyptians had no way to write a symbol for pi, and as their own mathematical documents use quite a different approximation, it is hard to see how they would have designed in a value they did not have.

That last point is worth emphasizing. The one Egyptian text that gives us their method for finding the area of a circle, the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (Problem 50), tells the scribe to subtract one-ninth of the diameter and square the result. That gives an effective value of pi of about 3.16, or 256/81, which is not the same as 22/7 (3.1428) and further from the true value of 3.1416. If the Egyptians had wished to build in an exact pi, they would have used the value they actually knew.

The golden ratio

A parallel claim is that the Great Pyramid embodies the golden ratio, phi, which is about 1.618. The claim goes back to the nineteenth century and was widely repeated in the twentieth. A form of it was even attributed to Herodotus, who is said to have reported that the square of the pyramid's height equals the area of each face.

Again, the arithmetic is close. If the slope is 14 to 11, the ratio of the slant height of a face to half the base is about 1.6186, which is very close to phi, which is 1.6180. This is another coincidence that follows directly from the chosen slope. And here is the telling point: a pyramid that matches pi and the golden ratio at the same time is evidence that neither was the goal. The two numbers are not exactly related (the closest link is that four di-

vided by pi happens to come out within about a tenth of a percent of the square root of phi), so a design could not aim exactly at both at once. The slope of 14 to 11 simply lands close to both. Both appear because of the same practical measurement.

WORKED EXAMPLE

How many coincidences should we expect by chance? Suppose we take 15 measurements of the Great Pyramid (the base, the height, the slant height, the diagonals, the dimensions of the chambers, and so on). From these we can form about 105 different ratios. Suppose we compare each ratio with 10 well-known constants such as pi, e, phi, and the square root of two, and we allow a match if the ratio comes within one half of one percent of the constant, after multiplying or dividing by any power of ten. A random number has about a 0.4 percent chance of falling in such a window for any one constant. With 105 ratios and 10 constants, that is 1,050 chances, and 1,050 times 0.4 percent is about four expected matches by pure chance. So finding a few striking "coincidences" in a large structure measured in many ways is not surprising. It is what chance predicts. Real evidence of design requires a prediction made before looking, not a pattern found afterwards.

The pyramid inch and pyramidology

In 1864, Charles Piazzi Smyth, who was Astronomer Royal for Scotland, published Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid. Smyth had measured the pyramid himself and became convinced that its builders had used a special unit, which he called the pyramid inch, a length very slightly greater than the British inch. He argued that the pyramid's dimensions, expressed in these units, encoded the circumference of the earth, the distance to the sun, the length of the year, and even the history and future of the human race, an idea that Smyth connected to biblical prophecy. This approach was called pyramidology, and it attracted many followers.

It had one weakness: it did not survive more careful measurement. In 1880, a young surveyor named Flinders Petrie, who had been inspired by Smyth's work, went to Giza and measured the pyramid with unprecedented care. His results did not support the pyramid-inch theory. The precision Smyth's numbers required was not in the monument, and Petrie came to reject the idea. His survey became the foundation of modern pyramid measurement, and it showed that the pyramid had been built with a degree of care that was high, but not mathematically perfect: the sides differ in length by only a few centimeters, a tiny fraction of their 230 meters, and the corner angles are not exactly right angles.

The real unit in use was the royal cubit, about 52.4 centimeters, which is used in other Egyptian buildings and is attested by surviving measuring rods. The Great Pyramid's base of about 230.3 meters corresponds to 440 royal cubits, and its original

height to 280. These are round numbers in the Egyptian system, which is exactly what one would expect from engineers working in cubits.

KEY POINT

When a monument's dimensions turn out to be round numbers in the builders' own units, that is evidence of design. When they turn out to be round numbers only in a unit invented centuries later, adjusted until it fits, that is evidence of the investigator's imagination.

"Pyramid power"

The last set of ideas is the most popular in daily life. It holds that the shape of a pyramid has special properties. Objects placed inside a pyramid, it is said, are preserved, sharpened, healed, or energized.

The modern version has a few well-known origins. In the 1930s, a Frenchman named Antoine Bovis claimed that when he visited the Great Pyramid, he noticed that small animals that had wandered into the King's Chamber and died there had not rotted, but had dried up, like mummies. He reasoned that the shape of the pyramid had preserved them. Back home, he built a small wooden model of the pyramid and reported that a dead cat placed inside also mummified rather than rotted.

In the 1940s and 1950s, a Czech radio engineer named Karel Drbal claimed that a used razor blade placed beneath a pyramid-shaped cardboard model, aligned with the earth's northsouth axis, would regain its sharpness. He reportedly obtained a

Czechoslovak patent for a "Cheops pyramid razor blade sharpener." In the 1970s, a bestselling book on Soviet-bloc parapsychology brought the idea to a wide public, and "pyramid power" spread across the world. People built pyramid-shaped tents, hats, and bed frames, and sold pyramid-shaped devices to preserve food, improve plant growth, and promote health.

When tested under controlled conditions, none of these effects has held up. Dead animals in the dry, still air of an Egyptian chamber do dry out, and they do so for the same reason that mummies do: low humidity prevents decay. The same result is achieved in any dry, sealed container, whatever its shape. Razor blades last longer or shorter depending on the metal, the shaving technique, and the care with which they are dried and used, and a blind test that compares blades under a pyramid with blades on a shelf finds no difference. Experiments on plants, fruit, and milk yield the same: no effect that depends on the pyramid shape.

Pyramid power persists, in part, because it is hard to disprove casually. A person who sets a razor blade under a pyramid and feels it is sharper has no easy way to know if the difference is real, and the expectation of a result can influence the judgment. Controlled testing, with blinded comparisons, is the reliable way to answer such questions, and it gives the same answer every time.

Why these ideas persist

It is worth asking why these claims keep coming back. Writers on the psychology of belief have given a number of reasons that apply well to the pyramids.

• Pattern-seeking. Human minds are tuned to see patterns,

even in random data. A monument with many measurements will always yield some striking numbers.

• The appeal of hidden knowledge. There is a deep satisfac-

tion in feeling that one knows a secret that others do not. • Awe and scale. The pyramids are so impressive that an

equally impressive explanation seems called for.

• Distrust of authority. If one suspects that experts conceal

things, a "forbidden" explanation is attractive.

• Media incentives. Mysteries sell books and attract viewers.

A television program that says "the pyramids were built with ramps, ropes, and a lot of well-fed workers" is not likely to draw the same audience as one that hints at secret chambers.

None of these motives is shameful, and many of them are part of what makes people curious about the past in the first place. The point of understanding them is not to ridicule anyone but to recognize the pull in ourselves, and to build the habit of asking for evidence.

Chapter summary

The Orion Correlation has a basis in Egyptian religion, but the match between the pyramids and the stars is loose, selective, and not supported by Egyptian texts; the possible stellar targeting of the shafts is a separate and still-open question. The notion that Giza was built by a lost ice-age civilization has not been supported by evidence, and the Sphinx is tied by its architecture to the reign of Khafre. The pi and golden-ratio "secrets" are byproducts of a practical slope of 14 to 11, and the pyramid inch collapsed when Petrie measured the monument carefully. Pyramid power has failed every controlled test. Taken together, these ideas show how readily pattern-seeking and a love of mystery can run ahead of evidence.

CHAPTER 22

The Frontier: What Science Is Finding Now

Cosmic rays, radar, buried rivers, papyrus logbooks, and a new museum: the discoveries of the last decade, and how to read the headlines about them.

The most exciting thing about the pyramids is that the story is not finished. For most of the twentieth century, research at Giza meant digging, measuring, and reading inscriptions. Those methods are still essential. But since about 2010, a flood of new technologies has joined them: particle detectors, ground-penetrating radar, satellite imagery, drone mapping, radiocarbon labs of unprecedented precision, and flexible cameras no thicker than a pencil. The result has been a run of discoveries that has changed some old debates and opened new ones.

This chapter surveys the main lines of current research, as of the autumn of 2026. It also tries to do something that may be even more useful: to show how to read a news story that says "hidden chamber discovered in pyramid." Such headlines appear regularly, and they are often more dramatic than the research behind them.

A logbook from the Red Sea

The most important single discovery for understanding how the Great Pyramid was built came, oddly, from a cave far from Giza. In 2013, the French archaeologist Pierre Tallet and his team, working at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, about 180 kilometers southeast of Cairo, uncovered among the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. They had been stored in a man-made gallery cut into the rock beside what turned out to be an ancient harbor, probably the oldest port yet found in Egypt, used for expeditions to the copper mines of Sinai.

The papyri are administrative records from the reign of Khufu. The best-known is the logbook of an official named Merer, who led a crew of about forty men. Over several months, his team transported blocks of fine white limestone from the quarries at Tura to Giza, using boats on the Nile and its canals, and they delivered them to the construction site that the document calls "the Horizon of Khufu." The diary gives dates, destinations, and rations. It also mentions a high official, Ankhhaf, a half-brother of the king, who was in charge of the harbor at Giza. For the first time, we have a primary source from the very people who were moving the stone.

The papyri have been studied and published by Tallet and Egyptologist Mark Lehner, who has spent decades excavating at Giza. Their joint account is told in a book, The Red Sea Scrolls, which appeared in 2021. Tallet's work continues. Each season brings new fragments, and each one adds to what we know of the administrative machine behind the pyramid.

KEY POINT

Merer's logbook is the oldest known papyrus archive, and the only first-hand account of work on the Great Pyramid. It proves that stone from Tura was sent by boat to Giza under Khufu's direct administration, and it shows an organized state bureaucracy, with dated records, named officials, and standard rations.

The lost branch of the Nile

In May 2024, a team led by Eman Ghoneim, a geomorphologist at the University of North Carolina Wilmington, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment the discovery of a long-lost branch of the Nile that once ran along the edge of the desert plateau where many of the pyramids were built. The team named it the Ahramat Branch, from the Arabic word for pyramids.

The researchers used a combination of satellite radar imagery, which can penetrate dry sand to detect buried features, ground-penetrating geophysics, and deep soil cores taken from the fields. They traced a buried channel roughly 64 kilometers long, running parallel to the plateau, and found that thirty-one pyramids from the Old and Middle Kingdoms, including the pyramids at Giza, the Step Pyramid of Djoser, and the Bent and Red Pyramids at Dahshur, lie along its former course. Many of the pyramids' causeways, the ceremonial roads leading from the pyramid to the valley temple, seem to end at the proposed riverbank.

The implication is that the pyramid builders did not have to move stone across miles of dry land. A branch of the river ran right at the foot of the plateau, close to the construction sites, and so boats could bring in materials, from quarries and from the south, almost to the building site. The study also suggests the branch shifted eastward over the centuries and eventually dried up, perhaps as a result of drought and the build-up of desert sand.

The study fits well with older evidence, such as Merer's logbook and the harbor found at Giza, but it also has limits. It was published without an exact date for when the branch dried up, and the details of how the branch worked in different seasons are still being worked out. Outside specialists praised the study as showing how different the floodplain was in the pyramid age. Some, including the Egyptologist Zahi Hawass, noted that it does not change the main picture, since the papyrus logbook had already shown that materials were delivered to the Great Pyramid through a nearby harbor.

Cosmic rays, voids, and the Great Pyramid's hidden spaces

Chapter 15 described the ScanPyramids project, which began in 2015 and has used muon imaging, thermography, and other methods to look inside the Great Pyramid. Its main results have been the Big Void, a space at least thirty meters long above the Grand Gallery, announced in 2017, and a smaller corridor-like void behind the north face, above the entrance, which was confirmed in 2023 when the team threaded an endoscope through a joint in the stonework and saw the interior of a gabled space. The researchers have suggested that the north-face space is most likely a structural device to relieve pressure on the entrance passage, and have been cautious about any further interpretation.

It is worth being careful about what these results show. They show that there are empty spaces inside the pyramid that were not known before. They do not show that there is a burial chamber, treasure, or any other particular thing. The Great Pyramid already contains several known voids and relief spaces, and the new ones are consistent with the same architectural logic, though the Big Void's purpose remains unexplained. A press story that says "secret chamber found" is true in a narrow sense, and misleading in the broad one.

The Menkaure scans

In November 2025, researchers from Cairo University and the Technical University of Munich, working as part of the Scan- Pyramids project, published results of a different kind of study, this time of the pyramid of Menkaure, the smallest of the three great pyramids at Giza. Rather than muons, they used a combination of ground-penetrating radar, ultrasound, and electrical resistivity tomography, and combined the data using a technique they call image fusion.

The team detected two air-filled voids behind the smooth granite facing on the eastern side of the pyramid. One is about 1.4 meters deep, about a meter high, and about 1.5 meters wide. The other is about 1.1 meters deep and smaller. They lie behind an area of polished granite blocks, about four meters high and six meters wide, which is unusual because similar granite facing elsewhere on the pyramid is found only around the known entrance on the north side.

That similarity led the team to suggest that the voids might be associated with a second entrance on the east face, an idea that had been proposed earlier, in 2019, by the researcher Stijn van den Hoven. The scientists were careful to describe their finding as "initial evidence" in support of that hypothesis and not as proof. One of the authors, Christian Grosse of the Technical University of Munich, called the entrance hypothesis "very plausible," but nothing has been opened, and no entrance has been found. The results were published in the journal NDT & E International.

This is a good example of how to read such a story. The result is a real measurement of a real anomaly. The interpretation, a hidden entrance, is a reasoned hypothesis. What is still needed is a way to look inside, perhaps with a small borehole and an endoscope, and the permission of Egypt's antiquities authorities to carry it out. Until then, the answer is "we do not know yet."

Radiocarbon and the calendar of kings

Another quiet revolution has been in dating. For a long time, the dates of the Egyptian kings depended on king lists, records of astronomical events, and the reconstruction of how long each king ruled. These methods are good but produce a margin of error of a few decades or more in the Old Kingdom.

In 2010, a team led by Christopher Bronk Ramsey of the University of Oxford published a major study in the journal Science. They dated short-lived plant material, such as seeds and reeds, from the sealed contexts of many Egyptian archaeological sites, and used statistical methods to link the radiocarbon dates to the historical chronology. Their results largely supported the framework of the traditional chronology, with the radiocarbon and historical dates agreeing to within a few decades for most reigns, though some dates shifted. Earlier radiocarbon work on pyramid mortar had given dates that seemed too old, but those samples included old wood used as fuel, which skews the result.

This matters for the claims in the last chapter. Radiocarbon dating gives an independent check on the age of the Great Pyramid, and it places the monument in the twenty-sixth century BCE, as the historical records say.

The workers' town and the human story

Archaeology at Giza has not been only about technology. Since the 1980s, Mark Lehner and his colleagues in the Giza Plateau Mapping Project, later AERA, have been excavating the settlement south of the pyramids, known as Heit el-Ghurab, "Wall of the Crow," and often called the "Lost City of the Pyramid Builders." They found bakeries, breweries, workshops, long galleries that may have housed work gangs, and a great deal of refuse showing what people ate. Chapter 13 described what they found.

The animal bone studies show that the workers ate substantial amounts of beef, as well as sheep and goat. This implies a state-supplied diet that was richer than the diet of the average Egyptian farmer, and it contradicts the picture of starving, whipped slaves. Their cemeteries, excavated by Zahi Hawass and his team in the 1990s, contain simple but carefully built tombs, some with bread and beer placed beside the body. A number of skeletons show healed injuries, which suggests medical care.

Excavation continues. Each season of work adds details about the layout of the town, how the work gangs were housed, and how supplies reached the plateau.

Quarries and ramps

Another area of active research is the study of how stone was moved up the pyramid. In earlier chapters, we met the steep ramp discovered at the alabaster quarry of Hatnub in the Egyptian desert. A joint French and British team has re-examined the site in recent years, and it has revealed a system of a central ramp flanked by staircases and post holes, which seems to have allowed heavy blocks to be hauled up on sledges at a steep angle using ropes anchored to the posts. It dates to about the time of Khufu and shows a plausible technique, though not necessarily the method used on the Great Pyramid itself.

Modern engineers have also tested ideas about ramps with computer models and with small-scale experiments. The debate remains open, but the range of possibilities has narrowed: whatever the builders used, it probably involved a combination of ramps of different types, levers, and a lot of well-organized rope work.

The new museum

In November 2025, after many years of construction, Egypt formally opened the Grand Egyptian Museum, on the desert plateau only a few hundred meters from the pyramids of Giza. It is the largest museum in the world devoted to a single civilization. Among its exhibits are the full collection of treasures from the tomb of Tutankhamun, shown together for the first time, and the conserved solar boat of Khufu, the ancient cedar ship that was buried beside the Great Pyramid.

The museum's significance for pyramid research is practical as well as symbolic. It houses conservation laboratories and displays objects that had been scattered across storerooms. For visitors, it offers a way to connect the monuments on the plateau with the objects and people who used them.

Technologies on the horizon

Looking ahead, several tools may change the picture again.

• Better muon detectors. New detectors, more sensitive and

easier to deploy, can image smaller structures and cover more of a pyramid's volume.

• Robotic and fiber-optic exploration. Small robots and

flexible cameras can enter spaces that people cannot, and their cameras keep getting smaller.

terns in satellite imagery, sort thousands of archaeological fragments, and read damaged papyri.

How to read a pyramid headline

Because pyramid discoveries attract so much attention, it is worth having a short guide for reading them. When you see a headline that promises a hidden chamber, a lost civilization, or a secret, you can ask a few questions.

1. Where was it published? A peer-reviewed journal is a bet-

ter sign than a press release, a social-media post, or a documentary. Peer review is imperfect, but it means that other specialists have examined the methods.

2. What exactly was detected? "An anomaly," "a void," and

"a chamber" are different statements. A void is a measurement. A chamber is an interpretation.

3. How certain do the authors say they are? Careful re-

searchers use words like "initial evidence," "consistent with," or "suggests." Be cautious of headlines that turn those into "proves" or "reveals."

4. Has anyone else confirmed it? An independent team using

a different method is the strongest check.

5. Who benefits from the story? A television program, a tour

operator, or a person selling a book has a reason to make a story sound bigger.

6. Does it change the main picture? Most new discoveries

refine the story without overturning it. Be wary of any claim that "everything we know is wrong."

MYTH AND FACT

Myth: Each new scan finds a secret chamber that the authorities are hiding. Fact: Most scans find structural voids and construction spaces, and the scientists who find them publish the results openly. Whether an anomaly is a room, a gap in the masonry, or a pressure-relieving space is determined by further investigation, and that takes time and permission, not a cover-up.

What we still do not know

For all the progress, many things are still unknown, and a good ending for this chapter is a list of open questions.

• The exact ramp system used to raise the stone, especially

to the upper levels of the Great Pyramid.

• The purpose of the Big Void above the Grand Gallery, and

whether it can be explored.

• What lies beyond the small stone doors in the Queen's

Chamber shafts.

• Whether Menkaure's pyramid has a second entrance

and what it leads to.

• Where the kings were actually buried. No intact Fourth

Dynasty royal burial has been found.

• How the workforce was recruited and rotated, in detail,

and how many people were involved at any one time.

• The precise methods of alignment used to orient the base

with such accuracy.

• How the Sphinx's builders organized the work and what,

exactly, it was meant to represent.

None of these is a "mystery" in the sense of something beyond explanation. Each is a question with a possible answer, waiting for evidence.

CHAPTER 23

Questions People Ask

Short, direct answers to the questions that come up most often, with pointers to the chapters that explain them.

Over the course of this book, a number of questions have come up repeatedly. This chapter gathers them in one place, in the form of short answers. If you want the reasoning and the evidence behind any answer, the chapter references will take you there.

About the pyramids themselves

How old is the Great Pyramid?

It was built around 2600 to 2560 BCE, during the reign of Khufu of the Fourth Dynasty, which makes it about 4,600 years old. It was already more than two thousand years old when Cleopatra VII was born. The dating rests on several independent lines of evidence: the work-gang marks inside the pyramid that name Khufu, the Wadi al-Jarf papyri from Khufu's reign, the style of the surrounding cemeteries, and radiocarbon dating of short-lived organic materials. See Chapters 5, 11, and 22.

How many pyramids are there in Egypt?

Counts vary depending on what is called a pyramid, since many are now only heaps of rubble. A commonly cited figure is around a hundred and twenty known pyramids in Egypt, built mostly between about 2670 and 1500 BCE. Sudan, in ancient Nubia, has more than Egypt, because the kings of Kush built pyramids for centuries. The best known Egyptian ones are at Giza, Saqqara, Dahshur, Meidum, Abusir, and Lisht. See Chapters 4 through 8.

Why isn't the Great Pyramid smooth and white anymore?

When new, the Great Pyramid was covered with a casing of fine white limestone from Tura, polished smooth, which would have shone in the sun. Most of the casing stones were removed in the Middle Ages, after earthquakes loosened them in the fourteenth century, and they were reused for buildings in Cairo. A few casing stones remain at the base. What we see today is the stepped core masonry. See Chapters 5 and 18.

Was the capstone made of gold?

We do not know for certain. The top of a pyramid was crowned by a small pyramid-shaped stone called a pyramidion. Pyramidia from other pyramids survive, made of limestone or granite, and some bear inscriptions. Egyptian texts speak of the sun's first rays striking the pyramid's tip, and some scholars have suggested that the pyramidion of the Great Pyramid may have been covered in electrum, an alloy of gold and silver, so that it would flash in the light. No such covering has survived, and the original pyramidion of the Great Pyramid has never been found. See Chapter 5.

Who designed the Great Pyramid?

We do not have a certain answer, but the best candidate is Hemiunu, a vizier and nephew of Khufu, who is called "overseer of all the king's works" in his tomb at Giza. A famous statue of him, found in his tomb chapel, shows an older, heavyset man, and is in a museum in Hildesheim, Germany. Many Egyptologists think he directed the project, though no text says in so many words that he designed it. See Chapter 5.

How tall is the Great Pyramid, and was it the tallest building in the world?

Its original height was about 146.6 meters, or 481 feet. Today it stands about 138.5 meters, because the top and the casing are missing. It was the tallest human-made structure in the world for roughly 3,800 years, until the central spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England was completed in the early fourteenth century. See Chapter 5.

About how it was built

How long did it take?

Ancient and modern estimates agree on about twenty years, matching the reign of Khufu, which was around twenty-three years by one reckoning. To finish in that time, the builders had to place, on average, many blocks per day, a rate that was achievable with several work crews operating at the same time on different parts of the monument. See Chapter 14.

How many people built it?

Estimates range from about ten thousand to thirty thousand workers at a time, with the most common range being twenty to thirty thousand, including quarrymen, haulers, masons, boat crews, bakers, brewers, and administrators. Many of them rotated in and out. The figure of a hundred thousand reported by Herodotus is almost certainly an exaggeration. See Chapter 13.

Were the builders slaves?

The evidence says no. They were housed in a town, fed bread, beer, meat, and fish, buried in tombs beside the pyramids with offerings, and given medical care. The tombs of the workers are decorated with the names of their gangs. The labor force seems to have combined permanent skilled specialists with farmers who were conscripted for a period of service, as part of the state's labor taxation. The conscripts were not free in the modern sense, but they were not slaves either. See Chapter 13.

How did they move the stones?

Most blocks were cut from limestone quarried within a few hundred meters of the pyramid, and dragged on wooden sledges. Wetting the sand in front of the sledge reduces friction considerably, as an Egyptian tomb painting seems to show and as modern physics experiments have confirmed. Finer stone, such as the limestone for the casing from Tura, and granite from Aswan, traveled by boat on the Nile. The logbook of Merer shows exactly how one boat crew did it. See Chapter 11.

How did they lift them to the top?

Nobody knows for sure, and this is one of the real open questions. The main proposals involve ramps: a straight ramp, a zigzagging ramp on one face, a spiral ramp around the pyramid, or an internal ramp, or a combination. Levers and rocking devices were probably used for final placement. A steep ramp with post holes found at the Hatnub quarry shows that steep hauling was practiced. See Chapter 12.

Could the pyramid be built today?

Yes. Modern engineers could build a copy with cranes and trucks, and the task would be a matter of cost, not possibility. The harder question is whether it could be done with only the tools of the Old Kingdom. Experiments, including televised attempts to build small pyramids with replica tools, have shown that small crews can quarry limestone with copper and stone tools and can drag multi-ton blocks on sledges, but that lifting blocks to a height is the difficult part, and that experiments at small scale do not tell us everything about work at large scale. See Chapter 12.

Is it true that the stones fit so tightly that you cannot slip a knife between them?

For the original outer casing stones, the joints were very fine, a fraction of a millimeter wide in places, and the claim is roughly true for those stones. For the inner core blocks, which were not meant to be seen, the joints are much wider, and the gaps were filled with mortar and rubble. The tight joints were a mark of care, not of magic. See Chapter 9.

How could they get the base so level and square?

By using simple tools with great care: a water-filled network of trenches cut into the bedrock as a level, plumb bobs, set squares, and knotted ropes. The north-south alignment was probably set by sighting stars or the sun. The base is level to within a few centimeters and aligned to true north within a small fraction of a degree. See Chapter 9.

About what they were for

Were the pyramids tombs?

Yes. The weight of the evidence supports that they were royal tombs and the centerpieces of cult complexes where the dead king was honored. The pyramid shape probably symbolized the sun's rays, or the mound of creation, or a staircase to the sky, or all three. No intact royal burial has been found in a Fourth Dynasty pyramid, since they were robbed in antiquity, and that remains a gap in the evidence. See Chapters 16 and 17.

Why is there no mummy in the Great Pyramid?

It was robbed long before the modern era. By the Middle Kingdom, if not earlier, the pyramid's contents were gone. When Caliph al-Ma'mun's men broke in during the ninth century CE, they found the chambers empty, according to later accounts. The sarcophagus in the King's Chamber is lidless and cracked, and the chamber has been open to visitors for more than a thousand years. See Chapters 17 and 18.

What about the "curse of the pharaohs"?

The story took off after the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, when its sponsor, Lord Carnarvon, died the following spring of an infection that followed a mosquito bite. Newspapers drew a connection. In fact, many of the people who worked on the tomb lived for decades afterward, and studies comparing the lifespans of those present at the opening with those who were not have found no difference. Inscriptions with curses do exist on some tombs, but they were mostly warnings to deter vandals, and had no more effect than a "no trespassing" sign. The curse has no connection to the pyramids as such.

Did Napoleon really say that forty centuries looked down on his troops?

He is reported to have said, before the Battle of the Pyramids in July 1798, "Soldiers, from the summit of these pyramids, forty centuries look down upon you." The line comes from accounts written after the fact, and its exact wording and even whether he said it are uncertain, but it was part of the legend that he and his supporters built around the Egyptian campaign. See Chapter 18.

About the controversies

Are the pyramids aligned with Orion's Belt?

Not in any way that the evidence supports. Egyptians associated Orion with the god Osiris and the dead king's afterlife, and the southern shaft of the King's Chamber may have been aimed at that region of the sky. But the claim that the three Giza pyramids are a map of Orion's Belt rests on a loose and selective match, and the pyramids were built by three different kings over about eighty years. See Chapter 21.

Do the pyramids hold secret mathematical codes?

The Great Pyramid's proportions are impressive and are based on a slope of 14 to 11, a simple practical slope that happens to produce ratios close to pi and the golden ratio. They are byproducts of that slope, not evidence of hidden knowledge. See Chapter 21.

Was there a lost civilization before the Egyptians?

There is no evidence of one in the archaeology of Egypt. The idea has been argued by some popular writers, but it has not been supported by physical evidence that has survived independent examination. See Chapter 21.

Did aliens help?

There is no evidence of that, and a great deal of evidence of human work. See Chapter 20.

Could the Great Pyramid generate energy?

No. The power-plant theory has no physical remains to support it, requires materials the Egyptians did not have, and cannot work as a source of net energy. See Chapter 19.

Why do so many people believe these theories?

Because the pyramids are awe-inspiring, because the human mind seeks patterns, because mystery is exciting, and because stories about hidden knowledge are more fun to tell than an account of ramps and rations. Most people who are drawn to these ideas are curious and sincere. Checking claims against evidence is the way to turn that curiosity into knowledge. See Chapters 19 through 22.

Practical questions

Can I go inside the Great Pyramid?

Visitors can usually enter the Great Pyramid, though access depends on the day, the ticket, and the conservation work in progress, and rules change over time. Entry is through a tunnel cut by tomb robbers in the Middle Ages, which joins the original passages. The ascent through the Grand Gallery to the King's Chamber is steep and cramped, and it is not suitable for anyone who has trouble with confined spaces. Check the current rules before you travel, as they change.

What is the best time to visit Giza?

Early morning, when it is cooler and the crowds are thinner, and the light on the limestone is soft. Winter and early spring are more comfortable than summer, when temperatures are very high. The nearby Grand Egyptian Museum is worth a separate visit.

Epilogue: What the Pyramids Teach

Four lessons from a mountain made by hand.

We began this book at the foot of the Great Pyramid, with a feeling that is familiar to almost everyone who sees it: that something so large and so exact cannot have been made by ordinary people. We end by saying that it was made by ordinary people, and that this is the most remarkable thing about it.

Let us gather the main lessons.

Lesson one: great things come from organization

The Great Pyramid is a triumph of logistics before it is a triumph of engineering. The stone was cut at the quarries, floated on the Nile, dragged on sledges, and set in place by tens of thousands of people who had to be fed, housed, and supervised. Bread and beer were the currency of the project. A boat foreman named Merer kept a log, a vizier named Hemiunu directed the work, and an army of bakers, brewers, carpenters, butchers, and scribes kept it running. The achievement was a collective one. It tells us that what we call technology is often a matter of coordinating people.

Lesson two: progress is made by trial and error

The pyramid did not appear fully formed. Djoser's builders learned to work in stone by stacking small blocks like bricks. Sneferu's builders tried a stepped design, saw it collapse, changed the angle halfway up a second pyramid when it began to crack, and got it right on the third. Khufu's builders applied what they had learned and perfected it. The failures are as instructive as the successes, because they show human minds at work: observing, adjusting, and improving. An advanced outside intelligence would not have needed to learn. The Egyptians did, and that is why we can respect what they achieved.

Lesson three: evidence beats mystery

It is thrilling to imagine that the pyramids hold secrets that no one has discovered. But the real secrets turned out to be better. A logbook found in a cave beside the Red Sea tells us how stone traveled to Giza. A buried town tells us who baked the bread. A series of failed pyramids tells us how the builders learned. Cosmic rays tell us that there are hollow spaces inside the monument that no one has entered. Each of these discoveries came from careful, patient work, and each is more satisfying than any story about lost machines or visitors from the stars. When people say "we don't know how it was done," the right answer is not to give up and imagine something exotic. It is to go and look.

Lesson four: the past deserves respect

Perhaps the most important lesson is the simplest. The people who built the pyramids were as intelligent as we are. They lacked iron, wheels for heavy loads, and engines, but they did not lack insight or will. They solved problems that would challenge a modern engineering firm, with materials that were at hand and skills passed from one generation to the next. To say that they could not have done it is to underestimate them. To learn how they did it is to honor them.

A closing image

Imagine a morning in the twenty-sixth century BCE, on the Giza plateau. Before dawn, the bakers have been up for hours. Smoke rises from the ovens in the workers' town. Gangs of men, with their names painted on their walls, gather their tools. At the quarry, a stonecutter strikes a copper chisel with a stone mallet. On the harbor, a boat arrives from Tura loaded with white limestone, and the crew, who have been traveling for days, hand over their load and receive their rations. A scribe records the delivery. The sun comes up over the ridge. On the plateau, a pyramid stands half-finished, its steps catching the light.

Everyone in that scene is doing something ordinary. The cutter is cutting. The baker is baking. The scribe is writing. The boatman is rowing. And the sum of all those ordinary acts is the Great Pyramid.

That is what this book has tried to show: that the greatest monument of the ancient world was not made by a miracle, but

by millions of small, skillful, patient acts, and that it has been standing for forty-six centuries to remind us what people can do together.

If you ever have the chance to stand at the foot of that great wall of stone, take a moment to look at one block, a single block, at about the height of your chest. Somebody cut it. Somebody dragged it. Somebody set it. Put your hand on it. That is as close as you will ever come to touching the hand of the person who did it.

Appendix C — Glossary

Terms used in this book, in alphabetical order.

• Akh. In Egyptian belief, the transfigured, effective spirit of

a dead person who has successfully entered the afterlife. • Ba. An aspect of a person's spirit, often shown as a human-

headed bird, that could travel between the tomb and the world of the living.

• Benben. The sacred mound or stone at Heliopolis associat-

ed with the sun god; the pyramid shape may recall it.

• Canopic jars. Containers for the preserved internal organs

of a mummy.

• Cartouche. An oval ring around a king's name in hiero-

glyphs.

• Casing stones. The finely cut outer limestone blocks that

gave a pyramid its smooth surface.

• Causeway. The covered or walled ceremonial road linking

a pyramid's valley temple to its mortuary temple.

• Corbelled vault. A roof or ceiling made by stepping suc-

cessive courses of stone inward until they meet.

• Cubit (royal). The standard Egyptian unit of length, about

52.4 centimeters.

• Djed. A hieroglyphic and religious symbol of stability,

often drawn as a pillar with horizontal bars.

• Dolerite. A very hard dark stone used for pounding balls

that shaped granite and other hard rock.

• Dynasty. A line of kings; Egyptologists, following the an-

cient historian Manetho, number the kings in about thirty dynasties.

• False door. A carved stone panel in a tomb chapel through

which the spirit of the dead was believed to receive offerings.

• Hieratic. The cursive handwriting form of Egyptian script,

used for everyday records on papyrus.

• Hieroglyphs. The picture-signs of formal Egyptian writing,

used on monuments.

• Inundation. The yearly Nile flood, called Akhet; it drove

the farming year and freed labor for state projects.

• Ka. The life-force or spiritual double of a person, which re-

quired offerings in order to survive.

• Kemet. "The Black Land": the fertile floodplain of Egypt,

as opposed to the red desert.

• King's Chamber. The granite-lined chamber high inside

the Great Pyramid that holds an empty sarcophagus.

• Maat. The Egyptian principle of truth, order, and balance,

which the king was bound to uphold.

• Mastaba. A flat-roofed, rectangular tomb structure with

sloping sides, from the Arabic word for "bench."

• Mortuary temple. The temple attached to the east face of a

pyramid, where offerings were made to the dead king.

• Muon. A subatomic particle created when cosmic rays

strike the upper atmosphere, used to image the inside of large structures.

• Natron. A natural salt mixture used to dry bodies for mum-

mification and for many other purposes.

• Necropolis. A "city of the dead," a large cemetery complex.

• Nome. An administrative province of ancient Egypt, from

the Greek word.

• Nubia. The region south of Egypt along the Nile, in presen-

t-day Sudan.

• Old Kingdom. The period of about 2700 to 2200 BCE, the

age of the great pyramids.

• Palimpsest. A surface that has been written or carved on

more than once, with traces of the earlier text still visible. • Papyrus. A paper-like writing material made from the pith

of the papyrus plant.

• Pharaoh. From the Egyptian per-aa, "great house"; the title

of the Egyptian king.

• Pyramidion. The small pyramid-shaped capstone at the top

of a pyramid.

• Pyramid Texts. The oldest known religious writings, spells

carved inside pyramids from the end of the Fifth Dynasty. • Queen's Chamber. The middle chamber of the Great Pyra-

mid; it was probably never used for a queen.

• Relieving chambers. Five empty spaces above the King's

Chamber, built to spread the weight of the stone above.

• Sarcophagus. A stone coffin.

• Sed festival. A royal jubilee in which the king renewed his

powers, usually after thirty years of rule.

• Seked. The Egyptian measure of the slope of a wall or pyra-

mid face.

• Serdab. A small closed chamber in a tomb holding a statue

of the dead; from the Arabic word for "cellar."

• Serekh. A rectangular frame representing a palace facade in

which early kings' Horus names were written.

• Shabti. A small figure placed in a tomb to do work for the

dead in the afterlife.

• Sledge. A wooden runner-based sled used to drag heavy

loads, such as stone blocks and statues.

• Stela. An upright stone slab with an inscription or image.

• Tura. The quarry area across the Nile from Memphis that

supplied fine white limestone for casings.

• Valley temple. The temple at the lower end of a pyramid

• Vizier. The chief minister of the king, head of the adminis-

tration and the judiciary.

• Wadi. A dry valley or watercourse in the desert.
